bipedalism.summary: Walking on two legs freed the hands from locomotion. Possible signs appear in fossils about 7 to 6 million years old (debated), and the Laetoli footprints show fully upright walking by about 3.7 million years ago.

precision-grip.summary: A long thumb opposing the fingertips lets a hand pinch, turn and strike accurately, the basis of toolmaking. Hand bones suggest human-like grips in australopiths by about 3 million years ago and a near-modern hand by about 1.8 million.

sources.title: Skinner et al. 2015, Human-like hand use in Australopithecus africanus (Science)

vision.summary: Forward-facing eyes with overlapping fields (depth perception) arose in early primates, and three-color vision evolved in the ancestors of Old World monkeys and apes about 30 to 40 million years ago. Humans inherited both.

sources.title: Evolution of color vision in primates (Wikipedia)

touch.summary: Primate fingertips carry flat nails, friction ridges and dense touch receptors, inherited from early primates. Fine touch lets people judge texture, pressure and fit when working materials.

hearing.summary: Human ears are most sensitive in the 1 to 5 kHz band that carries speech sounds. Australopiths heard much like chimpanzees; ear bones from Sima de los Huesos, about 430,000 years old, already approach the modern pattern.

sources.title: Quam et al. 2015, Early hominin auditory capacities (Science Advances)

large-brain.summary: Brain size roughly tripled over two million years, from about 450 cc in australopiths through Homo erectus to modern volumes by about 300,000 years ago. A big, slow-maturing brain made learning and culture central to human life.

cooperation.summary: Humans share food, care for each other's children, teach, and copy skills with high fidelity, so knowledge accumulates across generations instead of being reinvented. When this became distinctly human is uncertain; the spread of standardized Acheulean handaxes after 1.7 million years ago is one sign.

vocal-tract.summary: A low larynx, a mobile tongue and fine breath control let humans make a wide range of distinct vowels and consonants. Hyoid bones from Sima de los Huesos (about 430,000 years ago) and Neanderthals are modern in shape, though how fluent their speech was is debated.

language-capacity.summary: The mental ability to build unlimited meanings from words and grammar. Estimates range widely; all living human populations share it, so it existed before they began to split, at least about 135,000 years ago, and it may be much older.

res-flint.summary: Fine-grained stones that break with sharp, predictable edges: flint, chert, obsidian, quartzite and volcanic rock. They were the main material for cutting tools for over three million years.
res-flint.note: The oldest tools, at Lomekwi, used local lavas; later toolmakers sought high-quality flint and obsidian and traded it hundreds of kilometers. Good nodules near the surface were used up in some regions, so Neolithic people dug shaft mines over 10 m deep, as at Grimes Graves in England (about 2600 BC) and Spiennes in Belgium. Globally the stone was never scarce; it was displaced by metal.

res-wood.summary: The first fuel and building material, and as charcoal the fuel for all smelting until coke. Use-wear on early stone tools shows woodworking by at least 1.5 million years ago.
res-wood.note: Renewable but easily overcut. Smelting consumed whole forests around ancient mining centers in Cyprus, the Levant and Iberia. In 16th and 17th century England rising timber and charcoal prices pushed industry toward coal (the extent of this "timber crisis" is debated). The world has lost about a third of its forests since the last ice age, half of that in the last century.

sources.title: Our World in Data, The world has lost one-third of its forest

res-clay.summary: Fine plastic earth that hardens when fired. It made pottery, bricks, writing tablets and kilns possible; the earliest fired-clay objects are figurines from Dolni Vestonice, about 29,000 BC.
res-clay.note: Common clays are effectively unlimited. Special clays are more localized: high-purity kaolin for porcelain and paper coatings, and the palygorskite used in Maya blue.

res-fertile-soil.summary: Topsoil rich in organic matter and nutrients, built up over centuries to millennia. Farming began on the alluvial and loess soils of a few river valleys and hill flanks.
res-fertile-soil.note: Soil forms at roughly a centimeter per century and erodes much faster under plowing. Irrigated fields in southern Mesopotamia grew salty: records suggest wheat gave way to more salt-tolerant barley between about 3500 and 1700 BC as yields fell. The FAO estimates about a third of the world's soils are moderately to highly degraded.

res-fresh-water.summary: Water for drinking, crops, animals, mills and industry. It became a managed resource with farming; the earliest known wells, on Cyprus, date to about 8500 BC.
res-fresh-water.note: Renewable in rivers and rain, but groundwater can be mined faster than it refills. The Ogallala aquifer under the US Great Plains has fallen by over 30 m in parts of Kansas and Texas since pumping began in the 1940s, and aquifers in north India, the North China Plain and the Middle East show similar declines.

res-salt.summary: Needed by people and livestock and for preserving food, later the base of the chlorine and soda industries. Salt was boiled from springs at Poiana Slatinei in Romania and Lake Yuncheng in China by about 6000 BC.
res-salt.note: Rock salt deposits are vast and seawater is nearly unlimited; world production is about 280 million tonnes a year. Salt was scarce only locally and historically, which made it a major traded and taxed good.

res-copper.summary: The first metal worked by people, first as native copper hammered into beads (a pendant from Shanidar, Iraq, about 8700 BC), then smelted from ore. Today it carries most of the world's electricity.
res-copper.note: Early metalworkers took native copper and rich, colorful surface oxide ores (Timna, Cyprus, the Great Lakes). Those are long gone, and grades keep falling: ores of several percent copper were common in the 19th century, while Chile's average grade fell from about 0.93 percent in 2005 to around 0.6 percent, and Calvo et al. found global copper grades fell about 25 percent in ten years. Lower grades mean more rock, energy and water per tonne. USGS reserves are about 980 million tonnes (Chile largest), against mining of 23 million tonnes a year.

sources.title: Calvo et al. 2016, Decreasing Ore Grades in Global Metallic Mining (Resources)

res-tin.summary: Alloyed with copper to make bronze, later used for solder and tin plate. The earliest tin bronze, a foil from Plocnik in Serbia, dates to about 4650 BC.
res-tin.note: Tin ore is rare and patchy, so Bronze Age cities depended on long trade routes to a few sources: Cornwall, the Erzgebirge, Iberia and Central Asia. The Uluburun shipwreck (about 1300 BC) carried about 10 tonnes of copper and 1 tonne of tin, the 10 to 1 bronze ratio. Cornish mining ended in 1998. Today China, Indonesia and Myanmar lead; known reserves of about 4.2 million tonnes are only about 14 years of current production, and much of it is used in electronics solder.

sources.title: Tin sources and trade in ancient times (Wikipedia)

res-iron-ore.summary: Iron oxides were first used as red ochre pigment, by about 300,000 years ago in Africa. Meteoritic iron was worked by about 3200 BC and ore was smelted from the 2nd millennium BCE.
res-iron-ore.note: Iron is about 5 percent of the crust and reserves are some 200 billion tonnes of crude ore, so the metal is not scarce, but rich ore is. The Mesabi Range's natural ores, 51 to 57 percent iron, were mostly exhausted by the end of World War II, and the industry switched to taconite of 30 percent iron that must be crushed, concentrated and pelletized. High-grade supply now comes mostly from Australia's Pilbara and Brazil.

sources.title: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Iron Ore

res-gold.summary: Found as nuggets and river grains, gold was the first metal of display and money. The oldest large gold hoard is from the Varna necropolis in Bulgaria, about 4600 to 4400 BC.
res-gold.note: About 216,000 tonnes have been mined in all history, two thirds since 1950. Easy placer gold was worked out first in each gold rush. South Africa's Witwatersrand produced about 1,000 tonnes in 1970 and only about 100 tonnes in 2024, from mines up to 4 km deep. Reserves are about 64,000 tonnes.

sources.title: World Gold Council, How much gold has been mined

res-silver.summary: Extracted from lead ores by cupellation from about the 4th millennium BCE in Anatolia and Mesopotamia, silver became the standard of value in the ancient Near East and later of coinage.
res-silver.note: Great historic mines ran out or became uneconomic: Laurion funded Athens' fleet in the 5th century BCE; Potosi in Bolivia flooded the world with silver after 1545. Today most silver is a byproduct of lead, zinc and copper mining. Reserves are about 640,000 tonnes, against mining of 25,000 tonnes a year.

res-coal.summary: Fossil carbon that burns hotter and denser than wood. Systematic coal mining and burning is known from Jirentaigoukou in Xinjiang, China, about 3,600 years ago, apparently as local wood ran short.
res-coal.note: The easiest coal, at outcrops and in shallow seams, was used first; mines then went deeper and costs rose. In "The Coal Question" (1865) Jevons warned that Britain's cheap coal would run out; British output peaked in 1913 at 287 million tonnes and the last deep mine closed in 2015. World proven reserves are still about a trillion tonnes, concentrated in the US, Russia, Australia, China and India, so the limit on coal today is climate, not supply.

sources.title: Qiu et al. 2023, Earliest systematic coal exploitation for fuel extended to 3600 BP (Science Advances)
Coal mining in the United Kingdom (Wikipedia)

res-oil.summary: Natural bitumen seeping to the surface was used by Neanderthals as a glue for hafting stone tools in Syria and later to waterproof boats and bind bricks in Mesopotamia. Drilled oil became the main fuel of the 20th century.
res-oil.note: Chinese wells reached oil by the 4th century CE; the modern industry dates from 1859. The giant, shallow, high-pressure fields were found first. Hall and colleagues estimate the energy return on US oil production fell from roughly 100 to 1 in the 1930s to about 10 to 20 to 1 by the 2000s, as supply shifted to deep water, oil sands and shale. About half of proven reserves are in the Middle East.

sources.title: Hall, Lambert and Balogh 2014, EROI of different fuels (Energy Policy)
Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy

res-natural-gas.summary: In Sichuan, China, gas from deep brine wells was piped through bamboo and burned to evaporate salt by the Han dynasty at the latest. It is now about a quarter of world energy and the feedstock for nitrogen fertilizer.
res-natural-gas.note: Conventional fields in the US and North Sea declined from the 1970s; hydraulic fracturing of shale reversed US decline after 2008 at higher drilling intensity. Reserves are concentrated in Russia, Iran and Qatar. Gas is also the only commercial source of helium.

res-sulfur.summary: Yellow volcanic sulfur was burned for fumigation and bleaching in the ancient Mediterranean (Homer mentions it) and is one of the three ingredients of gunpowder. As sulfuric acid it is now the most-made industrial chemical.
res-sulfur.note: Sicilian mines dominated supply until the Frasch process tapped Gulf Coast salt domes in the 1890s. Today most of the 85 million tonnes a year is recovered from cleaning sulfur out of oil and natural gas, so supply is tied to fossil fuel refining and could tighten as that declines, while demand for fertilizer and metal leaching grows.

res-saltpeter.summary: Potassium nitrate, scraped from soils, caves and manure heaps. Chinese alchemists identified it around AD 500, and it became the oxidizer in gunpowder and a prized fertilizer.
res-saltpeter.note: For centuries natural saltpeter was scarce and strategic; states ran nitre beds to secure gunpowder. In the 19th century Chile's caliche deposits supplied the world's nitrate fertilizer and explosives, and the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884) was fought partly over them. The Haber-Bosch process made nitrogen effectively unlimited, given energy.

sources.title: Saltpeter War, War of the Pacific (Wikipedia)

res-potash.summary: Potassium salts, first made by soaking wood or plant ash in pots, used for soap, glass and dyeing since at least the 3rd millennium BCE. Today it is one of the three main fertilizer nutrients.
res-potash.note: Ash potash drove forest clearing in colonial North America (the first US patent, in 1790, was for a potash process). Mined potash began at Stassfurt, Germany, in 1861. Reserves exceed 4.8 billion tonnes of K2O, concentrated in Canada, Belarus and Russia, which makes supply politically exposed though not geologically scarce.

res-phosphate.summary: Phosphorus is essential to all life and cannot be substituted in fertilizer. Andean farmers spread seabird guano for centuries; industrial use began with superphosphate made from bones and phosphate rock in the 1840s.
res-phosphate.note: The resource has been depleted in stages: Peru's guano islands were stripped in a few decades after 1840, and the phosphate island of Nauru was mined nearly bare in the 20th century. USGS reserves are about 74 billion tonnes of rock, but about 50 billion (two thirds) are in Morocco and Western Sahara. Researchers debate whether high-grade rock will peak this century.

sources.title: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Phosphate Rock

res-silicon.summary: Silica sand is the raw material of glass, first made in Mesopotamia about 2500 BC, and later of silicon metal for alloys, solar cells and chips.
res-silicon.note: Silicon is the second most common element in the crust, but chipmaking depends on rare ultra-pure quartz: mines at Spruce Pine, North Carolina, supply most quartz for the crucibles that grow silicon crystals, and Hurricane Helene shut them briefly in 2024. China made almost 80 percent of the world's silicon materials in 2024.

res-cobalt.summary: Cobalt ores colored Egyptian and Mycenaean glass deep blue in the late Bronze Age. Today it is used in superalloys and in many lithium-ion battery cathodes.
res-cobalt.note: Mostly a byproduct of copper and nickel mining. Congo (Kinshasa) mined about 220,000 of the world's 290,000 tonnes in 2024 and holds over half of reserves, and China refines most of it, so supply is highly concentrated; Congo suspended and then capped exports in 2025 to support prices.

res-nickel.summary: Bactrian kings struck copper-nickel coins around 180 BC, and China made nickel-bearing paktong alloys. Nickel was isolated in 1751 and is now used mainly in stainless steel and battery cathodes.
res-nickel.note: The rich sulfide ores of Sudbury and Norilsk are being supplemented by lower-grade tropical laterites that need energy-hungry processing. Indonesia mined about 2.2 of the world's 3.7 million tonnes in 2024, with large deforestation and coal-power costs. Reserves exceed 130 million tonnes.

res-platinum-group.summary: Craftsmen of the La Tolita culture on the coast of Ecuador and Colombia worked platinum-gold alloys between about 600 BC and AD 200. Platinum, palladium and rhodium are now essential catalysts for cars, refining and hydrogen.
res-platinum-group.note: Extremely concentrated: South Africa's Bushveld Complex holds about three quarters of world reserves and South Africa mines about 70 percent of platinum; Russia and South Africa dominate palladium. Mines are deep and energy-intensive, and South African output has been held back by power shortages.

sources.title: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Platinum-Group Metals

res-uranium.summary: Identified in 1789, uranium was first used to color glass and ceramic glazes yellow-green from the 1830s. After fission was discovered in 1938 it became the fuel of nuclear power and weapons.
res-uranium.note: Identified resources recoverable at moderate cost are about 6 million tonnes, roughly 90 years of current reactor demand. Kazakhstan mines about 40 percent. Ore grades vary enormously: Cigar Lake in Canada averages around 15 percent uranium oxide, while many mines work ores of 0.1 percent or less.

sources.title: World Nuclear Association, Supply of Uranium

res-rare-earths.summary: Seventeen chemically similar metals first found in a Swedish quarry at Ytterby in 1787. Their first major use was Welsbach's gas mantle (patented 1885); now they make the strongest permanent magnets, for motors and wind turbines.
res-rare-earths.note: Not rare in the crust, but minable concentrations are uncommon and separating them is chemically dirty. China mined about 270,000 of 390,000 tonnes in 2024 and does about 90 percent of separation and magnet making, and it has used export controls on them as leverage. Reserves exceed 90 million tonnes.

sources.title: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Rare Earths

res-helium.summary: Found in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 and in Kansas natural gas in 1903, helium was first used in quantity to lift the US Navy airship C-7 in 1921. Liquid helium now cools MRI magnets and is used in chipmaking and research.
res-helium.note: Helium forms slowly from radioactive decay and escapes to space once released, so it is truly non-renewable. It is recovered only from a few gas fields; the US and Qatar lead production of about 180 million cubic meters a year. The US government sold its Federal Helium Reserve near Amarillo in 2024, ending a century-old strategic stockpile.

res-lithium.summary: Discovered in 1817, lithium was first produced commercially in Germany in 1923. It went into greases, glass and psychiatric medicine before lithium-ion batteries made it a major commodity after 1991.
res-lithium.note: Not geologically scarce: reserves are about 30 million tonnes and identified resources keep growing. Mining (about 240,000 tonnes in 2024) is concentrated in Australia (hard rock) and Chile and Argentina (brines), and China refines most of it, so processing capacity, water use in desert brines and price swings are the constraints.

res-germanium.summary: Predicted by Mendeleev and found in 1886, germanium had no use until wartime radar crystal detectors and the first transistor in 1947. It is now used in fiber optics, infrared optics and some solar cells.
res-germanium.note: Recovered in small amounts from zinc ore and coal ash, not mined for itself. China dominates refining; it required export licenses from August 2023 and banned exports to the United States in December 2024.

res-silphium.summary: A plant of the Libyan coast, prized across the Greek and Roman world as a seasoning and medicine, perhaps as a contraceptive. It was the wealth of the city of Cyrene, founded about 630 BC, and appeared on its coins.
res-silphium.lost: Extinct by the 1st century CE; the plant's identity is still uncertain.
res-silphium.note: It resisted cultivation and grew only in a narrow strip near Cyrene. Overharvesting, grazing and perhaps climate change wiped it out; Pliny the Elder reports the last known stalk was sent to Nero in the 1st century CE. It is often called the first recorded extinction caused by people. A claim (2022) that a Turkish Ferula species is silphium is unconfirmed.

res-limestone.summary: Rock made of calcium carbonate, burned to quicklime for plaster and mortar from about 12,000 years ago in the Levant. It is the raw material of lime, cement and concrete and the flux in iron smelting.
res-limestone.note: Limestone and dolomite cover a large share of the continents and are effectively unlimited. The constraint is climate: heating limestone releases its own carbon dioxide, so cement and lime making emit about 8 percent of global CO2.

res-zinc.summary: Zinc ore heated with copper makes brass, which the Romans used for coins from the 1st century BCE. Metallic zinc boils off before it can be smelted normally, so it was first produced in quantity by distillation at Zawar in India from about the 9th century CE.
res-zinc.note: Used today mainly to galvanize steel against rust. Mining is about 12 million tonnes a year, led by China, Peru and Australia, against USGS reserves of about 230 million tonnes, under 20 years of output, though identified resources are about 1.9 billion tonnes. Zinc ores are also the main source of germanium, gallium and indium.

res-natural-rubber.summary: Latex from tropical trees, which Mesoamericans processed with morning glory juice into tough, bouncy rubber by about 1600 BC for balls, bindings and figurines. Vulcanized rubber later became essential for tires, seals and insulation.
res-natural-rubber.note: Almost all supply comes from one species, Hevea brasiliensis, grown from a narrow genetic base taken from Brazil to Asia in 1876. Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam produce most of the world's 14 million or so tonnes a year; South American leaf blight prevents plantations in the tree's native range (Ford's Fordlandia failed), and its arrival in Asia could be catastrophic. Synthetic rubber covers much demand, but aircraft and heavy truck tires still need natural rubber.

sources.title: Hosler, Burkett and Tarkanian 1999, Prehistoric polymers (Science); MIT News summary

res-bauxite.summary: The ore of aluminum, named for Les Baux in France where it was identified in 1821. It became a major resource after the Hall-Heroult smelting process (1886) and the Bayer refining process (1888) made aluminum cheap.
res-bauxite.note: Aluminum is the most common metal in the crust, and bauxite reserves are about 29 billion tonnes against mining of about 450 million tonnes a year, with Guinea and Australia the largest producers and China refining most of the alumina. The real limit is energy: smelting takes roughly 14 to 15 MWh of electricity per tonne of metal, which is why smelters sit near cheap hydro, gas or coal power.

sources.title: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Bauxite and Alumina

stone-tools.summary: Striking flakes off a stone core makes sharp cutting edges. The oldest known tools, from Lomekwi in Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, older than the genus Homo.

efforts.note: Large, crudely knapped cores and flakes; whether this tradition continued is unknown.
Systematic flake production used to butcher hippos and pound plants.
Shaped bifacial handaxes, made to a standard plan for over a million years.

sources.title: Harmand et al. 2015, 3.3-million-year-old stone tools from Lomekwi 3 (Nature)
Plummer et al. 2023, Expanded geographic distribution and dietary strategies of the earliest Oldowan hominins and Paranthropus (Science)

woodworking.summary: Shaping wood with stone tools. The oldest worked structure, interlocking logs at Kalambo Falls in Zambia, is about 476,000 years old; the Schoningen spears in Germany are the oldest complete hunting weapons.

efforts.note: Two logs joined by a cut notch, perhaps part of a platform.
About ten balanced throwing spears; redated in 2025 from about 300,000 to about 200,000 years. The Clacton spear tip from England is about 400,000 years old.

sources.title: Barham et al. 2023, Evidence for the earliest structural use of wood (Nature)
University of York 2025, Age of Schoningen spears revised

control-of-fire.summary: Keeping and later making fire, for warmth, light, protection and cooking. When it began is contested: burned remains inside Wonderwerk Cave date to about 1 million years ago, and the earliest evidence of fire-making itself, at Barnham in England, is about 400,000 years old.

efforts.note: Ashed plants and burned bone deep inside the cave; whether fire was made or carried in from wildfires is unknown. Claims from Koobi Fora and Chesowanja (about 1.5 million years) are disputed.
Burned flint and seeds clustered in hearth-like patches across many layers.
Reported in Nature in 2025; heated sediments, fire-cracked flint and pyrite, a mineral struck with flint to make sparks.
A central hearth used repeatedly; from here on habitual fire use is widespread.

sources.title: Berna et al. 2012, Microstratigraphic evidence of in situ fire at Wonderwerk Cave (PNAS)
Control of fire by early humans (Wikipedia)
British Museum 2025, Groundbreaking discovery shows earliest evidence of fire-making

spoken-language.summary: Full spoken language let people share plans, teach skills, and pass on knowledge of things not present. Speech leaves no fossils, so its timing is inferred from anatomy, genetics and symbolic artifacts; a range of 300,000 to 100,000 years ago fits most views.

clothing.summary: Hides and later sewn garments let people live in cold climates. Body lice, which live in clothing, split from head lice about 170,000 to 83,000 years ago, and bone tools for scraping hides from Morocco date to about 120,000 to 90,000 years ago.

efforts.note: Specialized bone tools and cut-marked carnivore bones suggest fur and hide working.
Eyed bone needles appear, implying tailored, sewn clothing.

sources.title: Toups et al. 2011, Origin of clothing lice (Molecular Biology and Evolution)
Hallett et al. 2021, A worked bone assemblage from Contrebandiers Cave, earliest evidence of hide and fur working for clothing (iScience)

art-symbolic.summary: Beads, engraved patterns and paintings show people storing meaning outside their heads, a step toward writing. Shell beads from Morocco date to about 140,000 years ago; a hand stencil on Muna Island, Indonesia, at least 67,800 years old, is the oldest known cave art.

efforts.note: Perforated shell beads, about 142,000 to 150,000 years old.
Engraved ochre and the oldest known drawing, a crosshatched pattern about 73,000 years old.
Minimum age from uranium-series dating of overlying calcite (Nature, 2026). Neanderthal hand stencils in Spain dated to about 64,000 years are disputed.
The oldest known narrative scene, humanlike figures with a pig.
Carved figurines (the Lion-man), the Hohle Fels bone flute (the oldest musical instrument), and Chauvet's painted animals.

sources.title: Henshilwood et al. 2018, An abstract drawing from Blombos Cave (Nature)
Al Jazeera 2026, World's oldest cave art discovered in Indonesia's Muna island
Sehasseh et al. 2021, Early Middle Stone Age personal ornaments from Bizmoune Cave (Science Advances)

watercraft.summary: Rafts or canoes carried people across open sea to Australia and New Guinea at least 50,000 and possibly 65,000 years ago, a crossing never in sight of land. The oldest surviving boat, the Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, dates to about 8000 BC.

bow-and-arrow.summary: The first device to store energy slowly in a spring and release it fast. Impact-damaged stone and bone points from Sibudu Cave, South Africa (about 64,000 to 62,000 years ago), are the oldest likely arrowheads.

efforts.note: Small stone points with residues of glue; a bone point dated to about 61,700 years ago.
Hundreds of tiny points with impact damage, the earliest likely archery in Europe.
Bone arrow points in a tropical rainforest setting.

sources.title: Backwell et al. 2018, The antiquity of bow-and-arrow technology (Antiquity)
Metz et al. 2023, Bow-and-arrow technology at Mandrin (Science Advances)

weaving.summary: Twisting fibers into string and interlacing them into nets, baskets and cloth. A three-ply cord fragment made by Neanderthals in France is about 41,000 to 52,000 years old, and dyed flax fibers from Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia are about 30,000 years old.

efforts.note: Bark fibers twisted into a three-ply cord on a stone tool.
Spun, knotted and dyed wild flax.
Loom-woven linen and later wool cloth.

sources.title: Hardy et al. 2020, Direct evidence of Neanderthal fibre technology (Scientific Reports)
Kvavadze et al. 2009, 30,000-year-old wild flax fibers (Science)

tally-marks.summary: Notches cut in bone to keep count, the oldest record-keeping. The Lebombo bone (about 43,000 years old) and the Ishango bone (about 20,000 years old) are often cited, though whether their marks are counts is debated.

domestication-dogs.summary: Wolves became dogs while people were still hunter-gatherers, the first domesticated animal. Genetic estimates for the split range from about 40,000 to 20,000 years ago; the oldest genetically confirmed dog, from Pinarbasi in Turkey, is about 15,800 years old.

efforts.note: Inferred from genetics; one hypothesis places it in Siberia about 23,000 years ago.
Ancient DNA study (Nature, 2026) found dogs of distinct ancestries across Eurasia by 15,000 years ago. The Bonn-Oberkassel dog, buried with people about 14,200 years ago, is the oldest such burial.

sources.title: UCL 2026, Humans kept dogs 5,000 years earlier than thought

pottery.summary: Fired clay vessels for cooking and storage, the first synthetic material. The oldest known pots, from Xianrendong Cave in China, are about 20,000 years old, made by hunter-gatherers well before farming.

efforts.note: Fired clay figurines are older still, from Dolni Vestonice, Czechia, about 29,000 BC.
Possibly linked to the Chinese tradition.

sources.title: Wu et al. 2012, Early pottery at 20,000 years ago in Xianrendong Cave (Science)

lime-plaster.summary: Burning limestone to quicklime and mixing it with water gives a plaster that hardens back into stone, the first deliberate chemical transformation used in building. It appears in the Natufian and early Neolithic Levant.

sources.title: Kingery et al. 1988, Pre-pottery Neolithic lime plaster (Journal of Field Archaeology)

agriculture.summary: Planting and selecting crops until they depend on people, which fed far denser populations and made permanent villages, surpluses and cities possible. It arose independently in at least seven regions over several thousand years.

efforts.note: Wheat, barley, lentils, peas and flax; fully domesticated forms by about 8500 BC.
Broomcorn and foxtail millet.
Rice; domestication was gradual and complete by about 4000 BC.
Squash about 8000 BC (Guila Naquitz); maize from teosinte by about 7000 BC.
Squash, then potatoes, quinoa and manioc.
Taro, yams and bananas with drainage ditches.
Squash, sunflower, sumpweed and goosefoot.
Pearl millet, then sorghum and African rice.

sources.title: Larson et al. 2014, Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies (PNAS)

monumental-architecture.summary: Large buildings that need many people organized over years. Gobekli Tepe in Turkey, with carved pillars up to 5.5 m tall, was built about 9500 BC by people still largely hunting and gathering.

efforts.note: Sarsen stones of about 25 tonnes moved some 25 km and bluestones about 225 km from Wales.
The Great Pyramid of Khufu, about 2.3 million blocks, the tallest building on Earth for some 3,800 years.

effort.note: The Great Pyramid. Excavations of the workers' town at Giza suggest a paid, rotating workforce; modern estimates range from about 10,000 to 30,000 at a time over roughly 20 years.

animal-domestication.summary: Herding and breeding goats, sheep, cattle and pigs gave meat, milk, wool, leather, dung fuel and, later, pulling power. It began in the Fertile Crescent around 8500 BC and arose separately elsewhere.

efforts.where: Zagros and Taurus mountains, upper Euphrates
efforts.note: Goats, sheep, cattle (from aurochs) and pigs within a few centuries of each other.
Pigs, separately from western Asia.
Llama and alpaca, plus guinea pigs.
Chickens, from red junglefowl.

sources.title: Zeder 2008, Domestication and early agriculture in the Mediterranean Basin (PNAS)

clay-tokens.summary: Small clay shapes standing for measures of grain, animals or oil, used across the Near East from about 8000 BC. Sealed in clay envelopes and impressed on their surfaces, they are the leading theory for how writing began.

irrigation.summary: Canals that bring river water to fields let farming spread into dry lands and supported the first states. The earliest known canals are at Choga Mami in eastern Iraq, about 6000 BC.

efforts.note: Small canals dated to about 6,700 to 5,400 years ago.
Basin irrigation using the annual flood.
A diversion system that still irrigates over 5,000 square km.

sources.title: Dillehay et al. 2005, Preceramic irrigation canals in the Peruvian Andes (PNAS)

copper-smelting.summary: Heating ore with charcoal to about 1,100 C reduces it to metal, the start of extractive metallurgy. The earliest securely dated smelting is at Belovode in Serbia, about 5000 BC, after millennia of hammering native copper.

efforts.note: Native copper hammered and annealed into beads and awls, without smelting.
Slag and malachite show smelting far from the Near East, suggesting more than one origin.
Slagged crucibles; dating less certain.
Large-scale cold working of native copper, never smelted.

sources.title: Radivojevic et al. 2010, On the origins of extractive metallurgy (Journal of Archaeological Science)

plow.summary: The ard, a pointed beam dragged by oxen to break soil, multiplied the land one family could farm. It appears in Mesopotamia and Europe in the 4th millennium BCE; the heavy moldboard plow that turns the soil came later.

efforts.note: Iron plowshares with curved moldboards.
The heavy wheeled moldboard plow opened clay soils of the north.

sailing-ships.summary: Using wind on a sail, the first use of a non-muscle energy source to move things. Ubaid-period boats in the Persian Gulf (about 5500 BC) and sails painted on Egyptian pottery (about 3200 BC) are the earliest evidence.

efforts.note: Bitumen-coated reed boats; a model with a mast socket from Eridu.

efforts.where: Island Southeast Asia and the Pacific
efforts.note: Outrigger and double-hulled canoes settled the Pacific, reaching Hawaii and New Zealand by about AD 1300.

cities.summary: Dense settlements of tens of thousands with full-time specialists, temples, rulers and markets. Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grew to perhaps 40,000 or more people by about 3100 BC; cities then arose independently in several regions.

efforts.note: A large town of several thousand, without clear specialists or public buildings; often called proto-urban.
Planned grids, drains and standardized bricks.
Later Teotihuacan (about 100 BC to AD 550) held perhaps 100,000 people.

numerals.summary: Signs for numbers impressed on clay tablets in Uruk and Susa recorded quantities of goods before writing recorded words. Sumerian counting was sexagesimal (base 60), which survives in our hours and degrees.

efforts.note: Numerical tablets with impressed signs, followed by proto-cuneiform.
Decimal hieroglyphic numerals.
Decimal numerals on oracle bones.
Khipu, knotted cords recording decimal numbers.

writing.summary: A system of signs that records language, so knowledge, laws and accounts can outlast memory and travel without a messenger. It was invented at least three or four times; the earliest is proto-cuneiform at Uruk, about 3300 BC, which grew out of accounting.

efforts.note: Proto-cuneiform administrative tablets; full cuneiform could write sentences by about 2600 BC.
Labels in tomb U-j; whether hieroglyphs were fully independent of Mesopotamia or inspired by it is debated.
Oracle bone script, the ancestor of Chinese characters.
The Cascajal block (about 900 BC) is contested; Zapotec inscriptions date to about 600 BC and Maya writing to about 300 BC.
The Indus script is undeciphered and may not be full writing; it disappeared about 1900 BC.

wheel.summary: A wheel turning on an axle cuts rolling friction, enabling carts, and the same principle runs the potter's wheel, pulleys and gears. Wheeled vehicles appear almost at once across Mesopotamia, the steppe and Europe around 3500 BC.

efforts.note: The slow potter's wheel probably came before vehicle wheels.
The oldest picture of a wheeled wagon, on a pot.
The oldest surviving wooden wheel and axle.
Wheeled figurines, but no wheeled vehicles, probably for lack of draft animals.

bronze.summary: Copper alloyed with about 10 percent tin is harder than copper and casts well, giving durable tools, weapons and bells. Isolated tin bronze appears at Plocnik in Serbia about 4650 BC; the Bronze Age proper begins in the Near East about 3300 BC.

efforts.note: A tin bronze foil, probably smelted from mixed copper-tin ore.
Arsenical copper first, then tin bronze with tin traded from afar.
Large-scale piece-mold casting of ritual vessels; probably stimulated by contact via the steppe.
Arsenical and later tin bronzes, used widely under the Inca.

sources.title: Radivojevic et al. 2013, Tainted ores and the rise of tin bronzes in Eurasia (Antiquity)

calendar.summary: A counted year that tracks seasons for planting, festivals and taxes. Egypt's 365-day civil calendar of 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days was in use by early in the 3rd millennium BCE.

efforts.note: Lunisolar calendar; by about 500 BC a regular 19-year intercalation cycle.
The Long Count; the earliest dated monument, Chiapa de Corzo Stela 2, records 36 BC.
The Julian calendar with leap years, used in Europe until the Gregorian reform of 1582.

libraries.summary: Organized collections of texts let knowledge accumulate beyond what any one scribe knew. Ebla in Syria kept an archive of thousands of tablets about 2500 to 2250 BC; Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh and the Library of Alexandria followed.

efforts.note: Tens of thousands of tablet fragments, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.
A research library and museum; it declined over centuries rather than in one fire.
The House of Wisdom, a center for translating Greek, Persian and Indian works.

glassmaking.summary: Melting sand with plant ash or natron makes glass. Beads appear in Mesopotamia about 2500 BC, vessels about 1500 BC, and glassblowing on the Levant coast in the 1st century BCE made glass cheap.

efforts.note: Core-formed vessels, colored with cobalt and copper.
Glassblowing, quickly spread by Rome.
Clear cristallo glass by about 1450, the material for better lenses.

law-codes.summary: Publishing fixed rules and penalties made justice more predictable and less dependent on a ruler's mood. The Code of Ur-Nammu (about 2100 BC) is the oldest surviving; Hammurabi's code (about 1754 BC) is the best known.

efforts.note: 282 laws on a basalt stele, with fixed penalties for injury, fees and prices.
The Twelve Tables, later developed into Roman law and Justinian's code (529 to AD 534).

horse-domestication.summary: Horses for riding and pulling chariots made land travel several times faster and reshaped warfare and trade. Ancient DNA traces modern domestic horses to the western Eurasian steppe around 2200 BC.

efforts.note: Horses kept or herded, but they belong to the Przewalski's lineage, not modern domestic horses.
The DOM2 lineage spread across Eurasia within a few centuries, with spoke-wheeled chariots by about 2000 BC.

sources.title: Librado et al. 2021, The origins and spread of domestic horses from the Western Eurasian steppes (Nature)

geometry.summary: Rules for areas, volumes and right triangles were worked out for surveying and building in Babylon and Egypt by about 1800 BC. Greek mathematicians turned them into proofs from axioms, collected in Euclid's Elements about 300 BC.

efforts.note: Plimpton 322 lists Pythagorean triples; YBC 7289 gives the square root of 2 to six decimal places.
The Rhind papyrus, with areas and the volume of a pyramid.
The Sulba Sutras on altar construction state the Pythagorean theorem.
The Elements, used as a textbook for over 2,000 years.

astronomy-ancient.summary: Long written records of planets and eclipses let astronomers find cycles and predict the sky with arithmetic, and later geometric models. The Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa records observations from the 17th century BCE.

efforts.note: Astronomical diaries kept from 652 BC for six centuries; arithmetic lunar and planetary theory by about 400 BC.
Precession of the equinoxes; Ptolemy's Almagest (about AD 150) was standard for 1,400 years.
Venus and eclipse tables in the Dresden Codex.
Improved tables and instruments such as the astrolabe; Ulugh Beg's observatory in the 1420s.

water-clock.summary: A vessel that drains or fills at a steady rate measures hours at night and indoors. Egyptian examples date to about 1500 to 1400 BC; Ctesibius of Alexandria added a float regulator about 270 BC.

efforts.note: A feedback-regulated inflow clock.
Elaborate automata clocks described in his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices.

alphabet.summary: About two dozen signs for single sounds replaced hundreds of word and syllable signs, so literacy no longer took years of scribal training. Proto-Sinaitic, adapted from Egyptian hieroglyphs by Semitic-speaking workers, is the ancestor of almost all alphabets.

efforts.where: Wadi el-Hol and Serabit el-Khadim, Egypt
efforts.note: Clay cylinders from Umm el-Marra, Syria (about 2400 BC), proposed in 2024 as older alphabetic writing, are disputed.
The standardized consonant alphabet spread by trade.
Added letters for vowels; parent of Latin and Cyrillic.
Hangul, a featural alphabet designed from scratch.

iron-smelting.summary: Reducing iron ore in a charcoal bloomery gives a spongy metal that is hammered into tools. Iron ore is everywhere, unlike tin, so once smiths learned to carburize and quench it, cheap iron spread to farmers and armies across Eurasia and Africa after about 1200 BC.

efforts.note: Scattered early smelted iron and steel finds; experimental, prestige use only.
Iron became common after the Late Bronze Age collapse disrupted tin trade.
Whether African iron smelting was invented independently is debated; some sites have earlier contested dates.

sources.title: Archaeology Magazine 2019, New thoughts on the origins of iron smelting in Anatolia

blast-furnace.summary: Tall furnaces hot enough to fully melt iron let Chinese founders pour it into molds, making cheap tools and pots in bulk. China cast iron from about the 5th century BCE; Europe only from about the 12th century CE.

efforts.note: Later Song dynasty furnaces burned coal and produced perhaps 100,000 tonnes of iron a year by 1078.

coinage.summary: Stamped pieces of metal of guaranteed weight let strangers trade without weighing and assaying, and let states pay soldiers and collect taxes. The first coins were struck from electrum in Lydia in western Turkey in the late 7th century BCE.

efforts.note: Weighed silver (the shekel) as money, a precursor to coins.
Cast bronze spade and knife money.
Punch-marked silver coins.

crucible-steel-wootz.summary: Iron and plant matter sealed in clay crucibles in southern India and Sri Lanka made high-carbon steel cakes, traded as wootz. Forged in the Middle East into Damascus blades, it showed a watery pattern and was famed for sharpness and toughness.
crucible-steel-wootz.lost: Production of patterned blades faded by the late 18th century, possibly as the ores with trace vanadium ran out, and the method was forgotten. Verhoeven and Pendray reproduced the pattern in the 1990s by showing that trace impurities and repeated forging cycles were the key; Reibold and colleagues found carbon nanotubes in a 17th century saber in 2006.

sources.title: Reibold et al. 2006, Carbon nanotubes in an ancient Damascus sabre (Nature)

formal-logic.summary: Rules for which arguments are valid by their form alone. Aristotle's syllogistic, written about 350 BC, was the core of logic until the 19th century, when Boole and Frege turned it into algebra.

efforts.note: An early propositional logic.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Logic

abacus.summary: Pebbles or beads in columns let people add, subtract and multiply large numbers quickly, the first calculating machine. The Salamis tablet, a Greek counting board, dates to about 300 BC; the Chinese bead suanpan and Japanese soroban came later.

watermill.summary: A wheel turned by flowing water and geared to millstones, the first widely used machine powered by something other than muscle. Described by Philo of Byzantium in the 3rd century BCE; England's Domesday Book of 1086 counts over 5,600 mills.

efforts.note: Water-powered trip hammers, and by AD 31 Du Shi's water-powered bellows for iron furnaces.
Sixteen wheels in two parallel cascades, perhaps the largest ancient mill complex.

concrete-roman.summary: Lime mixed with volcanic ash (pozzolana) and rubble set into a strong, even underwater, artificial stone. It let Rome build harbors, aqueducts and the Pantheon dome (about AD 125), still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.

efforts.note: Vitruvius described the materials about 30 to 15 BC.
Explained self-healing lime clasts; a 2025 Nature Communications study of Pompeii followed.

concrete-roman.lost: Pozzolanic concrete largely fell out of use after the western empire, and modern Portland cement (1824) works differently. Why Roman concrete lasts so long was understood only recently: harbor concrete grows new minerals in seawater (Jackson, 2017), and MIT researchers (2023) showed that hot mixing with quicklime left lime clasts that seal cracks. An unfinished building site at Pompeii (2025) confirmed hot mixing directly.

sources.title: Seymour et al. 2023, Hot mixing and self-healing ancient Roman concrete (Science Advances)
MIT News 2023, Riddle solved, why was Roman concrete so durable
Smithsonian Magazine 2025, Pompeii construction site and Roman concrete

trigonometry.summary: Tables relating angles to lengths let astronomers and surveyors compute distances they could not measure. Hipparchus built the first chord table about 140 BC; Indian astronomers introduced the sine about AD 500.

efforts.note: Sine tables in the Aryabhatiya.
Trigonometry made a separate subject, with spherical trigonometry for astronomy.

antikythera-mechanism.summary: A hand-cranked bronze box of at least 30 gears that modeled the motions of the Sun, Moon and probably planets and predicted eclipses, an analog computer. It was found in a shipwreck off Antikythera that sank about 70 to 60 BC.
antikythera-mechanism.lost: No similar device survives and texts mention only a few. Gearing of this complexity did not appear again until astronomical clocks in 14th century Europe. The fragments were recovered in 1901 and fully decoded only with X-ray tomography in the 2000s.

sources.title: Freeth et al. 2021, A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism (Scientific Reports)

paper.summary: Plant fibers beaten to pulp in water and dried on a screen make a cheap, light writing surface. A map on paper from Fangmatan in China dates to the 2nd century BCE; Cai Lun improved the process in AD 105.

efforts.note: Bark, hemp, rags and fishnets; reported to the emperor.
Papermaking spread west via the Islamic world, reaching Spain by about 1100 and Italy (Fabriano) by 1264.

place-value-zero.summary: Ten digits whose value depends on position, with zero as a number in its own right, make arithmetic on paper easy for anyone. Indian mathematicians had it by the 5th century CE, and Brahmagupta gave rules for computing with zero in 628.

efforts.note: Sexagesimal place value; a placeholder sign for an empty place by about 300 BC, never used alone.
Vigesimal (base 20) place value with a zero glyph in the Long Count.
The Lokavibhaga (458) uses decimal place value; the Bakhshali manuscript may be older but its dating is disputed.
Spread through the Islamic world and to Europe in Liber Abaci (1202).

greek-fire.summary: A liquid incendiary that burned on water, sprayed from pressurized siphons on Byzantine warships. Credited to Kallinikos, a refugee from Syria, about 672, it helped break the Arab sieges of Constantinople.
greek-fire.lost: The formula was a state secret known to a few families and was lost, perhaps by 1203, when it was not used against the Fourth Crusade. It was probably based on crude petroleum from the Black Sea, but the exact recipe and siphon design are unknown.

woodblock-printing.summary: Carving a whole page in relief on a wooden block and inking it to print many copies. It spread in Tang China and Korea for Buddhist texts; the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book.

maya-blue.summary: A brilliant blue pigment made by heating indigo with palygorskite clay, which binds the dye so tightly that it survives centuries of tropical weather and acids. Mesoamerican painters used it from about the 8th century CE.
maya-blue.lost: Use continued in colonial Mexico into the 16th century, then the method was lost there. Its composition was worked out by X-ray diffraction in the 1950s and 1960s, and a working recipe was published in 1993. It has been a model for durable hybrid organic-mineral pigments.

algebra.summary: General methods for solving equations by manipulating unknowns. Al-Khwarizmi's book al-Jabr (about 820), written in Baghdad, gave algebra its name and treated it as its own subject.

efforts.note: Solved quadratic problems by recipe.
Arithmetica, with symbols for unknowns.
General solution of quadratics, negative numbers.
Geometric solutions of cubic equations.

sources.title: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing (Wikipedia)

windmill.summary: Sails turned by wind to grind grain and pump water, useful where rivers are weak or freeze. Vertical-axis windmills in eastern Persia are reported in the 9th century; the European post mill appears in England by 1185.

efforts.note: Horizontal panemone mills behind walls.
The post mill, with sails on a horizontal axis, probably developed independently.

gunpowder.summary: A mix of saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal that burns explosively, the first chemical explosive. Chinese alchemists noted its danger in the 9th century; the Wujing Zongyao of 1044 gives the first recipes, and guns followed.

efforts.note: Written formulas (1044), fire lances (about 1132), bombs, and metal hand cannons by about 1288.
A European recipe by 1267 and the first European image of a cannon in 1326.

bills-of-exchange.summary: A written order to pay money in another place lets merchants move value without carrying coin. Tang China's flying money, the Islamic suftaja, and the bills of Italian merchant-bankers after about 1150 made long-distance trade and banking possible.

efforts.note: Feiqian (flying money) drafts.
The suftaja and hawala transfer systems.
Bills of exchange underlay the Medici bank and later central banking.

optics-alhazen.summary: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics showed that we see by light entering the eye, analyzed reflection and refraction, and tested claims with controlled experiments. In Latin translation it shaped European optics and experimental method.

paper-money.summary: Printed notes backed by the state replaced heavy iron coins. Merchants in Sichuan issued notes in the 10th century, and the Song government took over issuing the jiaozi in 1024.

efforts.note: Yuan dynasty overissue later caused inflation, an early lesson in monetary policy.

sources.title: History of Chinese currency, paper money (Wikipedia)

movable-type.summary: Separate reusable characters arranged into pages and reset for the next job. Bi Sheng made ceramic type in China about 1040, and Korean printers cast metal type; Jikji (1377) is the oldest surviving book printed with it.

efforts.note: Clay type, described by Shen Kuo. Chinese scripts' thousands of characters limited the advantage over woodblocks.
Bronze type; Jikji is held in the National Library of France.

compass.summary: A magnetized iron needle points north, giving direction under clouds and at sea. Shen Kuo described the needle compass in 1088, and Zhu Yu reported its use by ships in 1117; it reached Europe by about 1190.

efforts.note: A lodestone spoon on a board for geomancy, if the descriptions are read that way; the evidence is debated.
Wujing Zongyao (1044) describes a magnetized iron fish; Shen Kuo the needle (1088).
The first European description, perhaps an independent invention.

universities.summary: Self-governing corporations of teachers and students granting degrees, with set curricula and legal privileges. Bologna (1088) and Paris (about 1150) set the pattern that spread across Europe and, later, the world.

efforts.note: A large residential center of learning until it was sacked about 1200.
Al-Qarawiyyin, a mosque school that became a university in the 20th century.
The model of the student-run university; Paris and Oxford followed with master-run models.

lenses.summary: Convex glass lenses in a frame, invented near Pisa about 1286, doubled the working life of scribes and craftsmen. Lens grinding was the craft from which telescopes and microscopes came three centuries later.

efforts.note: In 1306 the friar Giordano da Pisa said spectacles had been invented less than 20 years earlier.
Reading stones, polished glass or crystal laid on a page.

mechanical-clock.summary: A falling weight held back by a verge-and-foliot escapement drives gears that count time. It appeared in European monasteries and towns around 1280 to 1300, and set the standard of regular hours for work and science.

efforts.note: A water-driven escapement in an armillary sphere.
A 12 m astronomical clock tower driven by a water wheel with an escapement; dismantled after the Jin conquest.
Weight-driven verge escapement; Dunstable Priory had a clock by 1283, and Richard of Wallingford and Giovanni de Dondi built astronomical clocks in the 14th century.

sources.title: History of timekeeping devices, mechanical clocks (Wikipedia)

double-entry-bookkeeping.summary: Recording every transaction as both a debit and a credit, so the books must balance and errors show. Italian merchants used it by about 1300; Luca Pacioli's printed description of 1494 spread it across Europe.

efforts.note: The oldest surviving double-entry ledger.
The city's accounts in full double-entry form.

distillation.summary: Boiling a liquid and condensing the vapor separates substances by volatility. Akkadian tablets of about 1200 BC describe a perfumer, Tapputi, refining scents; Alexandrian alchemists built the alembic, and distilled alcohol appears at Salerno about 1150.

efforts.note: An early, simple form of distillation and extraction for perfume.

efforts.who: Mary the Jewess, Zosimos of Panopolis
efforts.note: The alembic and still, described in alchemical texts.
Distilled rosewater, essential oils and possibly alcohol.
The first clear evidence of distilled alcohol in Europe; later the basis of oil refining.

spinning-wheel.summary: A hand- or foot-turned wheel drives the spindle, making thread several times faster than a hand spindle. Its origin (China, India or Persia) is debated; the earliest clear picture is from Baghdad in 1237, and it reached Europe in the 13th century.

efforts.note: Known in the Middle East by about 1030; illustrated in al-Wasiti's Maqamat of 1237.
Some scholars argue for a much older Chinese origin; the earliest clear Chinese picture is about 1270.
Hand spindles stayed common until the 18th century, when mechanized spinning began the factory age.

printing-press.summary: Gutenberg combined cast metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press, making books cheap enough that knowledge could be copied exactly and spread across Europe within decades.

efforts.who: Johannes Gutenberg, financed by Johann Fust
efforts.note: The 42-line Bible was finished around 1454 to 1455. The hand mold for casting type drew on goldsmiths' punch-cutting.
Ceramic movable type, described by Shen Kuo. It did not displace woodblock printing.
The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.

effort.note: Gutenberg borrowed at least 1,600 guilders from Fust and lost the workshop to him in a lawsuit in 1455.

scientific-method.summary: The practice of testing claims about nature with controlled experiment, measurement and mathematics, rather than deferring to ancient authority, took shape with Galileo and Bacon.

efforts.note: Novum Organum argued for systematic induction from experiment.
Combined experiment, instruments and mathematical description.
His Book of Optics used controlled experiments centuries earlier.

scientific-societies.summary: Standing bodies such as the Royal Society and the Paris Academy, and the first scientific journals in 1665, gave natural philosophers a shared venue to report, replicate and argue.

efforts.note: An early society; Galileo was a member.
Chartered 1662. Philosophical Transactions began in March 1665.
State-funded; the Journal des scavans also began in 1665.

sources.title: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (Wikipedia)

peer-review.summary: Having other experts judge a paper before publication began with 18th-century society journals and became the standard gate for scientific publishing in the 20th century.

efforts.who: Royal Society of Edinburgh, Medical Essays and Observations
efforts.note: Submissions were sent to members judged knowledgeable on the topic.
Written referee reports followed in the 1830s. Universal external review only became normal after 1945.

sources.title: Csiszar, Peer review: Troubled from the start (Nature, 2016)

industrial-research-lab.summary: Firms began paying teams of scientists to invent on purpose, starting with Edison's Menlo Park and the German dye companies, then GE, DuPont and Bell Labs.

efforts.note: An "invention factory" with machinists, chemists and glassblowers.
Dye firms built in-house research labs staffed by university chemists in the 1870s and 1880s.
Followed by DuPont (1903) and Bell Telephone Laboratories (1925).

big-science.summary: In the Second World War governments organized science as a national project, contracting universities and firms through bodies like the US Office of Scientific Research and Development.

efforts.note: Funded radar, the proximity fuze, penicillin production and the early atomic program. Bush's 1945 report Science, the Endless Frontier led to the NSF.
A prewar model of large team physics built around big machines.

sources.title: Office of Scientific Research and Development (Wikipedia)

patents.summary: A legal right to exclusive use of an invention for a fixed term, in exchange for disclosing it, first codified in Venice and later in England's Statute of Monopolies and the US Constitution.

efforts.note: The Venetian Patent Statute granted 10-year privileges for new devices.
The Statute of Monopolies limited patents to true inventions for 14 years.
The Patent Act of 1790.

joint-stock-company.summary: Pooling capital from many investors into transferable shares of one permanent enterprise let merchants fund long, risky ventures like ocean trade that no single family could afford.

efforts.note: Chartered 1555. An early English joint-stock trading company.
First company with permanent capital and freely traded shares.

stock-exchange.summary: A standing market where shares of companies could be bought and sold at any time, which made long-lived company capital liquid for individual investors.

efforts.note: Trading in VOC shares; a dedicated exchange building opened in 1611.

efforts.who: London coffee houses, later the London Stock Exchange
efforts.note: Formally organized in 1801.

central-banking.summary: A bank chartered by the state to manage government debt, issue currency and act as lender of last resort, beginning with Sweden's Riksbank and the Bank of England.

efforts.note: Successor to Stockholms Banco, which issued Europe's first banknotes in 1661.
Founded as a joint-stock company to lend to the government. Bagehot's Lombard Street (1873) set out the lender-of-last-resort role.

insurance-modern.summary: Insurance priced from data and probability, so that premiums match measured risk, grew from marine underwriting at Lloyd's and fire offices to actuarial life insurance.

efforts.note: Set up after the Great Fire of 1666.
Center of marine underwriting, later Lloyd's of London.
First mutual life insurer to set premiums by age from mortality tables.

factory-system.summary: Gathering workers and powered machines under one roof, with set hours and division of labor, replaced home spinning and weaving and became the template for industrial production.

efforts.note: A water-powered silk mill, an early precursor.
Cromford Mill ran water frames around the clock in shifts and became the model copied across Britain and America.

analytic-geometry.summary: Describing curves with algebraic equations in coordinates joined geometry and algebra, and gave calculus its working language.

efforts.note: La Geometrie, an appendix to the Discourse on Method.
Circulated in manuscript, published after his death.

calculus.summary: The mathematics of rates of change and accumulation, which let physics state laws as equations of motion and solve them.

efforts.note: Developed fluxions in 1665 to 1666; published much later.
Published first, in 1684, with the notation still used today. A bitter priority dispute followed.
Infinite series for trigonometric functions, without a general calculus.

effort.note: Two people, each working largely alone, on the shoulders of Fermat, Barrow and Wallis.

probability-theory.summary: A mathematics of chance, begun in letters about gambling problems, that became the basis of insurance, statistics, statistical physics and information theory.

efforts.note: Correspondence solving the problem of points.
Liber de ludo aleae, written about 1564, published 1663.
First printed treatise. Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi (1713) proved the law of large numbers.

statistics.summary: Drawing conclusions from counts and measurements, from Graunt's mortality tables through least squares and the normal curve to Fisher's significance tests and experimental design.

efforts.note: Natural and Political Observations on the Bills of Mortality. Edmond Halley's life table followed in 1693.
Least squares (Legendre 1805, Gauss 1809) and the normal error curve.
Correlation and chi-squared (1900); Fisher's Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925) and randomized experimental design.

fourier-analysis.summary: Any periodic signal can be written as a sum of sine waves. Fourier found it while studying heat flow, and it became basic to acoustics, radio, quantum mechanics and signal processing.

efforts.note: Memoir on heat in 1807; Theorie analytique de la chaleur in 1822.

non-euclidean-geometry.summary: Consistent geometries in which Euclid's parallel postulate fails, generalized by Riemann to curved spaces of any dimension, later the language of general relativity.

efforts.note: Worked it out but did not publish.
Habilitation lecture on the foundations of geometry. Ricci and Levi-Civita's tensor calculus (1900) made it usable.

boolean-logic.summary: George Boole showed that logical reasoning could be done as algebra on true and false values, the mathematics that every digital circuit now implements.

efforts.note: The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (1847) and The Laws of Thought (1854).
Formal Logic, same year; De Morgan's laws.

mathematical-logic.summary: A precise symbolic language for quantifiers and proofs, built to put all of mathematics on logical foundations, which raised the question of what can be proved or computed.

efforts.note: Begriffsschrift, the first full predicate logic.
Axioms for arithmetic.
Principia Mathematica, 1910 to 1913. David Hilbert's program of the 1920s sought a complete and decidable foundation.

computability-theory.summary: Turing and Church defined precisely what an algorithm is and proved some problems can never be solved by one; Turing's universal machine is the abstract model of the stored-program computer.

efforts.note: Incompleteness theorems showed Hilbert's complete foundation was impossible.
On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem.
Lambda calculus; Emil Post's similar model appeared the same year.

switching-circuit-theory.summary: Claude Shannon showed that networks of relays and switches compute Boolean algebra, so logic could be designed on paper and built in hardware.

efforts.note: Master's thesis A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, published 1938.
Proposed in 1935, published 1941.

sources.title: A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits (Wikipedia)

information-theory.summary: Shannon defined information in bits and proved how much can be sent through a noisy channel, setting the limits for all later communication, compression and coding.

efforts.note: A Mathematical Theory of Communication.
Earlier results on telegraph speed and a logarithmic measure of information.
The sampling theorem.
A related statistical theory of communication in Cybernetics.

jacquard-loom.summary: A loom controlled by chains of punched cards, so a pattern became a stored program; the cards inspired Babbage's engine and Hollerith's tabulators.

efforts.who: Basile Bouchon, Jean-Baptiste Falcon, Jacques de Vaucanson
efforts.note: Punched paper and card loom controls from 1725 to 1745.

analytical-engine.summary: Charles Babbage designed a steam-age mechanical computer with memory, a processing unit and card input; Ada Lovelace wrote programs for it, but it was never built.

efforts.note: Difference Engine No. 1, funded by the British government, abandoned in 1842.
Analytical Engine design; Lovelace's 1843 notes include the first published program.
Mechanical calculators (Pascaline 1642, stepped reckoner 1673).

effort.note: The government spent about 17,000 pounds on the Difference Engine before abandoning it; the 2025-dollar figure is a rough conversion.

tabulating-machine.summary: Herman Hollerith's electric card readers tallied the 1890 US census in a fraction of the time of the hand-counted 1880 census, founding the data-processing industry that became IBM.

efforts.note: Patented 1889. His company merged into CTR in 1911, renamed IBM in 1924.

sources.title: US Census Bureau, Herman Hollerith and Mechanical Tabulation (History and the Census, 2016)

heliocentrism.summary: Copernicus put the Sun at the center with Earth as one moving planet, which Kepler and Galileo later confirmed and which opened the road to Newton.

efforts.note: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium.
Proposed a Sun-centered cosmos that did not catch on.

effort.note: About three decades of one astronomer's work.

telescope.summary: Two lenses in a tube magnified distant objects; turned to the sky, it showed Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus, evidence for a Sun-centered system.

efforts.note: First patent application; Jacob Metius and Zacharias Janssen made rival claims.
Improved it to about 20x and published Sidereus Nuncius in 1610.
The reflecting telescope.

keplers-laws.summary: Planets move in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times, and have periods tied to orbit size; Kepler fit these to Tycho Brahe's naked-eye data.

efforts.who: Johannes Kepler, using Tycho Brahe's observations
efforts.note: Astronomia nova (1609) gave the first two laws; Harmonices Mundi (1619) the third.

effort.note: About eight years of hand calculation on the orbit of Mars, from data Tycho's observatory gathered over some 20 years.

galilean-kinematics.summary: Galileo measured falling and rolling bodies and found uniform acceleration, parabolic trajectories and the principle of inertia.

efforts.note: Two New Sciences, written under house arrest and printed in Leiden.

vacuum-pump.summary: Pumps that removed air from a vessel showed that the atmosphere has weight and pressure, an idea behind the steam engine, and later made light bulbs and vacuum tubes possible.

efforts.note: The mercury barometer showed air pressure and made a vacuum.
First air pump; Magdeburg hemispheres demonstration in 1654.
An improved pump and Boyle's law (1662). Sprengel's mercury pump (1865) later gave the hard vacuum for light bulbs.

newtonian-mechanics.summary: Three laws of motion and universal gravitation explained both falling apples and planetary orbits with one set of equations, the model for all later physics.

efforts.note: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published with Edmond Halley's funding.
Suggested an inverse-square law of attraction to Newton but could not derive orbits.

aerodynamics.summary: George Cayley separated lift from thrust and flew fixed-wing gliders; Lilienthal's measured glider flights and wind tunnel data then showed how to build and control wings.

efforts.note: Model glider in 1804, a crewed glider in 1853.
About 2,000 glider flights before his fatal crash in 1896.
First wind tunnel.

transoceanic-voyages.summary: Ocean-going carracks and caravels, the compass and celestial navigation let European sailors cross the Atlantic, round Africa to India and circle the globe.

efforts.note: Three ships and about 90 men.
Sea route to India.
First circumnavigation. Five ships and about 270 men left; one ship and 18 men returned.
Large fleets sailed the Indian Ocean from 1405 to 1433, then were stopped.

longitude-chronometer.summary: A clock accurate enough at sea to carry home-port time let navigators find longitude, a problem Britain had offered a large prize to solve.

efforts.note: H4 lost about 5 seconds on the voyage to Jamaica.
The lunar distance method, a rival astronomical solution, published in the Nautical Almanac.

effort.note: About 30 years and four clocks (H1 to H4) by Harrison, chasing the 20,000-pound prize of the Longitude Act of 1714.

leyden-jar.summary: A glass jar lined with metal foil stored static electric charge, the first capacitor, and let experimenters study electricity with strong sparks; Franklin used it to show lightning is electric.

efforts.note: Friction machines that generated the charge.

electric-battery.summary: Stacked zinc and copper discs in brine gave the first steady electric current, enabling electrochemistry (Davy isolated sodium and potassium in 1807) and electromagnetism.

efforts.note: Built to refute Luigi Galvani's animal electricity (1791).
Electrolysis of water weeks after Volta's report.
Isolated potassium, sodium and later several other elements by electrolysis.

electromagnetism.summary: An electric current deflects a compass needle; electricity and magnetism are linked, and a coil of wire around iron makes a strong controllable electromagnet.

efforts.note: Mathematical law of forces between currents, weeks after Orsted.
The electromagnet (Sturgeon 1824); Henry's much stronger insulated-coil magnets around 1830.

electric-motor.summary: Electromagnetic forces turned into continuous rotation; practical motors arrived when the dynamo could supply cheap current, and they later freed factories from line shafts.

efforts.note: Electromagnetic rotation demonstration.
First useful rotating motor; powered a boat on the Neva in 1839.
First US motor patent.

electromagnetic-induction.summary: A changing magnetic field produces an electric current, the principle behind every generator, transformer and induction coil.

efforts.note: The induction ring experiment of 29 August 1831.
Found it independently and also discovered self-induction.

electric-generator.summary: Machines that turn mechanical rotation into current; the self-exciting dynamo made electricity cheap and plentiful enough for lighting, electroplating and industry.

efforts.note: Hand-cranked magneto generator.

efforts.who: Werner von Siemens; Charles Wheatstone; Samuel Varley
efforts.note: Self-excited dynamos announced almost simultaneously in 1866 to 1867. Anyos Jedlik had the idea earlier.
The ring-armature dynamo, the first commercially successful design.

maxwell-equations.summary: Maxwell unified electricity, magnetism and light into one field theory and predicted electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light.

efforts.note: A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field (1865); Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism (1873).
Recast Maxwell's 20 equations into the four vector equations used today.

effort.note: Built on Faraday's field lines, worked out over about 18 years.

sources.title: A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field (Wikipedia)

electromagnetic-waves.summary: Heinrich Hertz generated and detected electromagnetic waves with spark gaps, confirming Maxwell's prediction and showing that invisible waves could carry energy across a room.

efforts.note: Detected waves along wires about the same time.

relay.summary: An electromagnet that opens and closes another circuit, first used to extend telegraph lines, later the switching element of telephone exchanges and the first programmable computers.

efforts.note: Repeaters for long telegraph lines.

telegraph.summary: Coded pulses of current over wires sent messages across countries in seconds; by 1866 an Atlantic cable linked Europe and America, the first instant long-distance communication.

efforts.note: Needle telegraph, patented 1837, first used along railway lines.
Morse code; Washington to Baltimore line in 1844.
Optical semaphore telegraph network, displaced by the electric telegraph.
The 1858 cable failed in weeks; the Great Eastern laid a lasting one in 1866.

telephone.summary: Converting voice into a varying electric current and back carried speech over wires, and grew into switched networks run by the Bell System.

efforts.note: Patent filed 14 February 1876 and granted 7 March 1876.
Filed a caveat for a liquid transmitter the same day as Bell's application.
Filed a caveat in 1871 but could not afford to renew it.
Transmitted tones and some speech.
The carbon microphone made long-distance calls practical.

photography.summary: Light-sensitive silver chemistry fixed camera images permanently, a new record for science and the detector behind spectroscopy, astronomy and the discovery of X-rays and radioactivity.

efforts.note: The oldest surviving camera photograph, on bitumen.
The daguerreotype, released by the French state as a free gift to the world.
Paper negatives; the calotype (1841) allowed copies.

radio.summary: Wireless telegraphy, then voice and broadcasting, carried messages through the air by radio waves, first to ships and across oceans, then into homes from 1920.

efforts.note: British patent in 1896, transatlantic signal in December 1901. Nobel Prize 1909 with Karl Ferdinand Braun.
Millimeter-wave experiments and crystal detectors.
His US patents were upheld over Marconi's by the Supreme Court in 1943.
Amplitude-modulated voice transmission; KDKA began scheduled broadcasting in 1920.

vacuum-tube.summary: A heated filament emits electrons into a vacuum; the diode rectified radio signals and the triode amplified them, the active component of electronics until the transistor.

efforts.note: Patented the Edison effect, current from a hot filament, without explaining it.
The thermionic diode valve.
The Audion, a triode, though he did not understand how it amplified.
Hard-vacuum tubes made reliable amplifiers, enabling transcontinental telephony in 1915.

radar.summary: Pulsed radio echoes locate aircraft and ships; British chain stations and then microwave radar using the cavity magnetron shaped the Second World War.

efforts.note: The Daventry experiment; the Chain Home network was operating by 1939.
Pulse radar by Robert Page and colleagues.
Several nations developed radar in secret in the mid-1930s.
The cavity magnetron, taken to the US by the Tizard Mission in September 1940.
Developed about half of US wartime radar systems.

effort.note: The Rad Lab grew to about 4,000 staff. US wartime radar spending was roughly 2.7 billion 1940s dollars (Rad Lab designs were about 1.35 billion), roughly 50 billion 2025 dollars; this excludes the British program.

deep-coal-mining.summary: As English forests were cut, coal replaced wood as fuel; mines went deeper and flooded, and the need to pump them dry created the first market for steam engines.

efforts.note: British coal output grew roughly tenfold between 1560 and 1700 by most estimates.

steam-engine.summary: Newcomen's engine condensed steam under a piston so air pressure pushed it down, pumping water from mines; the first practical machine to turn fuel into work.

efforts.note: Hundreds were built in the 18th century, wasteful but cheap to fuel at the pithead.
A pistonless steam pump, whose broad patent Newcomen had to work under.
Piston-and-cylinder model.

precision-cylinder-boring.summary: John Wilkinson's boring mill, built for cannon, cut iron cylinders round and true enough to seal a steam piston, which made Watt's engine work.

efforts.note: Patented a cannon-boring method; his cylinders were accurate to roughly the thickness of a thin shilling.

watt-steam-engine.summary: A separate condenser roughly doubled or tripled efficiency, and rotary motion let steam drive mills and factories anywhere, not only at mines and rivers.

efforts.note: Separate condenser conceived in 1765, patented 1769; first commercial engines 1776; sun-and-planet rotary gear 1781.
High-pressure engines, light enough for locomotives and boats, after Watt's patent expired in 1800.

effort.note: About eleven years from idea to commercial engine, rescued by Boulton's capital and a patent extension to 1800.

carnot-heat-engine-theory.summary: Sadi Carnot showed that a heat engine's maximum efficiency depends only on the temperatures between which it runs, the seed of thermodynamics.

efforts.note: Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, largely ignored until Clapeyron (1834) and Kelvin revived it.

sources.title: Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire (Wikipedia)

thermodynamics.summary: Energy is conserved and heat flows from hot to cold, with entropy never decreasing; the laws that govern every engine, refrigerator, power plant and chemical reaction.

efforts.note: Mechanical equivalent of heat.
Precise experiments on the mechanical equivalent of heat.
General statement of conservation of energy.
The second law (1850 to 1851); Clausius named entropy in 1865. Gibbs extended it to chemistry in 1876.

statistical-mechanics.summary: Treating heat as the statistics of countless moving molecules explained gas laws and entropy from probability, and later guided Planck to the quantum.

efforts.note: Distribution of molecular speeds.
Entropy as the logarithm of the number of microstates.
Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics.

steamboat.summary: Steam engines driving paddle wheels and later screw propellers made river and ocean travel independent of wind and current.

efforts.note: The Pyroscaphe ran briefly on the Saone.
Ran a commercial service in 1790 that failed financially.
The Clermont, the first commercially successful steamboat.
SS Great Britain, an iron-hulled, screw-driven ocean liner.

railway.summary: High-pressure steam locomotives on iron rails moved goods and people overland faster and cheaper than ever, knitting together markets and reshaping time and geography.

efforts.note: First steam locomotive to haul a load on rails.
Stockton and Darlington Railway (1825).
The Liverpool and Manchester, the first intercity line run entirely by steam on a timetable, after the Rocket won the Rainhill Trials in 1829.

transcontinental-railroad.summary: About 1,800 miles of new line linking the US rail network to the Pacific, built largely by Chinese and Irish laborers through the Sierra Nevada with black powder and nitroglycerin.

efforts.who: Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads
efforts.note: Joined at Promontory Summit, Utah, on 10 May 1869.
Built 1891 to 1916, about 9,300 km.
