aging-reversal.criterion: A treatment, approved for use, that in a randomized controlled trial reverses biological age by at least 10 years on a validated measure across several organ systems at once (or equivalently restores muscle, cognitive and immune function by 10 or more years, the XPRIZE Healthspan bar), with the gain holding for at least two years.

efforts.note: First human trial of partial epigenetic reprogramming, in optic nerve diseases (glaucoma, NAION).

efforts.who: Altos Labs, Retro Biosciences, NewLimit, Calico
efforts.note: Altos launched in 2022 with about $3 billion.

forecast.note: Partial reprogramming reversed aging marks in mice from 2016 and reached a first human trial in 2026, in the eye. Senolytics have missed their endpoints so far. Pig kidneys keep people off dialysis for months but not yet a year, and no lab-grown solid organ has been implanted. Each route needs both the technology and an institutional change: an accepted aging endpoint, around 2036 here, without which nobody can run the trial this criterion asks for. Metaculus forecasters put longevity escape velocity, a looser bar, somewhere from the late 2030s to beyond 2100, with medians in the 2050s. I put a therapy meeting this bar around 2062, with very wide uncertainty and a real chance that the "replace" route gets there first on organ-by-organ grounds without anything that deserves the name rejuvenation.

sources.title: Metaculus: when will a country reach longevity escape velocity?

routes.name: Repair
routes.note: Reset cells where they are, with reprogramming, senolytics, gene editing and geroprotector drugs.

routes.name: Replace
routes.note: Swap out failing organs for new ones, grown in a lab or in a pig.

routes.name: Pause and wait
routes.note: Stop biological time until the other routes mature. Today's cryonics is a bet on this, not a demonstration of it.

whole-brain-emulation.summary: Scanning a human brain at synaptic resolution and simulating it closely enough that the simulation behaves like the person.
whole-brain-emulation.criterion: A human brain is scanned at synaptic resolution and simulated so that the simulation, questioned over days, is indistinguishable from the person to people who knew them, and reports the person's memories.

efforts.note: Complete connectome of an adult fruit fly brain, about 140,000 neurons and 50 million synapses.
A cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex, about 200,000 cells and 500 million synapses, with matched activity recordings.

forecast.note: The path runs through a whole mouse connectome (about 2036 here), an emulated fly or worm (about 2033), a mouse emulation (about 2052) and a human connectome (about 2062). Each step so far has taken longer than expected, and two things beyond wiring are unsolved: reading synapse strengths and molecular state from a preserved brain, and showing that a connectome plus physiology reproduces behavior at all. Metaculus forecasters have a community median in the early 2070s with a very wide range. I lean later, around 2090.

sources.title: Metaculus: when will the first whole human brain be emulated?
Zanichelli et al., State of Brain Emulation Report 2025 (arXiv)

electronic-computer.summary: ENIAC, finished at the University of Pennsylvania in late 1945 and unveiled in February 1946, was the first general-purpose programmable electronic computer, built from about 18,000 vacuum tubes and reprogrammed by rewiring plugboards.

efforts.who: J. Presper Eckert, John Mauchly (Moore School, for the US Army Ordnance Corps)
efforts.note: Built to compute artillery firing tables; one of its first real jobs was a calculation for the hydrogen bomb.

efforts.who: Tommy Flowers (Post Office Research Station, for Bletchley Park)
efforts.note: Colossus, an electronic but special-purpose code-breaking machine, kept secret until the 1970s.
The Z3 was programmable but electromechanical, built from relays.
Electronic but not programmable; a 1973 court ruling cited it to void the ENIAC patent.

effort.note: About $487,000 at the time (roughly $7 million in 2024 dollars per Wikipedia); 17,468 tubes, 30 tons, 150 to 200 kW.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Timeline of Computer History, 1945

monte-carlo-method.summary: Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann's idea of estimating hard quantities by running many random simulations, first run on ENIAC in 1948 for nuclear weapons design and now used everywhere from physics to finance to AI.

efforts.who: Stanislaw Ulam, John von Neumann, Nicholas Metropolis (Los Alamos)
efforts.note: Named by Metropolis after the casino; published 1949. The Metropolis algorithm followed in 1953.

transistor.summary: A semiconductor switch and amplifier, first made at Bell Labs in December 1947 from germanium and gold foil. It replaced the vacuum tube and is now the most-manufactured object in history.

efforts.note: The point-contact transistor. Nobel Prize in Physics 1956, shared with Shockley.
Conceived the more manufacturable junction transistor in 1948; first made in 1951.
The "transistron", developed from wartime radar detector work.
First commercial silicon transistor, which handled heat far better than germanium.

effort.note: A small solid-state group set up by Mervin Kelly at Bell Labs after the war.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Invention of the point-contact transistor

stored-program-computer.summary: A computer that keeps its program in the same memory as its data, so it can be reprogrammed by loading new instructions. The Manchester Baby ran the first stored program on June 21, 1948, and nearly every computer since has used this design.

efforts.who: John von Neumann, with Eckert and Mauchly (Moore School)
efforts.note: The "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" (June 1945) described the design; Turing's ACE proposal followed in 1946.

efforts.who: Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn, Geoff Tootill (University of Manchester)
efforts.note: The Manchester Baby, with memory on a cathode-ray tube (the Williams tube).
EDSAC, the first stored-program computer in regular service.
UNIVAC I, the first US commercial computer; the Ferranti Mark 1 shipped in the UK the same year.

sources.title: Wikipedia, First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC

single-crystal-growth.summary: Pulling large single crystals of germanium and later silicon from a melt, and purifying them by zone refining to impurity levels near one part per billion, which made reliable transistors and then silicon wafers possible.

efforts.note: Adapted Jan Czochralski's 1916 crystal-pulling method; William Pfann's zone refining followed in 1951 to 1952.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Development of zone refining

compiler.summary: A program that translates human-readable code into machine instructions, so people no longer had to write raw machine code.

efforts.note: The A-0 system, an early linker-loader she called a compiler.
Autocode for the Manchester Mark 1, often called the first compiled language.

magnetic-core-memory.summary: Memory made of tiny magnetic rings threaded on wires, each storing one bit. It was the main computer memory from the mid-1950s until DRAM chips replaced it in the 1970s.

efforts.note: An Wang patented a related pulse-transfer memory in 1949.

hard-disk-drive.summary: Spinning magnetic platters read by a moving head, giving computers fast random access to large stored data. IBM's first, the RAMAC 350, held about 5 MB on fifty 24-inch disks.

programming-languages.summary: Languages that let people write programs in something close to math or English and have a compiler produce efficient machine code. FORTRAN (1957) proved compiled code could rival hand-written code, and LISP, COBOL and ALGOL followed within three years.

efforts.note: FORTRAN, for scientific computing.
LISP, see the lisp node.

efforts.who: CODASYL committee, drawing on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC
efforts.note: COBOL, for business data processing.
Introduced block structure and formal grammar (BNF); ancestor of Pascal and C.

effort.note: Backus estimated the first FORTRAN compiler took about 18 person-years.

sources.title: Backus, The History of FORTRAN I, II and III (1978)

photolithography.summary: Printing circuit patterns onto a wafer by shining light through a mask onto a light-sensitive coating, then etching. It lets billions of devices be made at once and has driven every shrink in chip feature size since.

efforts.who: Jay Lathrop, James Nall (US Army Diamond Ordnance Fuze Laboratories)
efforts.note: Lathrop then joined Texas Instruments; Fairchild and Bell Labs developed it in parallel.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Photolithography techniques are used to make silicon devices

integrated-circuit.summary: Many transistors and other parts made together on one piece of semiconductor, wired up on the chip itself. It removed the hand-wiring bottleneck and started the exponential growth of chip complexity.

efforts.note: A germanium chip with flying gold wires, demonstrated September 12, 1958. Nobel Prize in Physics 2000.
The monolithic silicon IC built with the planar process; patented 1959, first working chips 1960. This is the form that won.
Proposed the idea publicly in 1952 but could not get it built.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, All semiconductor solid circuit is demonstrated

planar-process.summary: Building transistors into a flat silicon surface protected by a grown layer of silicon dioxide, so devices are reliable and can be wired together by a deposited metal layer. Every modern chip is made this way.

efforts.note: Built on oxide masking found by Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick at Bell Labs (1957) and Mohamed Atalla's surface passivation work.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Invention of the planar manufacturing process

mosfet.summary: The metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, switched by voltage on an insulated gate. It scales down well and uses little power, so it became the building block of nearly all modern chips.

efforts.note: Demonstrated late 1959 and presented in 1960; Bell Labs at first saw little use for it.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) transistor demonstrated

time-sharing.summary: Letting many users work interactively on one computer at once by switching rapidly between them, which created the interactive computing culture that led to networks, email and personal computers.

efforts.note: CTSS, demonstrated November 1961; John McCarthy had proposed time-sharing in 1959.

cmos.summary: Pairing complementary n-type and p-type MOS transistors so a logic gate draws almost no power except when it switches. It became the standard for digital chips from the 1980s on.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Complementary MOS circuit configuration is invented

operating-systems.summary: Software that manages a computer's memory, storage, devices and running programs so applications do not each have to. IBM's OS/360 and MIT's Multics in the mid-1960s set the template, and taught hard lessons about large software projects.

efforts.who: General Motors and North American Aviation
efforts.note: GM-NAA I/O for the IBM 704, an early batch-processing system.
OS/360, announced 1964 and shipped from 1966; the source of "The Mythical Man-Month".
Multics, which introduced many security and file-system ideas; Bell Labs left in 1969 and built Unix.

effort.note: Brooks put OS/360 at roughly 5,000 person-years, with over 1,000 people at the peak.

ibm-system-360.summary: A family of compatible computers, from small to large, that all ran the same software. It standardized the 8-bit byte and made software an asset that outlived any single machine.

efforts.who: Gene Amdahl, Fred Brooks, Gerrit Blaauw (IBM)

effort.note: Fortune called it IBM's $5 billion gamble (1960s dollars), more than IBM's annual revenue at the time.

moores-law.summary: Gordon Moore's observation that the number of components on a chip was doubling every year (revised in 1975 to every two years). It held for five decades, partly because the industry planned its roadmaps around it.

efforts.note: "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits", Electronics, April 19, 1965.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Moore's Law predicts the future of integrated circuits

packet-switching.summary: Breaking messages into small addressed packets that travel independently through a shared network and are reassembled at the end, instead of holding a dedicated circuit open. It is the basis of the internet.

efforts.note: "On Distributed Communications" (1960 to 1964), aimed at a network that could survive nuclear attack.
Coined "packet"; the NPL network ran from 1969 to 1970.
Queueing theory of message-switched networks.

arpanet.summary: The US defense research agency's packet-switched network linking university computers. The first message went from UCLA to SRI on October 29, 1969, and it grew into the core of the early internet.

efforts.who: Larry Roberts and Bob Taylor (ARPA IPTO); Frank Heart's IMP team (BBN)
efforts.note: BBN built the Interface Message Processors, the first packet routers.

effort.note: BBN's first contract, for four IMPs, was about $1 million (1968 to 1969 dollars).

sources.title: Engineering and Technology History Wiki, ARPANET
Computer History Museum, BBN's IMP and Network Operations Center team

dram.summary: Memory that stores each bit as charge on a tiny capacitor next to one transistor, refreshed thousands of times a second. It is dense and cheap, and has been computers' main working memory since the 1970s.

efforts.note: Invented the one-transistor cell in 1966; patented 1968.
The 1103, a 1-kilobit chip, the first commercial DRAM; by 1972 it was the best-selling chip in the world.

relational-database.summary: Storing data as tables queried by logical expressions, so programs ask for what they want rather than how to find it. It runs most of the world's business records through SQL.

efforts.note: "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks"; IBM System R and SEQUEL (1974), Oracle (1979).

optical-fiber.summary: Ultra-pure glass strands that carry laser light over long distances. They carry almost all intercontinental and backbone internet traffic.

efforts.who: Charles Kao, George Hockham (Standard Telecommunication Laboratories)
efforts.note: Showed that losses came from impurities and could fall below 20 dB per km. Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics.

efforts.who: Robert Maurer, Donald Keck, Peter Schultz (Corning)
efforts.note: First fiber under 20 dB per km. The first transatlantic fiber cable, TAT-8, opened in 1988.

unix.summary: A small, portable operating system and the C language it was rewritten in. Its ideas (files, pipes, small tools) live on in Linux, macOS, iOS and Android, which run most servers and phones.

efforts.note: Begun in 1969 on a PDP-7; First Edition November 1971; C in 1972; kernel rewritten in C in 1973. Turing Award 1983.

sources.title: Ritchie and Thompson, The UNIX Time-Sharing System (1974)

microprocessor.summary: A whole computer processor on one chip. Intel's 4004 (1971) had 2,300 transistors; today's largest chips have more than 100 billion.

efforts.who: Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor (Intel), Masatoshi Shima (Busicom)
efforts.note: The 4004, built for a Busicom calculator; the 8-bit 8080 (1974) made personal computers possible.
A multi-chip processor for the F-14 fighter, classified until 1998.
TMS1802 and TMS1000 single-chip calculator processors.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Microprocessor integrates CPU function onto a single chip

email.summary: Sending messages between users on different computers, with the @ sign separating user and host. It quickly became the ARPANET's most popular use.

ethernet.summary: A way for many computers to share one cable for local networking, listening for collisions and retrying. Its descendants wire nearly every office and data center.

efforts.note: Inspired by Norman Abramson's ALOHAnet radio network in Hawaii (1971). Metcalfe won the 2022 Turing Award.

graphical-user-interface.summary: Windows, icons, menus and a mouse pointer on a bitmapped screen. It made computers usable by people who would never type commands.

efforts.note: The December 1968 "Mother of All Demos" showed the mouse, hypertext and shared editing.

efforts.who: Alan Kay, Butler Lampson, Chuck Thacker and others (Xerox PARC)
efforts.note: The Xerox Alto, with a bitmapped display and windowed interface.
The Macintosh brought the GUI to the mass market; Microsoft Windows 3.0 (1990) made it dominant.

tcp-ip.summary: The pair of protocols that lets separate networks join into one network of networks, with hosts, not the network, handling reliability. It is the common language of the internet.

efforts.note: "A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication", May 1974. Turing Award 2004.

efforts.who: International Organization for Standardization and national telecoms
efforts.note: The OSI protocol suite, backed by governments, lost to TCP/IP by the early 1990s.

sources.title: Cerf and Kahn 1974, IEEE Transactions on Communications

dennard-scaling.summary: The rule that shrinking a MOSFET lets it run faster at the same power density. It made chips faster every generation until about 2005, when leakage current stopped voltage from falling and clock speeds stalled near 4 GHz.

public-key-cryptography.summary: Encryption with a public key anyone can use to lock a message and a private key only the owner can use to unlock it, so strangers can communicate securely without first sharing a secret. It secures web traffic, payments and software updates.

efforts.who: Whitfield Diffie, Martin Hellman (Stanford), building on Ralph Merkle
efforts.note: "New Directions in Cryptography", November 1976. Turing Award 2015.

efforts.who: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, Leonard Adleman (MIT)
efforts.note: RSA, the first practical public-key encryption and signature scheme. Turing Award 2002.

efforts.who: James Ellis, Clifford Cocks, Malcolm Williamson (GCHQ)
efforts.note: Discovered equivalents of RSA and Diffie-Hellman in secret from 1970 to 1974; declassified in 1997.

sources.title: Diffie and Hellman 1976, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman 1978, Communications of the ACM

personal-computer.summary: A computer cheap and small enough for one person to own. Hobby kits in 1975 were followed in 1977 by ready-made machines like the Apple II, and the IBM PC (1981) made it standard office equipment.

efforts.note: The Altair 8800 kit; Microsoft's first product was a BASIC for it.

efforts.who: Apple (Steve Wozniak, Steve Jobs), Commodore, Tandy
efforts.note: The "1977 trinity" of Apple II, Commodore PET and TRS-80.
The IBM PC, with an Intel 8088 and Microsoft DOS; its open design was cloned into the dominant platform.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, Timeline of Computer History, 1977

cellular-network.summary: Dividing an area into small cells that reuse radio frequencies and hand calls between towers as phones move. Automated networks opened in Tokyo in 1979, went digital with GSM in 1991, and reached most of humanity by the 2010s.

efforts.note: Proposed the hexagonal cell concept.
First handheld cellular call, April 3, 1973, on a DynaTAC prototype.
First commercial automated cellular network; AMPS opened in Chicago in 1983.
The digital 2G standard; 3G from 2001, 4G LTE from 2009, 5G from 2019.

risc-architecture.summary: Processors with a small set of simple, fast instructions, leaving optimization to the compiler. The low-power ARM design that came out of it is in nearly every phone and in hundreds of billions of chips.

efforts.who: David Patterson (Berkeley RISC), John Hennessy (Stanford MIPS)
efforts.note: Turing Award 2017.
ARM1. Arm licensees had shipped over 250 billion chips by the mid-2020s.

deep-uv-lithography.summary: Patterning chips with 248 nm and then 193 nm ultraviolet light from excimer lasers. With water immersion (from about 2006) and multiple patterning, 193 nm light printed features far smaller than its wavelength, down to the 7 nm class.

efforts.note: Demonstrated excimer laser lithography; KrF (248 nm) tools reached volume production in the 1990s.
193 nm immersion scanners, first used in volume at the 45 nm node around 2007; ASML took most of the market.

internet.summary: The global network of networks, which began when the ARPANET switched to TCP/IP on January 1, 1983. Opened to commercial traffic in 1995, it connected about three quarters of humanity by 2025.

efforts.who: ARPA, then the US National Science Foundation (NSFNET, 1986)
efforts.note: NSFNET's backbone was retired in 1995 as commercial providers took over.
Minitel, a centralized videotext network with millions of users, shut down in 2012.

sources.title: Internet Society, Brief History of the Internet

flash-memory.summary: Chip memory that keeps data with the power off and can be erased in large blocks at once. NAND flash replaced film, floppies and much of the hard disk, and made phones and solid-state drives possible.

efforts.note: NOR flash presented 1984 and NAND flash 1987; Intel shipped the first commercial NOR chip in 1988.

world-wide-web.summary: Linked hypertext pages addressed by URLs and fetched over HTTP, readable in a browser on any computer. Released freely by CERN, it turned the internet into a mass medium within a few years.

efforts.note: Proposed March 1989; first server running late 1990; public August 1991; put in the public domain April 1993. Turing Award 2016.
Gopher, a menu-based system, faded after the university sought license fees in 1993.
Mosaic, the browser that made the web popular; Netscape followed in 1994.

search-engines.summary: Crawling and indexing the whole web and ranking results, so anyone can find pages by typing words. Google's PageRank (1998) ranked pages by the links pointing to them.

efforts.who: Larry Page, Sergey Brin (Stanford, then Google)

gpu.summary: A chip with many small cores doing the same math on lots of data at once, built to draw 3D graphics for games. That same parallelism later made it the engine of deep learning.

efforts.note: GeForce 256, marketed as the first GPU because it did transform and lighting on the chip.
3dfx Voodoo cards (1996) and SGI workstations came first; ATI became AMD's graphics division.

itanium.summary: Intel and HP's 64-bit processor family that relied on the compiler to schedule instructions in parallel (EPIC). It was meant to replace x86 but lost to AMD's backward-compatible x86-64 and was discontinued.

efforts.note: First shipped May 2001; last shipments in 2021.

itanium.lost: Compilers could not extract the parallelism the design depended on, x86 software ran slowly on it, and AMD's x86-64 gave 64 bits without breaking compatibility. Intel adopted x86-64 in 2004, and Itanium faded to a niche in HP servers until it ended in 2021.

x86-64.summary: AMD's 64-bit extension of the x86 instruction set, which ran old software unchanged. Intel adopted it, and it still runs most PCs and servers.

efforts.note: The Opteron, April 2003; Intel shipped its compatible version in 2004.

multicore-processors.summary: Putting several processor cores on one chip once clock speeds stopped rising. More speed now had to come from parallel software.

efforts.note: POWER4, the first commercial dual-core processor.
Athlon 64 X2 and Pentium D brought dual cores to desktops.

cloud-computing.summary: Renting computing, storage and software over the internet by the hour from huge shared data centers instead of owning machines. It let small teams scale instantly and later hosted most AI training and serving.

efforts.note: S3 storage launched March 2006 and EC2 servers in August 2006.
Google App Engine (2008) and Microsoft Azure (2010).

sources.title: AWS, Announcing Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (2006)

gpu-computing.summary: Programming graphics chips for general math in an ordinary language. Nvidia's CUDA (2007) made thousands of GPU cores easy to use for science, and five years later for training neural networks.

efforts.who: Ian Buck and team (Nvidia), building on Buck's Brook language at Stanford (2004)
efforts.note: Announced November 2006 and released June 2007.
OpenCL, an open standard that never matched CUDA's software ecosystem.

smartphone.summary: A pocket computer with a touchscreen, mobile internet, camera, GPS and app store. The iPhone (2007) and Android (2008) put the internet in the hands of most adults on Earth within about 15 years.

efforts.note: The iPhone, announced January 9 and released June 29, 2007; the App Store opened in 2008.
Android, open-source, now on most of the world's phones.

efforts.who: IBM and BellSouth; Nokia; Research In Motion
efforts.note: IBM Simon (1994), Nokia Communicator (1996) and BlackBerry (from 2002) came first; Nokia and BlackBerry lost the market after 2010.

cryptocurrency.summary: A digital currency with no central issuer, kept honest by a shared ledger that miners extend by spending computation (proof of work). It started a large and volatile industry of cryptocurrencies.

efforts.note: White paper October 31, 2008; first block January 3, 2009.

sources.title: Nakamoto 2008, Bitcoin, A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System

finfet.summary: Transistors whose channel is a thin vertical fin wrapped by the gate on three sides, which cut leakage as planar transistors hit their limits. They carried chipmaking from 22 nm down to the 3 nm class.

efforts.who: Digh Hisamoto (Hitachi); Chenming Hu, Tsu-Jae King Liu, Jeffrey Bokor (UC Berkeley)
efforts.note: Hitachi's DELTA transistor (1989) and Berkeley's FinFET (1999).
First volume FinFETs ("Tri-Gate") at 22 nm, announced May 2011, shipped in 2012.

advanced-packaging.summary: Stacking memory dies and placing several chips side by side on a silicon interposer so they talk at very high bandwidth. HBM stacks and TSMC's CoWoS packaging became a key bottleneck for AI chips in 2023 to 2026.

efforts.note: SK hynix made the first HBM in 2013; AMD's Fiji GPU (2015) was the first product to use it.
CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate), used for most AI accelerators; AMD's chiplet CPUs followed from 2019.

euv-lithography.summary: Printing chips with 13.5 nm light made by hitting droplets of molten tin with a laser about 50,000 times a second, focused by mirrors in a vacuum. One Dutch company, ASML, makes the machines, which print the most advanced chips.

efforts.who: Hiroo Kinoshita (NTT); US national labs in the EUV LLC consortium (1997 to 2003)
efforts.note: Early soft X-ray projection lithography research.

efforts.who: ASML, with Zeiss (optics) and Cymer (light source), co-funded by Intel, TSMC and Samsung
efforts.note: Samsung's 7LPP (late 2018) and TSMC's N7+ (2019) were the first volume EUV processes.
Dropped out of EUV development.

effort.note: Rough order of magnitude. ASML's customer co-investment program alone raised about 1.4 billion euros of R&D funding in 2012. A production EUV scanner costs about $180 million; a leading-edge fab using them costs about $20 to 28 billion.

gate-all-around.summary: Transistors whose channel is a stack of thin horizontal sheets with the gate wrapped all the way around, the successor to FinFETs at the 2 to 3 nm nodes.

efforts.note: First production at 3 nm, June 2022.
N2 entered volume production in the fourth quarter of 2025.
18A, with RibbonFET transistors and backside power delivery (PowerVia).

effort.note: Consulting firm IBS estimated a 2 nm fab of 50,000 wafers a month at about $28 billion.

sources.title: Gigazine, TSMC quietly begins mass production of 2nm semiconductors (2026)
TechSpot, A 2nm-capable wafer fab will come with a $28 billion tag

high-na-euv.summary: EUV scanners with larger-aperture optics (numerical aperture 0.55) that print finer lines in one exposure. Each costs about $380 million; Intel, Samsung and SK hynix have bought them, while TSMC plans to skip them for its A14 node.
high-na-euv.criterion: High-NA EUV is used for at least one layer in high-volume manufacturing of a commercial chip.

efforts.note: First EXE:5000 to Intel in December 2023; first production-grade EXE:5200 shipped in 2025 (about 175 wafers an hour).
Finished acceptance of an EXE:5200B for its 14A node in December 2025; risk production 2027, volume 2028.
Both target High-NA in DRAM production by 2028.
Sticking with standard EUV and multiple patterning for A14.

forecast.note: No one was using High-NA in volume production by October 2026. Intel's 14A and the memory makers all point to 2027 to 2028, so 2028 is the likely first use in a product.

sources.title: TrendForce, Samsung and SK hynix set High-NA EUV timelines for DRAM (2026)
TrendForce, ASML confirms first EXE:5200 shipment (2025)
Tom's Hardware, ASML's roadmap for chipmaking lithography tools examined
DigiTimes, Intel completes High-NA EUV acceptance (2025)

mcculloch-pitts-neuron.summary: The first mathematical model of a neuron as a threshold logic unit, showing that networks of such units can compute any logical function. It is the common ancestor of neural networks and of von Neumann's computer design.

efforts.who: Warren McCulloch, Walter Pitts (University of Illinois, University of Chicago)
efforts.note: "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity". Donald Hebb added a learning rule in 1949.

sources.title: McCulloch and Pitts 1943, Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics

turing-test.summary: Alan Turing's proposal to judge machine intelligence by whether a machine can pass as human in text conversation. It framed the goal of AI for decades; large language models passed controlled versions of it by 2025.

efforts.note: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", Mind. In a 2025 UC San Diego study, GPT-4.5 with a persona prompt was judged human 73% of the time.

sources.title: Turing 1950, Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Mind
Jones and Bergen 2025, Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test

dartmouth-workshop.summary: A summer 1956 workshop at Dartmouth College whose 1955 proposal coined the term "artificial intelligence" and claimed every aspect of intelligence could in principle be simulated by a machine. It founded AI as a research field.

efforts.who: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, Claude Shannon
efforts.note: Ran about eight weeks, June 18 to August 17, 1956, funded by the Rockefeller Foundation; only McCarthy, Minsky and Ray Solomonoff stayed throughout.

symbolic-ai.summary: Building intelligence by manipulating explicit symbols with logical rules and search, as in theorem provers, planners and chess programs. It was the dominant approach to AI from 1956 to the late 1980s, in rivalry with neural networks.

efforts.who: Allen Newell, Herbert Simon, Cliff Shaw (RAND, Carnegie Tech)
efforts.note: Logic Theorist proved 38 of the first 52 theorems of Principia Mathematica; the General Problem Solver followed in 1957.
Stated the physical symbol system hypothesis; Turing Award 1975.

perceptron.summary: Frank Rosenblatt's learning machine, which adjusts the weights of artificial neurons from examples until it classifies inputs correctly. It was the first neural network that learned, and the start of the connectionist tradition behind modern AI.

efforts.who: Frank Rosenblatt (Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory), funded by the US Office of Naval Research
efforts.note: First simulated on an IBM 704 (1957 report, 1958 paper); the Mark I Perceptron hardware used a 20 by 20 grid of photocells.
ADALINE and the least-mean-squares rule, still used in signal processing.

effort.note: Epoch estimates the Mark I Perceptron's training at about 700,000 FLOP.

lisp.summary: John McCarthy's language built on lists and recursive functions, which introduced garbage collection and code that can treat itself as data. It was the main language of AI research for about 30 years.

efforts.note: Paper 1960; Steve Russell wrote the first interpreter. McCarthy won the 1971 Turing Award.

sources.title: McCarthy 1960, Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions

perceptrons-book-limits.summary: Minsky and Papert proved that single-layer perceptrons cannot compute simple functions such as XOR or parity. With the UK Lighthill report (1973) and US defense cuts, it led to the first AI winter of roughly 1974 to 1980, when funding for neural nets and much of AI dried up.

efforts.note: The book "Perceptrons". Multi-layer networks could solve these problems, but no one yet knew how to train them.

efforts.who: James Lighthill (for the UK Science Research Council)
efforts.note: The Lighthill report criticized AI's failure to reach its goals and UK funding was cut.

reverse-mode-autodiff.summary: A method for computing the gradient of a function with respect to millions of inputs at about the cost of evaluating it once, by applying the chain rule backward through the computation. Backpropagation is its special case for neural nets, and PyTorch and JAX are built on it.

efforts.note: Master's thesis on cumulative rounding error; Bert Speelpenning's 1980 thesis made it a practical tool.

expert-systems.summary: Programs that capture a specialist's knowledge as hundreds or thousands of if-then rules. They were AI's first commercial success in the early 1980s, but proved brittle and costly to maintain, and the bust that followed (about 1987 to 1993) was the second AI winter.

efforts.who: Edward Feigenbaum, Joshua Lederberg, Bruce Buchanan (Stanford)
efforts.note: DENDRAL, inferring molecular structure from mass spectra.
MYCIN diagnosed blood infections about as well as specialists but was never used clinically.

efforts.who: John McDermott (Carnegie Mellon) for Digital Equipment Corporation
efforts.note: XCON (R1) configured VAX orders and was reported to save DEC tens of millions of dollars a year.

lisp-machines.summary: Workstations with hardware built to run LISP fast, sold to AI labs and companies during the expert-system boom. The market collapsed in 1987, a marker of the second AI winter.

efforts.who: Richard Greenblatt, Tom Knight (MIT AI Lab)
efforts.note: The CADR machine; spun out as Symbolics and Lisp Machines Inc. in 1979 to 1980.
Revenue collapsed after 1987; bankrupt in 1993. Symbolics.com was the first registered .com domain (1985).

lisp-machines.lost: General-purpose workstations from Sun and others, and then PCs, ran LISP well enough at a fraction of the price, while the expert-system market they served shrank. Their integrated development environments were admired and not matched for years.

neocognitron.summary: A layered neural network for recognizing shapes, with alternating feature and pooling layers modeled on the visual cortex cells found by Hubel and Wiesel. It is the direct ancestor of convolutional networks, but it was not trained by backpropagation.

efforts.who: Kunihiko Fukushima (NHK Science and Technology Research Laboratories)

fifth-generation-project.summary: Japan's government program to build massively parallel logic-programming computers for AI. It alarmed the US and Europe into rival programs, but produced little commercial value and ended as specialized hardware was overtaken by ordinary chips.

efforts.note: Ran 1982 to about 1994 and built five Parallel Inference Machines based on Prolog-style logic programming.

efforts.who: UK Alvey Programme, US MCC consortium, EU ESPRIT

effort.note: Just under 57 billion yen, about $320 million at the time.

fifth-generation-project.lost: Its premise that logic programming on special parallel machines was the road to AI turned out wrong; commodity processors improved faster and statistical methods took over. MITI stopped funding large computer projects afterward.

hopfield-network.summary: Neural networks described by an energy function, borrowed from the physics of magnets, that settle into stored memories. Boltzmann machines (1985) added randomness and a learning rule, and the work won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.

efforts.who: David Ackley, Geoffrey Hinton, Terrence Sejnowski (Carnegie Mellon, Johns Hopkins)
efforts.note: The Boltzmann machine.

backpropagation.summary: Training a multi-layer neural network by sending the error backward through the layers to compute how each weight should change, then taking a small gradient step. Shown to learn useful internal representations in 1986, it still trains nearly every neural network.

efforts.who: David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, Ronald Williams (UC San Diego, Carnegie Mellon)
efforts.note: "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", Nature, October 1986.
Proposed it for neural networks in his PhD thesis; little noticed.

efforts.who: Shun-ichi Amari; David Parker; Yann LeCun
efforts.note: Amari trained multi-layer nets by gradient descent in 1967; Parker and LeCun found versions of backprop in 1985.

effort.note: Epoch puts the 1986 experiments at about 7e8 FLOP.

bayesian-networks.summary: Representing uncertain knowledge as a graph of variables with probability tables, and reasoning by Bayes' rule. It replaced brittle certainty factors in expert systems and led to the statistical turn in AI.

efforts.note: Named in 1985; the book "Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems" (1988). Turing Award 2011, which also cited his work on causal inference.

reinforcement-learning.summary: Learning to act by trial and error from rewards, estimating how good each situation and action is and improving the policy. Temporal-difference learning (1988) and Q-learning (1989) made it practical, and it now trains game players, robots and reasoning language models.

efforts.note: Dynamic programming and the Bellman equation.
A checkers program that improved by self-play; Samuel popularized the term "machine learning".
Temporal-difference learning; their 1998 textbook defined the field. Turing Award 2024.
Q-learning.
TD-Gammon reached near world-class backgammon by self-play with a small neural net.

sources.title: Sutton 1988, Learning to predict by the methods of temporal differences, Machine Learning
Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, An Introduction (2nd ed.)

convolutional-networks.summary: Neural networks that slide the same small learned filters across an image, so they detect a feature anywhere with few parameters. Trained by backprop, they read handwritten digits in 1989 and drove the deep learning breakthrough in vision in 2012.

efforts.who: Yann LeCun and colleagues (AT&T Bell Labs)
efforts.note: Read handwritten zip codes; LeNet-5 (1998) was used to read a large share of US bank checks around 2000.
The time-delay neural network applied shared weights to speech.

effort.note: Epoch estimates the 1989 zip-code network at about 1.5e12 FLOP.

sources.title: LeCun et al. 1989, Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition, Neural Computation
LeCun et al. 1998, Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition

support-vector-machines.summary: Classifiers that find the widest-margin boundary between classes, using a kernel to work in a high-dimensional feature space. Backed by learning theory, they outperformed neural nets on many tasks from the mid-1990s until about 2012.

efforts.who: Bernhard Boser, Isabelle Guyon, Vladimir Vapnik (AT&T Bell Labs)
efforts.note: The kernel trick for maximum-margin classifiers.

efforts.who: Corinna Cortes, Vladimir Vapnik (AT&T Bell Labs)
efforts.note: Soft-margin "support-vector networks". Random forests (Breiman, 2001) and boosting were other strong rivals.

sources.title: Cortes and Vapnik 1995, Support-vector networks, Machine Learning

lstm.summary: A recurrent neural network with gated memory cells that can carry information across long sequences, fixing the vanishing gradient problem. It ran most speech recognition and machine translation from about 2015 until transformers replaced it.

efforts.who: Sepp Hochreiter, Jurgen Schmidhuber (TU Munich, IDSIA)
efforts.note: Hochreiter analyzed vanishing gradients in his 1991 thesis; the forget gate was added by Felix Gers and colleagues in 1999 to 2000.

efforts.who: Alex Graves and others (IDSIA, Toronto, Google)
efforts.note: CTC training (2006) enabled LSTM speech recognition, deployed in Google voice search in 2015.

sources.title: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997, Long Short-Term Memory, Neural Computation

deep-blue.summary: IBM's chess computer, which beat world champion Garry Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5 in May 1997. It won by brute-force search of about 200 million positions a second on custom chips, with a hand-tuned evaluation, not by learning.

efforts.who: Feng-hsiung Hsu, Murray Campbell, Joe Hoane and team (IBM Research)
efforts.note: Grew from Hsu's ChipTest and Deep Thought at Carnegie Mellon (1985 to 1989); the 1997 machine had 480 custom chess chips.

deep-belief-networks.summary: Training deep networks one layer at a time as unsupervised models before fine-tuning with backprop. It revived interest in deep networks and the name "deep learning", then was dropped after 2012 once better activations, initialization and GPUs let plain backprop work.

efforts.who: Geoffrey Hinton, Simon Osindero, Yee-Whye Teh (University of Toronto)
efforts.note: Funded in part by the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, which kept neural net research alive in the 2000s.
Stacked autoencoders and other layer-wise schemes.

sources.title: Hinton, Osindero and Teh 2006, A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets, Neural Computation

imagenet.summary: A dataset of millions of labeled photos in thousands of categories and an annual recognition contest (2010 to 2017). It showed that large data could matter as much as algorithms and became the proving ground for deep learning.

efforts.who: Fei-Fei Li, Jia Deng, Kai Li and colleagues (Princeton, Stanford)
efforts.note: Built on the WordNet hierarchy of categories; the contest used 1.2 million images in 1,000 classes.

effort.note: About 14 million images were labeled by roughly 49,000 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers in 167 countries.

sources.title: Deng et al. 2009, ImageNet, A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database (CVPR)

deep-learning.summary: Training large many-layered neural networks on GPUs with big datasets. In 2012 AlexNet cut the ImageNet error rate from about 26% to 15%, and within a few years deep networks took over vision, speech, translation and much of science.

efforts.who: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton (University of Toronto)
efforts.note: AlexNet, 60 million parameters, trained for about a week on two GeForce GTX 580 gaming GPUs; used ReLU and dropout. Their startup was bought by Google in 2013.

efforts.who: Hinton's group with Microsoft, Google and IBM
efforts.note: Deep networks for speech recognition (2009 to 2012) were the first big industrial win.
GPU-trained CNNs won several image contests in 2011 to 2012 before AlexNet.

effort.note: Epoch estimates AlexNet at 4.7e17 FLOP and about $16 of compute (2023 dollars). Hinton, LeCun and Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award.

word-embeddings.summary: Representing each word as a learned vector so that words used in similar contexts sit close together, with directions that capture meaning (king minus man plus woman lands near queen). Learned token embeddings are the input layer of every language model.

efforts.note: A neural probabilistic language model that learned word vectors.
word2vec, fast enough to train on billions of words.

efforts.who: Jeffrey Pennington, Richard Socher, Christopher Manning (Stanford)
efforts.note: GloVe, based on global co-occurrence counts.

sources.title: Mikolov et al. 2013, Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

deep-reinforcement-learning.summary: Combining reinforcement learning with deep networks that learn straight from raw input. DeepMind's DQN learned dozens of Atari games from screen pixels and score alone.

efforts.who: Volodymyr Mnih, Koray Kavukcuoglu, David Silver and colleagues (DeepMind)
efforts.note: Preprint December 2013; Nature paper on 49 games in 2015. Google bought DeepMind in January 2014, reportedly for about $500 million or more.

sources.title: Mnih et al. 2013, Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning

gans.summary: Training a generator network to fool a discriminator network that tries to tell real data from fakes. GANs made the first photorealistic synthetic faces, then were largely replaced by diffusion models for images after 2021.

efforts.who: Ian Goodfellow and colleagues (University of Montreal)
Diederik Kingma, Max Welling (University of Amsterdam)
efforts.note: The variational autoencoder, a rival generative model whose encoder later became part of latent diffusion.
StyleGAN, the peak of GAN image quality.

sources.title: Goodfellow et al. 2014, Generative Adversarial Networks

attention-mechanism.summary: Encoding one sequence with a neural network and decoding another from it, with an attention step that lets the decoder look back at the most relevant input positions. It made neural machine translation work and was the seed of the transformer.

efforts.who: Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, Quoc Le (Google)
efforts.note: Sequence-to-sequence LSTMs, about 5.6e19 FLOP per Epoch.

efforts.who: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, Yoshua Bengio (Montreal)
efforts.note: Additive attention for translation.
GNMT replaced phrase-based statistical translation in Google Translate in September 2016.

sources.title: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio 2014, Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
Sutskever, Vinyals and Le 2014, Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

residual-networks.summary: Adding shortcut connections so each layer learns a change to its input, which let networks grow to over 100 layers and still train. Residual connections, together with batch normalization and the Adam optimizer from the same years, are in nearly every modern model, including transformers.

efforts.who: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun (Microsoft Research Asia)
efforts.note: A 152-layer ResNet won ImageNet 2015 with 3.57% top-5 error.

efforts.who: Rupesh Srivastava, Klaus Greff, Jurgen Schmidhuber (IDSIA)
efforts.note: Highway networks, gated shortcuts published months earlier.

sources.title: He et al. 2015, Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

alphago.summary: DeepMind's Go program, which combined deep networks for move choice and position value with tree search, and beat Lee Sedol 4 to 1 in March 2016, a decade earlier than many expected. Its successors learned Go, chess and shogi from self-play alone.

efforts.who: David Silver, Aja Huang, Demis Hassabis and colleagues (DeepMind)
efforts.note: Beat Fan Hui 5 to 0 in October 2015, then Lee Sedol in Seoul in March 2016.
AlphaGo Zero (October 2017) learned with no human games; AlphaZero (December 2017) generalized to chess and shogi; MuZero (2019) learned its own model of the rules.
Darkforest and Fine Art (Jueyi) were strong rival Go programs.

effort.note: Epoch estimates AlphaGo Lee at about 1.9e21 FLOP (speculative) and AlphaGo Zero at about 6.5e20 FLOP.

sources.title: Silver et al. 2016, Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search, Nature
Silver et al. 2017, Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge, Nature

ai-accelerators.summary: Chips built for the dense matrix math of neural networks, with low-precision arithmetic units and very fast memory. Google's TPU (2016) and Nvidia's tensor-core GPUs from 2017 on became the industrial base of modern AI.

efforts.note: TPU v1, in Google's data centers since 2015 and announced May 2016; TPU v7 Ironwood in 2025.
V100 tensor cores (2017), A100 (2020), H100 (2022), Blackwell B200 and GB200 (2024 to 2025); Vera Rubin began shipping in the second half of 2026.

efforts.who: AMD, AWS (Trainium), Huawei (Ascend), Cerebras (wafer-scale), Groq and others
efforts.note: Huawei's Ascend became China's main alternative under US export controls.

sources.title: Jouppi et al. 2017, In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit

transformer.summary: A neural network built entirely from attention, in which every position in a sequence looks directly at every other, with no recurrence. It parallelizes well on accelerators and scales with data and compute, and is the architecture of nearly all large language, vision and protein models.

efforts.who: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin (Google Brain and Google Research)
efforts.note: "Attention Is All You Need", June 2017. All eight authors later left Google, several to found companies.

efforts.who: Albert Gu, Tri Dao and others
efforts.note: State-space models such as Mamba, used in some hybrid architectures but not displacing attention at the frontier.

effort.note: The big model trained for 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs, about 7.4e18 FLOP and $440 of compute per Epoch.

sources.title: Vaswani et al. 2017, Attention Is All You Need

mixture-of-experts.summary: Splitting a network's layers into many expert sub-networks and routing each token to only a few, so a model can have trillions of parameters while using a small fraction per token. Most frontier and open models of 2024 to 2026 are built this way.

efforts.who: Robert Jacobs, Michael Jordan, Steven Nowlan, Geoffrey Hinton
efforts.note: Adaptive mixtures of local experts.
The sparsely gated MoE layer; then GShard (2020) and Switch Transformer (2021).
Mixtral (December 2023); DeepSeek-V3 (671 billion total, 37 billion active parameters, 2024); DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6 trillion total, 49 billion active, 2026).

sources.title: Shazeer et al. 2017, Outrageously Large Neural Networks

rlhf.summary: Training a reward model on human judgments of which of two outputs is better, then optimizing a policy against it. Applied to language models in 2020 to 2022, it turned raw text predictors into helpful assistants.

efforts.who: Paul Christiano, Jan Leike and colleagues (OpenAI and DeepMind)
efforts.note: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences, demonstrated on simulated robots and Atari.
InstructGPT; labelers preferred a 1.3 billion parameter RLHF model to the 175 billion parameter GPT-3. Followed Stiennon et al. on summarization (2020).
Constitutional AI, using AI feedback guided by written principles (RLAIF).
Direct preference optimization (DPO), which skips the separate reward model.

sources.title: Christiano et al. 2017, Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
Ouyang et al. 2022, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

generative-pretraining.summary: Pretraining a transformer to predict the next word on large amounts of text, then adapting it to tasks. GPT-2 (2019) showed that scale alone produced fluent text and some zero-shot ability.

efforts.who: Alec Radford, Ilya Sutskever and colleagues (OpenAI)
efforts.note: GPT-1 (June 2018, 117 million parameters); GPT-2 (February 2019, 1.5 billion), released in stages over misuse concerns.

efforts.who: Jeremy Howard, Sebastian Ruder (fast.ai); Matthew Peters and colleagues (Allen Institute for AI)
efforts.note: ULMFiT and ELMo showed pretrained language models transfer to many tasks.

sources.title: Radford et al. 2018, Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
Radford et al. 2019, Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners

bert.summary: Google's bidirectional transformer encoder, pretrained by filling in masked words. It set records on most language-understanding benchmarks and entered Google Search in 2019; its approach spread to biology as protein and DNA language models.

efforts.who: Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova (Google)
efforts.note: 340 million parameters. RoBERTa (Meta) and T5 (Google) followed in 2019.

effort.note: About 2.9e20 FLOP on 64 TPU v2 chips over four days, about $1,750 per Epoch.

scaling-laws.summary: The finding that language model loss falls as a smooth power law in model size, data and compute across many orders of magnitude. It let labs predict the payoff of bigger runs and justified spending billions on them.

efforts.who: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and colleagues (OpenAI)
efforts.note: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models", January 2020. Several authors later co-founded Anthropic.
Found predictable power-law scaling across translation, speech and vision in 2017.

sources.title: Kaplan et al. 2020, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
Hestness et al. 2017, Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically

large-language-models.summary: Transformers with billions of parameters trained to predict the next token on much of the public internet. GPT-3 (2020) showed that such a model can do new tasks from a few examples in its prompt, with no retraining.

efforts.who: Tom Brown, Dario Amodei and colleagues (OpenAI, on Microsoft Azure)
efforts.note: GPT-3, 175 billion parameters, 300 billion tokens, May 2020.
LaMDA (2021) and PaLM (540 billion parameters, 2.5e24 FLOP, April 2022).

efforts.who: DeepMind; Microsoft and Nvidia; Meta; BigScience; Baidu
efforts.note: Gopher (280 billion), Megatron-Turing NLG (530 billion), OPT, BLOOM and ERNIE, 2021 to 2022.

effort.note: GPT-3 used about 3.1e23 FLOP on V100 GPUs, about $2.1 million of compute in 2023 dollars per Epoch (other estimates run to $4.6 million).

sources.title: Brown et al. 2020, Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

diffusion-models.summary: Generating data by learning to reverse a process that gradually adds noise, starting from pure noise and denoising step by step. Since 2020 they have produced the best images, video and audio, and are used for molecule and protein design.

efforts.note: Proposed diffusion probabilistic models, inspired by nonequilibrium thermodynamics.
Score-based generative modeling; unified with diffusion as stochastic differential equations in 2020.

efforts.who: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, Pieter Abbeel (UC Berkeley)
efforts.note: DDPM, the paper that made diffusion competitive with GANs.

efforts.who: Robin Rombach, Bjorn Ommer and colleagues (LMU Munich, Runway)
efforts.note: Latent diffusion, the basis of Stable Diffusion; flow matching (2022) became a common variant.

sources.title: Ho, Jain and Abbeel 2020, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015, Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics

multimodal-models.summary: Models that learn from and produce several kinds of data, such as text, images, audio and video, in one network. CLIP (2021) linked images and text, and by 2024 frontier assistants could see, listen and speak in real time.

efforts.note: CLIP, trained on 400 million image-caption pairs; the Vision Transformer (Google, 2020) showed transformers work on images.
Flamingo, a visual language model.
GPT-4 with vision (2023); Gemini 1.0 trained natively multimodal (December 2023); GPT-4o with native speech (May 2024).

sources.title: Radford et al. 2021, Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
Gemini Team 2023, Gemini, A Family of Highly Capable Multimodal Models

ai-coding-assistants.summary: Language models trained on public code that complete, write and fix programs. They went from autocomplete in 2021 to agents that carry out multi-hour software tasks by 2025 to 2026, and became the largest commercial use of AI.

efforts.note: Codex and GitHub Copilot (preview June 2021).
AlphaCode reached about median human level in programming contests.
Claude Code (February 2025), OpenAI Codex agent (May 2025), Cursor's in-house Composer models (2025 to 2026), Gemini CLI.

sources.title: Chen et al. 2021, Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code

chinchilla-scaling.summary: DeepMind's finding that for a fixed compute budget, models should be trained on far more data than earlier practice, about 20 tokens per parameter. Its 70 billion parameter Chinchilla beat the 280 billion parameter Gopher using the same compute.

efforts.who: Jordan Hoffmann, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Laurent Sifre and colleagues (DeepMind)
efforts.note: Chinchilla, 70 billion parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens, about 5.8e23 FLOP. Later models trained even longer than this optimum to cut inference cost, such as Llama 3 8B on 15 trillion tokens.

sources.title: Hoffmann et al. 2022, Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models

generative-media.summary: Models that make images, and then video with sound, from a text prompt. In 2022 DALL-E 2, Midjourney and the open Stable Diffusion brought them to millions of users, and video models followed from 2024.

efforts.note: DALL-E (January 2021), DALL-E 2 (April 2022), Sora (preview February 2024).
Stable Diffusion, open weights, August 2022, about 5e22 FLOP and $110,000 of compute per Epoch.
Midjourney (open beta July 2022); Google's Imagen (May 2022) and Veo 3 (May 2025, video with synchronized audio).

sources.title: Rombach et al. 2021, High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

chatgpt.summary: A language model tuned with RLHF to follow instructions in conversation, offered free on the web on November 30, 2022. It became the fastest-growing consumer app in history and made AI a mass technology.

efforts.note: Built on GPT-3.5. An estimated 100 million users within two months; OpenAI reported 800 million weekly users in October 2025.
Bard (later Gemini), Claude and Ernie Bot all launched in March 2023.

efforts.who: Meta, xAI, DeepSeek, Mistral, Alibaba, Moonshot and others
efforts.note: Meta AI, Grok, the DeepSeek app (top of app stores in January 2025), Le Chat, Qwen and Kimi.

frontier-models.summary: The most capable general models, trained with 1e25 FLOP or more from 2023 and near 1e27 FLOP by 2026, each costing tens to hundreds of millions of dollars to train. A handful of labs in the US and China leapfrog each other every few months.

efforts.note: GPT-4 (March 2023, about 2.1e25 FLOP on about 25,000 A100s, per Epoch); GPT-4.5 (February 2025, about 3.8e26 FLOP); GPT-5 (August 2025); GPT-6 Astra (September 3, 2026, about 9.4e26 FLOP on at least 100,000 GB200s in Abilene, Texas, per Epoch; first model rated "Critical" for cybersecurity under OpenAI's framework).

Claude (March 2023), Claude 3 Opus (March 2024), Claude 4 (May 2025), Opus 4.6 and 4.8 (2026); Claude Mythos Preview (April 2026) was withheld from public release for its cyberattack ability and shared with defenders through Project Glasswing; Claude Fable 5 (June 2026) and the 5.1 and 5.5 models (September to October 2026) followed.
Gemini 1.0 Ultra (December 2023, about 5e25 FLOP per Epoch, speculative), Gemini 2.5 Pro (2025), Gemini 3 Pro (November 2025); Gemini 4 was in post-training as of late September 2026.
Grok 3 (February 2025, about 3.5e26 FLOP on 80,000 H100s) and Grok 4 (July 2025, about 5e26 FLOP, speculative); Grok 4.7 (September 2026).
Llama 3.1 405B (July 2024, 3.8e25 FLOP on 16,384 H100s), the largest openly disclosed run of 2024; Llama 4 (April 2025) disappointed and Meta reorganized its AI effort.

effort.note: Epoch's amortized compute costs (2023 dollars) are about $37 million for GPT-4, $30 million for Gemini 1.0 Ultra, $53 million for Llama 3.1 405B, $366 million for GPT-4.5 and $390 million for Grok 4 (speculative); total development costs are several times higher. Frontier training cost has grown about 2.4 times a year since 2016. Technical reports list hundreds (GPT-4) to over a thousand (Gemini) contributors.

sources.title: Cottier et al. 2024, The rising costs of training frontier AI models
Constellation Research, OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra

open-weight-llms.summary: Large models whose trained weights are published for anyone to run and modify. Led first by Meta and then by Chinese labs such as DeepSeek and Alibaba, they trail the closed frontier by months rather than years.

efforts.note: LLaMA (February 2023, weights leaked within a week), Llama 2 (July 2023, commercial use allowed), Llama 3 (2024).
Mistral 7B (September 2023) and Mixtral (December 2023).

DeepSeek-V3 (December 2024, final run on 2,048 H800s for about $5.6 million) and R1 (January 2025), after which Nvidia lost about $590 billion of market value in one day; V4 (April 2026), adapted to Huawei Ascend chips.

efforts.who: Alibaba (Qwen), Moonshot (Kimi), Zhipu (GLM), OpenAI (gpt-oss, August 2025), Nvidia (Nemotron)

effort.note: Epoch puts DeepSeek-V3 at 3.3e24 FLOP and about $5.4 million, the final run only; DeepSeek's total hardware investment was far larger.

reasoning-models.summary: Language models trained by reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers to think in long chains of thought before replying. Their accuracy grows with thinking time, adding a second scaling axis (test-time compute) and large gains in math and coding.

efforts.who: Jason Wei and colleagues (Google); Takeshi Kojima and colleagues (Tokyo, Google)
efforts.note: Chain-of-thought prompting and "let's think step by step" showed models reason better when they write out steps.
o1-preview (September 12, 2024) and o3 (announced December 2024, scoring 75.7% to 87.5% on ARC-AGI-1; released April 2025).
R1 (January 20, 2025) published the recipe, RL with verifiable rewards using GRPO; R1-Zero showed reasoning emerging from RL alone. Its Nature paper put the RL stage at about $294,000.
Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking (December 2024) and Deep Think, Claude 3.7 Sonnet extended thinking (February 2025), Grok 3 Think, QwQ and Qwen3.

sources.title: Wei et al. 2022, Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
OpenAI, Learning to reason with LLMs

ai-mathematics.summary: AI systems that solve hard competition problems and contribute to research math. In July 2025 general reasoning models from Google DeepMind and OpenAI reached gold-medal scores at the International Mathematical Olympiad.

efforts.note: AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 scored 28 of 42 (silver) at IMO 2024 using formal Lean proofs; AlphaEvolve (May 2025) found improved algorithms, including 4 by 4 complex matrix multiplication with 48 multiplications.
Gemini Deep Think and an experimental OpenAI model each scored 35 of 42 at IMO 2025, in natural language within the time limits.

sources.title: Google DeepMind, AI achieves silver-medal standard solving IMO problems

ai-agents.summary: Language models that act on their own over many steps, using tools, code, browsers and whole computers to finish tasks. The length of software task they finish half the time grew from about an hour (early 2025) to about 12 to 17 hours of expert work (2026), doubling about every four months.

efforts.note: ReAct, interleaving reasoning and tool use.
Computer use (October 2024), the Model Context Protocol for tools (November 2024), Claude Code (February 2025).
Operator (January 2025), Deep Research (February 2025), Codex (May 2025), ChatGPT agent (July 2025).

efforts.who: Google DeepMind, xAI, Moonshot, Cursor, Cognition and many startups

effort.note: METR's 50 percent time horizon crossed 1 hour with Claude 3.7 Sonnet (February 2025) and 8 hours with Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026, about 12 hours); an early Claude Mythos Preview measured about 17 hours (April 2026). Since 2023 it has doubled about every 130 days. METR says its tasks cannot measure reliably above about 16 hours.

sources.title: Kwa et al. 2025 (METR), Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks
METR, benchmark results (time horizons by model)

ai-datacenters.summary: Purpose-built campuses with hundreds of thousands of AI chips drawing a gigawatt or more, for training and serving frontier models. By 2026 Epoch counted one campus above 1 GW of IT power and several near it; power and chip supply, more than algorithms, now set the pace of scaling.

efforts.note: About 1,037 MW of IT power in Epoch's data, the only site above 1 GW.
Colossus was built in about four months in 2024; Colossus 2 had about 440,000 GB300 chips and about 946 MW by late 2026.
A 10 GW commitment from January 2025; the Abilene, Texas site (about 618 MW) trained GPT-6 Astra.

effort.note: Epoch estimates the hardware for GPT-6 Astra's 100,000-plus GB200 run at about $4.2 billion, drawing about 230 MW. Epoch projected in 2024 that runs of about 2e29 FLOP would be feasible by 2030, with power the tightest constraint.

sources.title: Epoch AI, Can AI scaling continue through 2030?

autonomous-vehicles.summary: Cars that carry paying passengers with no one in the driver's seat, using cameras, lidar, radar and neural networks. Waymo began fully driverless public rides in Phoenix in 2020; scaling to many cities is the next step.

efforts.note: Won the DARPA Grand Challenge desert race; no car finished in 2004.
Driverless service in Phoenix from October 2020, then San Francisco, Los Angeles and other cities.
Camera-only approach; robotaxi pilot in Austin from June 2025.
Shut down in December 2024 after a 2023 crash and permit suspension.

robot-foundation-models.summary: Vision-language-action models that turn camera images and instructions directly into robot motions and transfer across tasks and robot bodies. They work in demonstrations and pilots; general-purpose robots doing paid work at scale are the next step.

efforts.note: RT-2 (July 2023); Gemini Robotics (March 2025).
pi0 (October 2024), pi0.5 (April 2025), pi*0.6 (November 2025), pi0.7 (April 2026), and an API in October 2026.

shor-algorithm.summary: A quantum algorithm that factors large numbers exponentially faster than any known classical method, which would break RSA and elliptic-curve encryption. It turned quantum computing from a curiosity into a strategic goal.

efforts.note: Built on Richard Feynman (1981 to 1982) and David Deutsch (1985), who proposed quantum computers; Lov Grover's search algorithm followed in 1996.

sources.title: Shor 1995, Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer

quantum-error-correction.summary: Spreading one logical qubit across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and fixed without measuring the stored information. The threshold theorem says arbitrarily long computations are possible once physical error rates fall below a fixed level.

efforts.note: The first quantum codes.

efforts.who: Dorit Aharonov, Michael Ben-Or; Emanuel Knill, Raymond Laflamme, Wojciech Zurek; Alexei Kitaev
efforts.note: The threshold theorem (1996 to 1997) and Kitaev's toric code, ancestor of the surface code; IBM's qLDPC "gross" codes (2024) cut the overhead.

quantum-computing.summary: Machines that compute with qubits held in superposition and entanglement. First demonstrated with two qubits in 1998, they reached hundreds to thousands of physical qubits by 2026 on several competing platforms; doing useful work better than classical computers is the next step.

efforts.who: Isaac Chuang, Neil Gershenfeld, Mark Kubinec (IBM, MIT, Berkeley); Jonathan Jones, Michele Mosca (Oxford)
efforts.note: First two-qubit algorithms, using nuclear spins in liquid NMR; Yasunobu Nakamura's superconducting qubit followed in 1999.
Sycamore (2019), Willow (105 qubits, December 2024); "Quantum Echoes" (October 2025) claimed a verifiable advantage on a physics simulation.
Condor (1,121 qubits, 2023), Heron and Nighthawk processors; Starling, a fault-tolerant machine, targeted for 2029.
Helios (November 2025), 98 barium-ion qubits with 99.92% two-qubit gate fidelity; its 2026 IPO filing claims 48 logical qubits from those 98.
Bought Oxford Ionics in 2025; sold its first 256-qubit chip-based system in 2026; targets 1,600 logical qubits in 2028 (company claim).
Raised $1 billion in September 2025; building utility-scale sites in Brisbane and Chicago; selected with Microsoft for the final phase of DARPA's US2QC program.
Majorana 1 (February 2025) claimed eight topological qubits; many physicists say the evidence that they are truly topological is not yet convincing.

efforts.who: QuEra and Harvard, Atom Computing, Pasqal (neutral atoms); USTC (superconducting and photonic); D-Wave (annealing)
efforts.note: Harvard and QuEra ran 48 logical qubits in December 2023; USTC built Jiuzhang (2020) and Zuchongzhi 3.0 (2025).

sources.title: Chuang, Gershenfeld and Kubinec 1998, Experimental Implementation of Fast Quantum Searching, Physical Review Letters

quantum-supremacy.summary: The first demonstration of a quantum computer doing a calculation, sampling from random circuits, far faster than the best classical supercomputers could. The task has no practical use, and better classical algorithms later narrowed the gap.

efforts.who: Google AI Quantum (John Martinis and colleagues)
efforts.note: Sycamore, 53 qubits, 200 seconds versus a claimed 10,000 years; IBM disputed the estimate.
Jiuzhang, a photonic boson-sampling machine.

sources.title: Arute et al. 2019, Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor, Nature

below-threshold-error-correction.summary: The first proof that adding more physical qubits to an error-correcting code makes a logical qubit better rather than worse. It is the basic requirement for scaling to a fault-tolerant machine.

efforts.note: On Willow, each step up in surface code size (distance 3 to 5 to 7) cut the logical error rate by about 2.14 times, to 0.143% per cycle.

efforts.who: Quantinuum and Microsoft; Harvard and QuEra
efforts.note: Logical qubits with lower error rates than their physical qubits on trapped ions and neutral atoms.

sources.title: Google Quantum AI 2024, Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, Nature
Google, Meet Willow, our state-of-the-art quantum chip

post-quantum-cryptography.summary: Public-key schemes based on math problems, such as lattices, that quantum computers are not known to solve. NIST standardized the first three in August 2024, and browsers and messaging apps have begun switching.

efforts.who: NIST, with cryptographers worldwide (Kyber and Dilithium from the CRYSTALS team, SPHINCS+)
efforts.note: FIPS 203, 204 and 205 (August 13, 2024) after a competition begun in 2016; NIST's draft IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic curves by 2030 and disallows them by 2035.
Signal's PQXDH (2023), iMessage PQ3 (2024) and hybrid key exchange in Chrome.

sources.title: NIST IR 8547 (draft), Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards

fault-tolerant-quantum-computer.summary: A quantum computer with about 100 or more error-corrected logical qubits that can run very long computations reliably, enough for useful chemistry and materials simulation. Five hardware platforms are racing, with company targets around 2029.
fault-tolerant-quantum-computer.criterion: John Preskill's "megaquop" bar: about 100 or more logical qubits with error rates near one in a million per logical operation, running circuits of at least about 10,000 layers (a million or more logical operations) correctly.

efforts.note: Starling, about 200 logical qubits running 100 million gates, planned for Poughkeepsie by 2029 using qLDPC codes; Blue Jay (2,000 logical qubits) after 2033.
Below-threshold surface code (2024); magic states at 99.99 percent fidelity by cultivation (Science, October 2026).
Apollo, a universal fault-tolerant machine, targeted for 2029.

Aims to judge by 2033 whether any approach can reach utility scale; stage C (government verification) included Atom Computing, Diraq (silicon spins), IBM, IonQ, Microsoft and PsiQuantum as of October 2026.

forecast.note: Logical qubit counts went from 1 to about 48 between 2023 and 2026, at small code sizes and short circuits, and IBM, Quantinuum and others target 100 to 200 logical qubits around 2029. Such roadmaps have usually slipped a year or two, but progress since 2024 has been on or ahead of schedule and several platforms are competing, so my best guess is 2030, with a tail into the late 2030s if error rates stall.

routes.note: IBM (Starling, 200 logical qubits and 100 million operations, by 2029), Google (magic-state cultivation shown 2026), USTC, Rigetti, AWS.

cryptographically-relevant-quantum-compu.summary: A quantum computer able to run Shor's algorithm against 2048-bit RSA or 256-bit elliptic-curve keys, breaking much of today's internet encryption, including data recorded now and decrypted later. Estimates of the hardware needed fell sharply in 2025 and 2026.
cryptographically-relevant-quantum-compu.criterion: A quantum computer factors a 2048-bit RSA modulus, or solves a 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete logarithm, and the result is publicly verified.

forecast.note: Craig Gidney estimated in May 2025 that RSA-2048 could be factored in under a week with fewer than a million noisy qubits; a March 2026 paper put 256-bit elliptic curves at under 500,000 physical qubits running for minutes. That is still hundreds of times larger than 2026 machines. In the Global Risk Institute's 2025 survey (published March 2026), experts gave 28 to 49 percent odds within 10 years and 51 to 70 percent within 15. NIST's final transition plan (October 2026) deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve signatures after 2030 and disallows them after 2035. I put the median about five years after the first fault-tolerant machines.

brain-computer-interfaces.summary: Electrode arrays in or on the brain whose signals are decoded, increasingly by neural networks, to move cursors and robot arms or produce speech for paralyzed people. Roughly 50 to 100 people had high-channel implants by 2026, almost all of them in trials.

efforts.who: John Donoghue and colleagues (Brown University, BrainGate)
efforts.note: The first person to control a cursor with a Utah array implant, Matt Nagle.

efforts.who: UCSF (Edward Chang) and Stanford (Francis Willett, Jaimie Henderson) groups
efforts.note: Speech neuroprostheses decoding about 60 to 80 words a minute.
Neuralink's first human implant was in January 2024; secondary reports put its total near 26 people by mid-2026.

bci-at-scale.summary: Implanted high-bandwidth brain interfaces in routine medical use, with tens of thousands of people restored to fluent communication or movement. Elective use by healthy people would come later, if at all.
bci-at-scale.criterion: At least 100,000 people worldwide are living with an implanted high-bandwidth brain interface, reimbursed by health systems as ordinary care.

forecast.note: Cochlear implants, the closest analogue, took about 20 years from first approval (1984) to 100,000 recipients worldwide. If the first BCI approvals land around 2030, the same curve gives about 2050; faster electronics and a large eligible population (roughly 5 million people with paralysis worldwide) argue for sooner, surgical capacity and cost for later. I put 2045. Elective use by healthy people, if it ever comes, is a separate and later question.

sources.title: MIT Technology Review: China approves a brain chip (June 2026)

automated-ai-research.summary: AI that does the whole job of a frontier lab's best research scientists, choosing questions, designing and running experiments and inventing new methods, so AI progress itself speeds up. OpenAI has set it as a goal for 2028; it is the main mechanism in fast-takeoff scenarios.
automated-ai-research.criterion: The AI 2027 "superhuman AI researcher" bar: AI that can do the work of a frontier lab's best human AI researcher, at least as well and about 30 times faster, with about 30 times as many copies as the lab has researchers. In practice, a frontier lab reports that AI systems, not people, now originate and carry out most of its research, with humans mainly setting goals and checking safety.

efforts.note: In October 2025 Sam Altman said OpenAI was tracking toward an intern-level research assistant by September 2026 and a fully automated "legitimate AI researcher" by 2028.

efforts.who: Anthropic; Google DeepMind; xAI; Meta Superintelligence Labs
efforts.note: All use their own models heavily for research coding by 2026.

forecast.note: This needs the automated coder first (judged about 2028 here) plus research taste and long-horizon judgment. In August 2026 the AI 2027 authors put "top-expert-dominating AI" at November 2028 (Kokotajlo) and July 2032 (Lifland). METR judged that GPT-6-era models (GPT-5.6 Sol, June 2026) would not yet enable fully automated AI research. I put it two years after the automated coder, at 2030, with a long tail if continual learning proves necessary and hard.

agi.summary: AI that can do essentially any cognitive work a skilled human can do, including learning a new job on the job, at similar or lower cost. It would transform the economy and science, and how to make it safe is one of the central open problems of the time.
agi.criterion: A single AI system that (1) can do at least 90 percent of the tasks in jobs done at a computer, across the economy, at the level of a competent professional and at lower cost than one; (2) learns a new job from experience about as fast as a capable human hire; and (3) would resolve Metaculus's "first general AI system" question, whose tests include a two-hour adversarial Turing test and controlling a robot through a complex assembly task.

efforts.who: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, xAI, Meta Superintelligence Labs
efforts.note: All state AGI or superintelligence as a goal; OpenAI presented GPT-6 Astra (September 2026) as the start of an "AGI era".

efforts.who: DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, Zhipu and others

forecast.note: Frontier training compute has grown about 4 to 5 times a year, to about 1e27 FLOP (GPT-6 Astra, 2026, per Epoch), and METR's time horizons doubled about every four months to around 12 to 17 hours by 2026. Carried forward, and on the forecasts drawn on the time-horizon trend line, AI handles month-long projects around 2027 to 2028 and year-long ones around 2028 to 2030; the question is whether that reaches messy, open-ended work and on-the-job learning. In August 2026 the AI 2027 authors put top-expert-level AI at 2028 (Kokotajlo) and 2032 (Lifland); Dwarkesh Patel put human-like on-the-job learning at 2032; Metaculus's strong-AGI question sat around the early 2030s in 2025 to 2026; the 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers gave 50 percent for human-level machine intelligence by 2047, earlier with each survey. I put the median at 2031, with a long tail if scaling slows when compute growth meets power and capital limits around 2030.
