routes.name: Scaling today's methods
routes.note: Larger pretraining, reinforcement learning on longer tasks and more inference compute keep closing gaps, as time horizons have grown since 2019.

routes.name: AI-automated research
routes.note: AI researchers find the remaining ideas themselves, possibly quickly (the intelligence explosion of AI 2027).

routes.name: New paradigm
routes.note: Scaling stalls short of general ability, and on-the-job learning or learned world models (as LeCun's AMI Labs argues) supply the missing piece.

nuclear-power.summary: Fission reactors that boil water to drive turbines, first feeding a grid at Obninsk in 1954. About 440 reactors now supply roughly 9 percent of the world's electricity with almost no carbon emissions.

efforts.note: First electricity from fission, enough to light four bulbs (December 20, 1951).
First reactor to feed a power grid (5 MW), June 27, 1954.
First commercial-scale nuclear station, opened October 1956.
First full-scale US plant, a pressurized water reactor adapted from the naval program that powered USS Nautilus (1955). The PWR became the world's dominant design.
Builds more reactors than the rest of the world combined in the 2020s.

effort.note: Rides on the Manhattan Project (about 130,000 people, about $30 billion in 2025 dollars). Vogtle 3 and 4 in Georgia cost about $35 billion for two units and Hinkley Point C is estimated near 46 billion pounds, which is why cost, not physics, is the constraint in the West.

small-modular-reactors.summary: Factory-built reactors under about 300 MW, meant to cut nuclear costs through series production rather than one-off megaprojects. The first run in Russia (2020) and China (2023); Western units are under construction for about 2030, and US test reactors went critical in 2026.

efforts.note: Two 35 MWe KLT-40S reactors on a barge at Pevek, fully commissioned May 2020.
High-temperature gas-cooled pebble-bed reactor, commercial operation December 2023.
125 MWe land-based PWR at Changjiang, Hainan, construction from July 2021; commercial operation was expected in 2026.

efforts.note: Construction license April 2025; first grid power targeted for the end of 2030.

efforts.who: TerraPower Natrium (Kemmerer, Wyoming); Kairos Power Hermes; X-energy with Dow
efforts.note: Natrium construction permit March 2026 and construction start April 2026; Kairos's 50 MWe Hermes 2 broke ground April 2026.

efforts.who: US DOE Reactor Pilot Program (Antares, Valar Atomics, Aalo, Oklo)
efforts.note: Small test reactors went critical from June 2026 (Antares Mark-0 first, then Valar, Aalo by July 4 and Oklo in August).

efforts.who: NuScale (with ENTRA1 and TVA); Rolls-Royce SMR

molten-salt-thorium.summary: Reactors with fuel dissolved in molten fluoride salt that can breed fissile uranium-233 from abundant thorium. Oak Ridge ran a test reactor in the 1960s; China's Wuwei reactor converted thorium to uranium in 2025.
molten-salt-thorium.criterion: A molten salt reactor of at least 100 MW thermal runs on a thorium fuel cycle (breeding uranium-233 from thorium) and produces electricity.

efforts.who: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Molten Salt Reactor Experiment
efforts.note: Ran 1965 to 1969, including on U-233; program cut in favor of sodium fast breeders.

efforts.who: Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics (CAS), TMSR-LF1
efforts.note: 2 MWt; critical October 2023, thorium added October 2024, first thorium-to-uranium conversion announced November 2025. A 373 MWt follow-on is planned around 2030.

efforts.who: Copenhagen Atomics, Terrestrial Energy, Flibe Energy

efforts.note: Solid-fuel route through fast breeders rather than molten salt.

forecast.note: China moved fastest: construction from 2018, criticality of the 2 MWt TMSR-LF1 in October 2023, and thorium-to-uranium conversion announced November 2025 (with a conversion ratio of only about 0.1). Its stated next goal is a 100 MWt demonstration by 2035, which state projects have usually met within a few years. Salt corrosion, tritium and fuel reprocessing are unsolved at commercial scale, and thorium is not needed while uranium is cheap, so Western efforts lag. Best guess 2038 in China.

laser.summary: A light source that amplifies light by stimulated emission into an intense, coherent beam, first built by Theodore Maiman with a ruby crystal in 1960. It underlies fiber optics, precision measurement, laser fusion and much of modern manufacturing.

efforts.note: The microwave precursor; Townes and Schawlow proposed the optical version in 1958.

efforts.who: Nikolay Basov and Alexander Prokhorov (Lebedev Institute)
efforts.note: Shared the 1964 Nobel with Townes.
First working laser, May 16, 1960.

tokamak.summary: A doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle that holds plasma hot enough for fusion, proposed by Tamm and Sakharov in 1951. Soviet T-3 results in 1968 made it the world's main fusion approach.

efforts.note: Reported 10 million degree plasmas; a British Culham team confirmed with laser scattering in 1969.
Record 69 MJ of fusion energy in its final experiments before closing in December 2023.
1,066 seconds of high-confinement plasma, January 2025.
1,337 second plasma, February 2025.

efforts.who: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory stellarator program; Wendelstein 7-X (Max Planck)
efforts.note: Stellarators, the twisted alternative, revived by W7-X (first plasma 2015).

fusion-ignition-nif.summary: On December 5, 2022, the National Ignition Facility got more fusion energy out of a fuel pellet (3.15 MJ) than its lasers put in (2.05 MJ), the first controlled fusion ignition. By 2025 shots reached 8.6 MJ, a target gain above 4.

efforts.who: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, National Ignition Facility
efforts.note: Gain counts laser energy at the target only; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid. Record 8.6 MJ from 2.08 MJ in April 2025.

effort.note: About $3.5 billion to build (finished 2009), plus over a decade of operation, mostly funded for weapons stewardship.

sources.title: Physics World, NIF laser fusion milestone ignites debate

fusion-power.summary: A power plant that makes net electricity by fusion for months at a time, with abundant fuel and no long-lived high-level waste. Laser fusion has passed scientific gain; no device has yet made net electricity, and four rival confinement routes are racing.
fusion-power.criterion: A fusion plant delivers at least 50 MW of net electricity to a grid and runs for months, with at least six months of operation at 50 percent or higher availability.

efforts.who: ITER (EU, China, India, Japan, Korea, Russia, USA)
efforts.note: 2024 baseline moved start of research operations to 2034 and deuterium-tritium to 2039, adding about 5 billion euros. Aims at Q=10, not electricity.
Ignition December 2022; laser drivers need roughly 100 times better wall-plug efficiency for a plant.

efforts.who: Commonwealth Fusion Systems, SPARC then ARC
efforts.note: High-field REBCO tokamak; 20 T magnet test 2021, SPARC first plasma targeted 2027, ARC plant in Virginia early 2030s.
Pulsed field-reversed configuration with direct energy recovery; broke ground on Orion in Malaga, Washington in 2025 for a 50 MW Microsoft contract by 2028.
Beam-driven FRC; announced a merger with Trump Media and Technology Group in December 2025 and plans a 50 MWe plant.
BEST, a compact superconducting tokamak aiming at burning plasma with Q above 1 (design Q=5), due end of 2027; CFEDR demo to follow.
Spherical tokamaks; STEP prototype plant at West Burton targeted 2040.

efforts.who: General Fusion, Zap Energy, Type One Energy, Proxima Fusion, Marvel Fusion, Pacific Fusion
Energy Singularity; China Fusion Energy Co.
efforts.note: Chinese private and state HTS tokamaks (HH70 first plasma 2024).

effort.note: ITER alone is officially over 20 billion euros plus the 2024 overrun; the US DOE once estimated the full in-kind total near $65 billion. Private fusion firms raised roughly $10 billion by 2025 (Fusion Industry Association). Public fusion research worldwide has run on the order of $1 to 2 billion a year since the 1970s.

forecast.note: Read as first fusion electricity sold steadily to a grid. Company dates (Helion 2028, CFS early 2030s, STEP 2040) have a poor record: SPARC slipped from 2025 to 2027, ITER from 2016 to 2034 for first research operation, and Helion missed a 2024 electricity goal. Private firms raised about $14 billion by mid-2026 (FIA) and most say the early 2030s. Metaculus's 100 MW question sat near 2041 in earlier snapshots. Tritium breeding, materials under neutron flux and plant availability are untested. I put the first net-electric run around 2034 and a plant running for months around 2040.

solar-photovoltaic.summary: A semiconductor junction that turns sunlight directly into electricity, first made practical at Bell Labs in 1954 at about 6 percent efficiency. Module prices fell over 99 percent since 1975, making it the cheapest new electricity in much of the world.

efforts.who: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller, Gerald Pearson (Bell Labs)
efforts.note: Announced April 25, 1954.
First solar-powered satellite; space was PV's first real market.

efforts.who: Germany's feed-in tariff (EEG, 2000) and Chinese manufacturers (LONGi, Jinko, Trina, Tongwei)
efforts.note: German demand then Chinese scale drove the learning curve; China makes over 80 percent of the world's modules.

effort.note: Price fell about 20 percent per doubling of cumulative capacity (Wright's law), from about $132/W in 1975 to $0.27/W in 2024 (2025 dollars). The world added about 510 GW in 2025, past 2.4 TW cumulative. Silver paste is a constraint at terawatt scale; makers are shifting to copper metallization.

perovskite-solar-cells.summary: Solar cells made from cheap, solution-processed metal halide perovskite crystals, first reported at 3.8 percent efficiency in 2009 and above 26 percent within 15 years. Their weakness is degradation under heat, light and moisture.

efforts.who: Akihiro Kojima, Tsutomu Miyasaka and colleagues (Toin University of Yokohama)
Henry Snaith (Oxford) and Nam-Gyu Park (Sungkyunkwan) groups
efforts.note: Solid-state cells near 10 percent launched the field.

perovskite-silicon-tandem.summary: A perovskite layer stacked on a silicon cell to harvest blue and red light separately, beating silicon's practical limit of about 27 percent. Lab cells reached 35.5 percent in 2026, but commercial modules are small-volume and about 25 percent; durable mass production is the open problem.
perovskite-silicon-tandem.criterion: Tandem modules ship at more than 1 GW a year with certified module efficiency of at least 28 percent and pass standard IEC durability certification.

efforts.note: Certified 35.5 percent cell (ESTI, July 2026), after 33.9 percent in 2023; said in June 2026 it had no active mass-production plan.
First commercial tandem module shipments (2024) at about 25 percent; targets 27 percent in 2027 and 30 percent in 2030.
Pilot lines.

efforts.who: Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin, KAUST, EPFL and CSEM, Fraunhofer ISE

forecast.note: Cell records rise about half a point a year, but perovskite layers still degrade faster than silicon, and silicon modules at about 11 cents a watt are a hard price to beat. Oxford PV's own roadmap puts 27 percent modules in 2027. Judgment: GW-scale, certified 28 percent modules around 2031.

wind-power.summary: Three-bladed, upwind, grid-connected turbines on the Danish design, scaled from tens of kilowatts in the late 1970s to 15 MW machines today. Global capacity passed about 1,300 GW in 2025.

efforts.note: 200 kW three-bladed prototype that set the "Danish concept".
Small commercial turbines sold into the California wind rush of the early 1980s.
Large two-bladed government turbines that mostly failed; incremental Danish scaling won.
China added about 120 GW in 2025 alone and holds over half of world capacity.

effort.note: Direct-drive generators use neodymium-iron-boron magnets (roughly 600 kg of magnet per MW, about a third of it rare earths); geared designs with induction generators avoid them at some cost in maintenance.

offshore-wind.summary: Wind farms built at sea, where winds are stronger and steadier, starting with Vindeby in Denmark in 1991. Floating platforms now open deep water.

efforts.note: Eleven 450 kW turbines.
First floating wind farm.
China has about half of world offshore capacity.

lithium-ion-battery.summary: A rechargeable battery that shuttles lithium ions between a layered oxide cathode and a carbon anode, commercialized by Sony in 1991. Cell prices fell about 99 percent since then, enabling phones, laptops, electric cars and grid storage.

efforts.note: Lithium titanium disulfide cathode; metallic lithium anode was a fire risk.
Lithium cobalt oxide cathode, doubling voltage.
Carbon (petroleum coke) anode, the first safe practical cell.
First commercial cells, in a camcorder.

efforts.who: CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, Samsung SDI, SK On
efforts.note: Demand passed 1 TWh a year in 2024; Chinese makers hold about three quarters of production.

effort.note: Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino shared the 2019 Chemistry Nobel. The graphite anode and the cobalt in early cathodes are supply risks; nickel- rich and cobalt-free chemistries (LFP) and sodium-ion substitute.

lithium-iron-phosphate.summary: A lithium-ion cathode of iron phosphate, reported by Goodenough's group in 1997, that needs no cobalt or nickel and resists fire. Cheap and long-lived, it now powers nearly half of new electric cars and most grid batteries.

efforts.who: Akshaya Padhi, John Goodenough and colleagues (University of Texas)

efforts.note: Cell-to-pack designs closed the energy density gap.

sodium-ion-battery.summary: A battery chemistry like lithium-ion but using abundant sodium, trading some energy density for lower cost and good cold-weather performance. CATL's sodium cells went into a mass-produced car in 2026, and sodium storage orders reached tens of GWh.

efforts.note: 175 Wh/kg cells; a car CATL calls the first mass-produced sodium-battery passenger car was unveiled in February 2026, with 10,000 to 20,000 cars expected that year; a 60 GWh, three-year sodium storage order from HyperStrong (April 2026) and 40 GWh of new capacity in Fujian.
Small production runs in cars from 2023 to 2024.
Prussian-blue sodium startup that shut down in 2025.

solid-state-batteries.summary: Batteries with a solid ceramic or sulfide electrolyte instead of a flammable liquid, allowing a lithium-metal anode for more energy and less fire risk. Prototype cells exist; making them cheaply at scale is the hurdle.
solid-state-batteries.criterion: All-solid-state cells (no liquid electrolyte) power a series-production car sold in at least 10,000 units in one year.

efforts.note: Sulfide electrolyte; production for EVs targeted 2027 to 2028. Toyota once aimed at the 2020 Olympics.
Anode-free ceramic separator; B-sample cells 2025, Eagle line 2026, license up to 80 GWh.

efforts.who: Factorial Energy with Mercedes-Benz and Stellantis
efforts.note: Road tests of a semi-solid pack in 2025.

forecast.note: Every major player points to 2027 to 2028 for small runs, but these dates have slipped repeatedly (Toyota's from 2020, QuantumScape's from 2024), and as of early 2026 none had commercialized all-solid cells in cars. Liquid LFP (about $81 per kWh for packs in 2025) and sodium keep getting cheaper, which raises the bar. Small runs late 2020s; 10,000 cars a year around 2030.

sources.title: BloombergNEF, Lithium-ion battery pack prices fall to $108 per kilowatt-hour (2025)
Janek and Zeier 2016, A solid future for battery development, Nature Energy

electric-vehicles.summary: Highway-capable cars powered by lithium-ion packs, beginning with the Tesla Roadster in 2008. Sales passed 20 million in 2025, a quarter of new cars, led by China.

efforts.note: Lead-acid then NiMH; recalled and crushed by 2003.
Chinese firms made about 60 percent of EVs sold in 2025; EVs were nearly 55 percent of China's car sales.

effort.note: Most motors use rare-earth permanent magnets; induction and externally excited motors (Tesla, BMW, Renault) substitute.

sources.title: IEA, Global EV Outlook 2026, trends in electric cars

grid-batteries.summary: Large lithium-ion installations that store solar and wind power for hours and stabilize grid frequency, made economic by falling cell prices. South Australia's Hornsdale reserve in 2017 showed what they could do.

efforts.who: Tesla and Neoen, Hornsdale Power Reserve
efforts.note: 100 MW / 129 MWh, built in under 100 days.
Over 10 GW of batteries shifting solar into the evening peak.
Largest installer of new-type storage in the 2020s.

sources.title: IEA, Batteries and Secure Energy Transitions (2024)

long-duration-storage.summary: Storage that holds energy for a day or more rather than hours, using iron-air or flow batteries, compressed air or heat, to cover windless, dark spells on a renewable grid. Pumped hydro already does this where geography allows; the newer kinds are just reaching commercial use.
long-duration-storage.criterion: Storage systems that can discharge at full power for 24 hours or more, other than pumped hydro, reach at least 10 GWh in commercial operation worldwide.

efforts.note: 100-hour batteries; a 1.5 MW, 150 MWh first system with Great River Energy in Minnesota; a 12 GWh deal with Crusoe (March 2026) and a $750 million round (August 2026).

efforts.who: Dalian Rongke Power, vanadium flow battery
efforts.note: 100 MW and 400 MWh in Dalian, about four hours.
China's 300 to 600 MW plants store about four to five hours.
Thermal batteries for industrial heat.

forecast.note: Almost all storage built so far lasts two to eight hours, because lithium batteries got cheap so fast. Form Energy's contracted 12 GWh alone would meet the bar once built, probably near the end of the decade. Judgment: 2030.

sources.title: Great River Energy, Cambridge energy storage project
MIT Technology Review, Form Energy (2026 climate tech companies to watch)

shale-fracking.summary: Drilling sideways through shale and cracking it with pressurized water and sand to release trapped gas and oil. Proven in Texas's Barnett Shale around 1998, it made the US the world's largest oil and gas producer.

efforts.note: First experimental hydraulic fracture.

efforts.who: DOE Eastern Gas Shales Project and Gas Research Institute
efforts.note: Public research on shale, microseismic mapping and horizontal wells.
About 17 years of persistence in the Barnett before it paid.

efforts.who: Devon Energy and others, horizontal multistage wells

effort.note: Mitchell Energy drilled for about 17 years before the economics worked.

sources.title: Breakthrough Institute, Where the shale gas revolution came from
US EIA, Hydraulic fracturing accounts for about half of current US crude oil production (2016)

green-hydrogen.summary: Splitting water with renewable electricity to make hydrogen for steel, ammonia and fuels without fossil carbon. It works, but costs two to four times hydrogen from natural gas, and low-emission hydrogen was under 1 percent of the roughly 100 million tonnes used in 2024.
green-hydrogen.criterion: Hydrogen from electrolysis powered by low-carbon electricity reaches 10 million tonnes a year, about a tenth of world hydrogen use.

efforts.note: About 260 MW of electrolyzers, then the largest.

efforts.who: NEOM Green Hydrogen Company (ACWA Power, Air Products)
efforts.note: About 4 GW of solar and wind for 600 tonnes of hydrogen a day; 90 percent built by March 2026, with first product due 2027.
Hydrogen-reduced steel; hit funding trouble in 2025.

efforts.who: LONGi Hydrogen, Peric, thyssenkrupp nucera, Electric Hydrogen
efforts.note: Electrolyzers cost $600 to 1,200 per kW in China and $2,000 to 2,600 outside it (IEA 2025); China has about 65 percent of installed and committed capacity.

forecast.note: Low-emission hydrogen was on track for about 1 million tonnes in 2025, and projects operating or committed reach 4.2 million tonnes a year by 2030, while the announced 2030 pipeline shrank from 49 to 37 million tonnes in a year (IEA). Growth from there depends on carbon prices and mandates. Judgment: 10 million tonnes of electrolytic hydrogen around 2040.

sources.title: IEA, Global Hydrogen Review 2025, executive summary

enhanced-geothermal.summary: Making geothermal power away from volcanic hot springs by drilling into hot dry rock and fracturing it to circulate water, borrowing shale drilling methods. Fervo's Project Red sent power to the grid in 2023, and its Cape Station in Utah began commercial operation in October 2026.

efforts.who: Los Alamos, Fenton Hill hot dry rock project
efforts.note: Proved the concept but not the economics; ended 1995.
Small EGS plant, about 1.5 MW.
3.5 MW to NV Energy from November 2023, from a horizontal well pair at 191 °C.
First power September 24, 2026; first 33 MW block in commercial operation October 1, 2026; about 100 MW due by January 2027.

sources.title: Canary Media, America's first enhanced geothermal plant just got up and running (2023)
ThinkGeoEnergy, Fervo reports first power at Cape Station (2026)

superconductors-high-temp.summary: Copper oxide ceramics that lose all electrical resistance at far higher temperatures than metals, found by Bednorz and Muller in 1986; YBCO works in cheap liquid nitrogen. REBCO tapes now enable compact fusion magnets.

efforts.who: Georg Bednorz and K. Alex Muller (IBM Zurich)
efforts.note: Lanthanum barium copper oxide at 35 K; Nobel 1987.

efforts.who: Maw-Kuen Wu and Paul Chu (Alabama, Houston)
efforts.note: YBCO at 93 K, above liquid nitrogen's 77 K.

efforts.who: Commonwealth Fusion Systems and MIT PSFC
efforts.note: 20 tesla large-bore REBCO fusion magnet.

efforts.who: Faraday Factory Japan, Shanghai Superconductor, SuperPower (Furukawa), Fujikura
efforts.note: REBCO tape makers scaling for fusion and cables.

effort.note: Older niobium superconductors need liquid helium at 4 K; HTS at 20 K or 77 K cuts helium demand, a real substitution since helium is scarce.

sources.title: MIT News, Tests show high-temperature superconducting magnets are ready for fusion

room-temperature-superconductor.summary: A material that superconducts at everyday temperature and pressure, which would transform power lines, motors, magnets and computing. Hydrides come close only under crushing pressures, and recent claims (LK-99, Dias) collapsed.
room-temperature-superconductor.criterion: A material shows zero resistance and expels magnetic fields (the Meissner effect) above 273 K (0 °C) at ordinary atmospheric pressure, in a bulk sample, replicated by at least two independent laboratories.

efforts.who: Mikhail Eremets (Max Planck Mainz), hydrides H3S and LaH10
efforts.note: Superconductivity up to about 250 K, but at about 1.7 million atmospheres.
Room-temperature claims retracted from Nature in 2022 and 2023; Rochester found misconduct in 2024.
A viral July 2023 claim of a room-temperature superconductor; within weeks replications traced its behavior to copper sulfide impurities.

efforts.who: Paul Chu and colleagues (University of Houston)
efforts.note: Kept a mercury cuprate superconducting at 151 K at ambient pressure after a "pressure quench" (PNAS, March 2026), above the 133 K record that stood since 1993, though it degrades above 200 K.

efforts.who: Nickelate and AI materials-discovery efforts (Google DeepMind GNoME, Microsoft)

forecast.note: The ambient-pressure record sat at about 133 K (mercury cuprates) from 1993 until a metastable 151 K in 2026, while hydrides reach about 250 K only above a million atmospheres. No theory rules out room temperature at ambient pressure, but none says how to get there, and the field has a run of collapsed claims (Dias; LK-99). AI materials screening raises the number of candidates tried, not the odds per candidate. Judgment with very low confidence; it may never happen.

sources.title: Deng et al. 2026, pressure-quenched Hg-1223 at 151 K, PNAS
Drozdov et al. 2019, Superconductivity at 250 K in lanthanum hydride, Nature

satellites.summary: Objects placed in orbit around Earth, beginning with the Soviet Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957. Satellites now carry the world's navigation, weather forecasting, broadband and Earth imaging.

efforts.who: Sergei Korolev's OKB-1, Sputnik 1 on an R-7 missile
JPL and Army Ballistic Missile Agency, Explorer 1
efforts.note: Found the Van Allen radiation belts.

efforts.who: China (Dong Fang Hong 1, 1970), Japan (Ohsumi, 1970), France (Asterix, 1965), India (Rohini, 1980)

effort.note: Built on the R-7 ICBM program. By 2026 roughly 19,000 payloads were in orbit, over half of them Starlink.

sources.title: NASA, Sputnik and the origins of the Space Age

communications-satellites.summary: Satellites that relay telephone, television and data across oceans, first with Telstar in 1962 and from geostationary orbit by 1964, as Arthur C. Clarke had proposed in 1945. Intelsat made them a global utility.

efforts.who: Arthur C. Clarke, Extra-Terrestrial Relays (Wireless World)
efforts.note: Proposed three geostationary relays.

efforts.who: AT&T Bell Labs and NASA, Telstar 1

efforts.note: Syncom 3 broadcast the Tokyo Olympics from geostationary orbit.
Highly elliptical orbits to cover high latitudes.

sources.title: Communications satellite, Wikipedia (Clarke 1945 and early history)

earth-observation.summary: Satellites that image clouds, land, ice and oceans, from TIROS-1 in 1960 and Landsat in 1972 to daily whole-Earth imaging today. They made global weather forecasts and climate records possible.

efforts.note: First weather satellite images.
The longest continuous record of Earth's land surface; free data since 2008.

efforts.who: ESA Copernicus Sentinels; China Fengyun; Planet Labs
efforts.note: Planet's cubesat flock images the whole land surface daily.

human-spaceflight.summary: Sending people into space and returning them alive, first done by Yuri Gagarin on April 12, 1961. Russia, the US and China fly crews on their own rockets, and private companies now fly them too.

efforts.who: Alan Shepard (suborbital, May 1961), John Glenn (orbital, 1962), Project Mercury

efforts.note: First private company to fly astronauts to orbit, May 30, 2020.

sources.title: ESA, Yuri Gagarin, first man in space

moon-landing.summary: Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Twelve people walked on the Moon in six landings through 1972, and no one has returned since.

efforts.who: NASA Apollo program (with North American, Grumman, Boeing, MIT Instrumentation Lab and others)

efforts.note: Four N1 launch failures 1969 to 1972; Luna 9 made the first soft landing (uncrewed) in 1966.

effort.note: $25.8 billion in then-year dollars, about $309 billion in 2025 dollars (Planetary Society, NASA New Start Index), peaking near 4 percent of the federal budget in 1966. The Apollo Guidance Computer was the largest early buyer of integrated circuits.

sources.title: Planetary Society, How much did the Apollo program cost?

planetary-probes.summary: Robotic spacecraft sent to other worlds, from Mariner 2 passing Venus in 1962 to Voyager leaving the solar system. Every planet, and Pluto, has now been visited.

efforts.note: First impact on the Moon and first images of its far side.
First soft landing on another planet.
Grand tour of the outer planets; Voyager 1 reached interstellar space in 2012.
Rosetta comet landing (2014), Mangalyaan (2014), Chang'e 4 far-side landing (2019).

space-stations.summary: Crewed outposts in orbit for long stays and research, starting with Salyut 1 in 1971. The International Space Station has been occupied without a break since November 2000, and China runs its own Tiangong.

efforts.who: International Space Station (NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, CSA)
efforts.note: To be deorbited around 2030.

efforts.who: Axiom Space, Vast (Haven-1), Starlab, Blue Origin Orbital Reef
efforts.note: Commercial successors to the ISS.

effort.note: The ISS is often cited at about $150 billion across partners, the most expensive single object ever built.

space-shuttle.summary: NASA's partly reusable winged spacecraft, flown 135 times from 1981 to 2011. It built the ISS and launched Hubble, but refurbishment made it far more expensive per kilogram than promised, and two orbiters were lost with crews.

efforts.note: Challenger (1986) and Columbia (2003) disasters killed 14 astronauts.
One uncrewed orbital flight.

effort.note: About $209 billion in 2010 dollars over the program, roughly $1.5 billion per flight; CSIS puts it at about $65,400 per kg to LEO.

sources.title: Space.com, NASA's shuttle program cost $209 billion

atomic-clock.summary: A clock that counts the microwave frequency of a cesium atom's transition, first built by Louis Essen in 1955. Since 1967 the second has been defined this way, and satellite navigation depends on such clocks.

efforts.who: Louis Essen and Jack Parry (National Physical Laboratory)

efforts.note: Optical clocks 100 times more precise may redefine the second around 2030.

gps.summary: A US military constellation of satellites with atomic clocks that lets any receiver compute its position to meters, first launched in 1978 and fully operational in 1995. Opened fully to civilians in 2000, it now times phone networks, power grids and finance as well as guiding people.

efforts.who: US Air Force NAVSTAR program (Bradford Parkinson and others)
efforts.note: First Block I satellite February 1978; full operational capability 1995; Selective Availability turned off May 2000.

effort.note: About $7.2 billion in R&D and procurement through 1994 in then-year dollars (roughly $15 to 20 billion today), and about $1.5 to 2 billion a year since. Relativity matters: uncorrected, clocks would drift about 38 microseconds a day, about 10 km of position error.

sources.title: National Academies, The Global Positioning System (1995), costs

space-telescopes.summary: Telescopes above the atmosphere, which blurs visible light and blocks infrared, X-rays and ultraviolet. Hubble (1990) and the James Webb Space Telescope (2021) changed what we know about the universe's age, expansion and first galaxies.

efforts.who: NASA and ESA, Hubble Space Telescope
efforts.note: Launched with a flawed mirror, fixed by astronauts in 1993.

efforts.who: NASA, ESA, CSA, James Webb Space Telescope
NASA Nancy Grace Roman; China's Xuntian

effort.note: Hubble cost about $1.5 billion at launch (about $16 billion over its life); JWST about $10 billion, from 1996 to 2021.

exoplanet-detection.summary: The discovery of planets around other stars, first around a normal Sun-like star (51 Pegasi b) by Mayor and Queloz in 1995. More than 6,000 are now confirmed, many by the Kepler and TESS space telescopes.

efforts.note: Planets around a pulsar.
Nobel 2019.

nasa-cots.summary: NASA's 2006 Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program paid companies fixed sums for milestones instead of owning rocket designs. It funded Falcon 9 and Dragon, and became the model for commercial crew and lunar landers.

efforts.who: NASA (Alan Lindenmoyer), SpaceX and Orbital Sciences
efforts.note: Dragon reached the ISS in May 2012.

effort.note: NASA paid about $800 million across COTS partners (then-year dollars).

sources.title: NASA, Commercial Orbital Transportation Services, a new era in spaceflight

reusable-rockets.summary: Rocket first stages that fly back and land upright to be reused, first done by a SpaceX Falcon 9 on December 21, 2015. Some boosters have flown more than 35 times, and SpaceX now launches most of the world's mass to orbit.

efforts.note: Suborbital vertical-landing test vehicle.

efforts.who: Blue Origin, New Shepard (suborbital) and New Glenn
efforts.note: New Shepard landed November 2015; New Glenn's orbital booster first landed November 13, 2025.
First landing December 2015; first reflight March 2017; booster B1067 flew its 37th mission in August 2026.

efforts.who: LandSpace (Zhuque-3), Space Pioneer, CALT (Long March 12A); Rocket Lab Neutron; ArianeGroup Themis

effort.note: SpaceX put Falcon 9 v1.0 development at about $300 million (2011), and reusability at roughly $1 billion more. A 2011 NASA cost model estimated $1.7 to 4 billion for the same rocket under NASA practices.

sources.title: NASA, Falcon 9 cost analysis with NAFCOM (2011)
Spaceflight Now, Falcon 9 booster's record-breaking 35th flight (2026)
Blue Origin, New Glenn lands booster on ESCAPADE launch

satellite-megaconstellations.summary: Thousands of mass-produced satellites in low orbit that give broadband to anywhere on Earth through phased-array dishes. Starlink passed 11,000 satellites in orbit and about 10 million subscribers in 2026.

efforts.note: First batch May 2019; 10.3 million subscribers at March 2026 per SpaceX's IPO filing.

effort.note: Raises orbital debris and astronomy concerns; most satellites deorbit within about five years.

mars-rovers.summary: Wheeled robots exploring the Martian surface, from Sojourner in 1997 to Perseverance, which is caching samples for return. They found evidence of past liquid water and habitable lakes.

efforts.who: NASA JPL (Sojourner 1997, Spirit and Opportunity 2004, Curiosity 2012, Perseverance 2021)
efforts.note: Perseverance's Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet, April 2021.

efforts.who: CNSA Tianwen-3; NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return
efforts.note: China aims to return samples around 2031; the NASA plan faced cancellation over cost.

asteroid-sample-return.summary: Spacecraft that collect rock from an asteroid and bring it to Earth, first done by Japan's Hayabusa in 2010. Hayabusa2 and OSIRIS-REx returned grams of pristine carbon-rich material with amino acids.

efforts.note: 121.6 grams returned.
Launched May 2025.

planetary-defense.summary: Changing an asteroid's path by hitting it with a spacecraft. NASA's DART struck Dimorphos in September 2022 and shortened its orbit by about 33 minutes, the first time humans moved a celestial body on purpose.

efforts.who: NASA and Johns Hopkins APL, DART

efforts.note: Arrives at Didymos in late 2026 to measure the result.

efforts.who: Vera C. Rubin Observatory; NASA NEO Surveyor
efforts.note: Finding the asteroids comes first.

fully-reusable-rockets.summary: A rocket whose booster and upper stage both return and refly, aiming to cut launch cost per kilogram another tenfold or more. SpaceX's Starship has caught boosters in the launch tower, but its ship has not yet been recovered and reflown.
fully-reusable-rockets.criterion: An orbital rocket's upper stage returns intact from orbit and flies to orbit again, with its booster also reused.

efforts.note: First flight April 2023; first tower catch of a booster October 2024 and first booster reflight May 2025; V3 debut May 22, 2026; first orbital flight September 28, 2026 (26 Starlink satellites deployed, splashdown off Hawaii). No ship had been caught or reflown; a first ship catch was planned for the next flight.

effort.note: Very rough; SpaceX said in 2023 it was spending about $2 billion a year on Starship. NASA's lunar lander contracts cover about $4 billion.

forecast.note: The booster side is done, and Starship reached orbit in September 2026. The ship still needs a catch (first attempt planned for Flight 15, late 2026 at the soonest), a heat shield that survives without heavy refurbishment and a reflight. The first booster reflight came about seven months after the first booster catch. SpaceX has usually met its technical goals two to three times later than Musk's dates, but the remaining steps are incremental. Judgment: late 2027.

crewed-lunar-return.summary: Landing people on the Moon for the first time since 1972, this time near the south pole where ice may supply water and fuel. Artemis II flew four astronauts around the Moon in April 2026; the US aims to land in 2028 and China by 2030, by different routes.
crewed-lunar-return.criterion: A crew lands on the Moon, works on the surface and returns safely to Earth.

efforts.who: NASA Artemis (SLS, Orion; SpaceX Starship HLS and Blue Origin Blue Moon landers)
efforts.note: Artemis II crewed flyby April 1 to 11, 2026. In February 2026 NASA made Artemis III a 2027 Earth-orbit docking test and moved the first landing to Artemis IV, targeted early 2028; the uncrewed Starship lunar demo slipped to late 2027.
Pad abort (June 2025) and a Long March 10 first-stage test with an in-flight abort (February 2026); first uncrewed Mengzhou flight about 2027; landing planned by 2030.

effort.note: NASA's Inspector General estimated Artemis at about $93 billion through 2025.

forecast.note: US landings depend on ship-to-ship propellant transfer, not yet shown (now planned for early 2027), and Artemis dates have slipped from 2024 to 2028. China's program has met its milestones on schedule so far and needs no refueling. Best guess 2029, by either.

sources.title: CSIS, Artemis rewritten, NASA's new Moon plan
NASA OIG, NASA's management of the Artemis missions (2021)

routes.name: Refueled lander (Artemis)
routes.note: NASA's Orion carries the crew to lunar orbit; a Starship or Blue Moon lander filled in Earth orbit takes them down.

routes.name: Expendable heavy lift (China)
routes.note: Two Long March 10 launches, the Mengzhou crew ship and the Lanyue lander meet in lunar orbit, with no refueling.

crewed-mars-landing.summary: Landing a crew on Mars and bringing them home, a trip of about two to three years through deep-space radiation. It needs heavy lift, orbital refueling, propellant made from Martian air and reliable life support.
crewed-mars-landing.criterion: A crew lands on Mars and later returns safely to Earth.

efforts.note: Musk gave 50 percent odds for an uncrewed 2026 attempt in May 2025, then said in February 2026 that Mars would wait about five to seven years while SpaceX focuses on the Moon.

efforts.who: NASA Moon to Mars architecture; Space Reactor-1 Freedom
efforts.note: A nuclear electric pathfinder with Mars flybys is proposed for December 2028.
Officials have floated crewed missions in the 2030s.

forecast.note: Metaculus's question had a median in the mid-2030s in earlier snapshots. I am later: propellant transfer, Mars propellant production and long-duration life support are all undemonstrated, launch windows come every 26 months, and SpaceX has now deferred Mars for the Moon. If uncrewed Starships land around 2031 to 2033 and make propellant, crews could follow in the late 2030s; early to mid 2040s is my median.

sources.title: Metaculus, Date first human lands on Mars

routes.name: Refueled Starship
routes.note: SpaceX's plan, refueling in Earth orbit and making return propellant on Mars.

routes.name: Nuclear propulsion
routes.note: NASA's longer-term architectures, which shorten the trip and carry return propellant.

mars-settlement.summary: A permanently inhabited, growing settlement on Mars that could in time survive without supply ships from Earth. Beyond rockets, it needs closed-loop life support, local manufacturing, radiation shelter and an answer to whether people can raise children in 38 percent gravity.
mars-settlement.criterion: At least 100 people live on Mars continuously for five years or more, with crew rotations, making their own water, oxygen and propellant and most of their food locally.

efforts.note: Musk's stated goal of a self-sustaining city of a million people.

forecast.note: Read as a continuously inhabited base of at least about 100 people. The Antarctic analog took 50 years from first landing to permanent stations, with no rocket needed. Self-sufficiency is far harder: no closed ecological system (Biosphere 2) has run for years. Cheap launch is necessary, not sufficient. Very uncertain.

sources.title: Metaculus, Date first human lands on Mars
Weinersmith and Weinersmith, A City on Mars (2023)

space-based-solar.summary: Large solar arrays in orbit that beam power to Earth as microwaves, catching sunlight around the clock. Proposed by Peter Glaser in 1968, it has only been shown in tiny demonstrations; launch cost is the deciding factor.
space-based-solar.criterion: At least 1 MW of power is beamed from a satellite in orbit and fed into a grid on Earth.

efforts.who: Caltech Space Solar Power Project, MAPLE
efforts.note: First wireless power beamed in space and detected on Earth, milliwatts.

efforts.who: JAXA and Japan Space Systems, OHISAMA
efforts.note: Small satellite to beam about 1 kW-class power to Usuda.
Plans MW-scale orbital demo in the 2030s.

forecast.note: Only milliwatts have been beamed from space (Caltech, 2023). Japan's OHISAMA, meant to beam about 1 kW from orbit, had slipped to 2026 or later without launching, and Aetherflux turned toward orbital data centers. NASA's 2024 study found it costlier than ground renewables unless launch and in-space assembly costs fall dramatically, while ground solar plus batteries keeps getting cheaper. China is the most likely first mover.

sources.title: Caltech, In a first, Caltech's space solar power demonstrator beams power to Earth
Glaser 1968, Power from the Sun, its future, Science

asteroid-mining.summary: Extracting water, metals or platinum-group elements from asteroids, most likely first as water for rocket fuel in space rather than metal shipped to Earth. Sample-return missions show the access, not the economics.
asteroid-mining.criterion: Material mined from an asteroid (water or metal) is sold to a paying customer, in space or on Earth.

efforts.note: Both well-funded startups were sold off in 2018 to 2019 without mining.
Its Odin flyby probe was lost days after launch in February 2025; a next mission (DeepSpace-2) is listed for late 2026 or 2027.
Karman+ plans a first mission to the asteroid Apophis.

forecast.note: Read as first commercial sale of material mined from an asteroid. Two earlier waves of startups failed for lack of buyers; in-space customers (depots, stations) do not yet exist, and shipping metal to Earth would crash its price. Depends on cheap launch and a space economy that needs local water.

sources.title: The Space Review, The asteroid mining bubble has burst (2019)
The Space Review, The new wave of asteroid mining ventures (2025, includes the Odin mission)

orbital-manufacturing.summary: Making products in orbit that benefit from microgravity, such as pure drug crystals, optical fiber and semiconductor crystals, and returning them to Earth. Varda Space returned the first commercially made drug crystals in 2024.
orbital-manufacturing.criterion: At least one company returns products made in orbit to Earth on a regular schedule (at least monthly) and sells them commercially.

efforts.note: W-1 crystallized ritonavir and landed in Utah in February 2024; W-2 to W-6 flew in 2025 to 2026, about one every two to three months, carrying defense and NASA payloads; W-4 was lost on reentry in May 2026.
Launched June 2025 and ran its 1,000 °C furnace in orbit.

efforts.who: ISS National Lab, Redwire, Flawless Photonics
efforts.note: ZBLAN optical fiber drawn in orbit.

forecast.note: Varda's flight rate rose from one in 2023 to four in 2025, but its payloads are mostly test and government work, not products for sale. Cheaper launch and reentry should allow monthly returns by about 2030. Judgment.

interstellar-probe.summary: A spacecraft sent to reach another star system within a human lifetime, for example gram-scale light sails pushed to a fifth of light speed by ground-based lasers. Voyager 1, the fastest-leaving probe, would take about 75,000 years to reach the nearest star.
interstellar-probe.criterion: A spacecraft is launched at a speed (at least about 1 percent of light speed) and on a trajectory that would carry it to another star system within 100 years.

efforts.note: $100 million research program; work largely paused after 2022.

efforts.who: Johns Hopkins APL, Interstellar Probe concept
efforts.note: Heliopause probe, not a star mission.

forecast.note: Read as launching a probe designed to reach another star within a century. Laser sails need gigawatt-class phased lasers and materials that survive thousands of g; nothing is funded at that scale. Pure judgment.

standard-model.summary: The theory of the known elementary particles and three of the four forces, assembled from electroweak unification (1967) and quantum chromodynamics (1973). Every collider test since has agreed with it, though it leaves out gravity and dark matter.

efforts.who: Sheldon Glashow, Steven Weinberg, Abdus Salam
efforts.note: Electroweak theory; Nobel 1979.

efforts.who: David Gross, Frank Wilczek, David Politzer
efforts.note: Asymptotic freedom in QCD; Nobel 2004.

efforts.who: CERN (W and Z bosons, 1983), Fermilab (top quark, 1995)

higgs-boson.summary: The particle that confirms how other particles get mass, predicted in 1964 and found at CERN's Large Hadron Collider on July 4, 2012. It completed the Standard Model.

efforts.note: Peter Higgs and Francois Englert shared the 2013 Nobel.

efforts.who: CERN Future Circular Collider; China CEPC
efforts.note: Proposed Higgs factories of about 15 billion Swiss francs.

effort.note: The LHC machine cost about 4.6 billion Swiss francs to build; ATLAS and CMS each have about 3,000 to 5,000 members.

sources.title: CERN, The Large Hadron Collider (facts and figures)

gravitational-wave-detection.summary: Measuring ripples in spacetime from colliding black holes with laser interferometers 4 km long, sensitive to a thousandth of a proton's width. LIGO made the first detection on September 14, 2015, a century after Einstein's prediction.

efforts.who: LIGO (Caltech, MIT; Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, Barry Barish)
efforts.note: Nobel 2017.
Space-based detector.

effort.note: NSF's largest single investment, about $1.1 billion over four decades.

plate-tectonics.summary: The theory that Earth's surface is made of moving plates that spread at ocean ridges and sink at trenches, settled by seafloor magnetic stripes between 1962 and 1968. It explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountains and where ores and oil form.

efforts.who: Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews (Cambridge); Lawrence Morley
efforts.note: Magnetic stripes on the seafloor, mapped with Navy magnetometers.

efforts.who: J. Tuzo Wilson, Dan McKenzie, Jason Morgan, Xavier Le Pichon

effort.note: Built on Alfred Wegener's rejected continental drift (1912) and Cold War ocean surveys and seismograph networks set up to detect nuclear tests.

sources.title: USGS, This Dynamic Earth, developing the theory

climate-science.summary: Measurements and models showing that carbon dioxide from fossil fuels is accumulating and warming Earth, from the Keeling curve (1958) to Manabe and Wetherald's 1967 model. Its predictions of about 3 degrees C per doubling of CO2 have held up.

efforts.who: Charles David Keeling (Scripps), Mauna Loa CO2 record

efforts.note: Manabe shared the 2021 Nobel.
Estimated 1.5 to 4.5 C of warming per CO2 doubling.

sources.title: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Trends in atmospheric CO2 (Mauna Loa record)

scanning-tunneling-microscope.summary: A microscope that images individual atoms by measuring the quantum tunneling current to a sharp tip, built at IBM Zurich in 1981. In 1989 IBM used one to spell its name in 35 xenon atoms.

efforts.who: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer (IBM Zurich)
efforts.note: Nobel 1986; the atomic force microscope followed in 1986.
Positioned single atoms.

jet-airliner.summary: Passenger aircraft powered by jet engines, starting with the de Havilland Comet in 1952 and the Boeing 707 in 1958. Jets made intercontinental travel routine; airlines carried about 5 billion passengers in 2025.

efforts.note: Grounded after 1954 crashes from metal fatigue around square windows; the lessons reshaped aircraft design.
Wide-bodies and high-bypass turbofans cut cost per seat.

sources.title: IATA, Global Outlook for Air Transport (December 2025, about 5 billion passengers in 2025)

concorde.summary: Concorde flew passengers at twice the speed of sound from 1976 to 2003, but noise, fuel cost and a 2000 crash ended it, and no one flies supersonic passengers today. Quieter designs are being tested to revive the idea.

efforts.who: BAC and Aerospatiale (Air France, British Airways)

efforts.note: Passenger service lasted 55 flights.

efforts.who: Boom Supersonic (XB-1 broke the sound barrier January 2025); NASA and Lockheed X-59 low-boom demonstrator (first flight October 2025)

effort.note: Development cost about 1.3 billion pounds by 1976, several times the 1962 estimate, all paid by the two governments.

concorde.lost: Retired October 24, 2003 after the Air France crash (2000) and the post-2001 travel slump; only 14 aircraft ever flew in service. Overland supersonic flight is banned in the US since 1973 because of sonic booms.

sources.title: AIAA, NASA's X-59 performs first flight

container-shipping.summary: Moving goods in standard steel boxes that transfer unopened between ships, trains and trucks, launched by Malcom McLean's Ideal X in 1956. It cut port labor and loading costs by over 90 percent and made global supply chains possible.

efforts.note: 58 containers, Newark to Houston, April 26, 1956.
The largest ships now carry about 24,000 twenty-foot boxes.

effort.note: Loading cost fell from about $5.86 per ton loose to about 16 cents by container in 1956 (Levinson). Bernhofen et al. (2016) estimate containerization raised trade among rich countries more than all trade agreements of the era.

sources.title: Bernhofen, El-Sahli and Kneller 2016, Estimating the effects of the container revolution on world trade

high-speed-rail.summary: Electric trains on dedicated track running at 200 to 350 km/h, starting with Japan's Tokaido Shinkansen on October 1, 1964. China built about 50,000 km by 2025, over two thirds of the world's network.

efforts.who: Japanese National Railways, Tokaido Shinkansen (Hideo Shima)
efforts.note: No passenger deaths from train accidents in over 60 years.
4.28 billion high-speed trips in 2025.

efforts.who: Shanghai Transrapid maglev (2004); JR Central Chuo Shinkansen maglev
efforts.note: The Chuo line, 500 km/h, is delayed to the mid-2030s or later.

effort.note: The Tokaido line cost about 380 billion yen (about $1 billion then), roughly double its budget, with a World Bank loan.

sources.title: Railway News, China high-speed rail completes 50,000 km by 2025

electric-aviation.summary: Small battery-powered aircraft that take off and land vertically on many rotors, aimed at short city hops. China certified the first for commercial passenger operations in 2025; Western makers are in final certification.
electric-aviation.criterion: Electric air taxis with an FAA or EASA type certificate carry paying passengers on regular service in at least one US or European city.

efforts.note: Chinese type certificate in 2023 and approval for pilotless commercial passenger operations in March 2025.
Its first FAA-conforming aircraft began type inspection flight testing in March 2026, the fifth and final stage of certification; no type certificate by October 2026.
Archer flew its Midnight in Abu Dhabi in 2025 but had not begun FAA type inspection testing.
Lilium shut down in 2025; Volocopter went insolvent and was sold.

forecast.note: Joby is closest: it began type inspection flight testing in March 2026, the final stage of certification, and expects FAA pilots' for-credit flights to follow; that stage usually takes a year or more, and first certified service would follow soon after. Its 2026 passenger flights under the FAA's eVTOL pilot program come before a type certificate and do not meet this bar. China already allows commercial eVTOL passenger flights. Judgment: 2028.

carbon-fiber.summary: Fibers of nearly pure carbon, made by baking acrylic (PAN) filaments, set in epoxy to give parts stronger than steel at a fifth of the weight. Developed in Japan and Britain in the early 1960s, they now make up half of a Boeing 787.

efforts.note: High-performance graphite whiskers.

efforts.who: Akio Shindo (Osaka Government Industrial Research Institute)
efforts.note: PAN-based carbon fiber.

efforts.who: William Watt, Leslie Phillips, William Johnson (Royal Aircraft Establishment)

synthetic-diamond.summary: Diamond made from graphite at high pressure and temperature, first reproducibly at General Electric in 1954, later grown from gas by vapor deposition. Synthetic grit cuts and drills most of the world's hard materials.

efforts.note: Made diamonds but did not publish.

efforts.who: Chemical vapor deposition (Soviet and Japanese groups, 1970s to 1980s); Henan and Indian growers
efforts.note: Lab-grown gems passed half of US engagement rings in the 2020s.

graphene.summary: A single layer of carbon atoms in a honeycomb, isolated with sticky tape by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov in 2004. It is the strongest, most conductive thin material known, though mass-market uses are still mostly additives and coatings.

efforts.who: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov (University of Manchester)
efforts.note: Nobel 2010.
About 1 billion euros over ten years.
Superconductivity at a "magic angle".

carbon-nanotubes.summary: Hollow molecules of pure carbon: soccer-ball fullerenes found in 1985 and the tubes Sumio Iijima imaged in 1991. They are used to strengthen materials and in battery electrodes, but never became the wonder cables once hoped.

efforts.who: Harold Kroto, Robert Curl, Richard Smalley (Rice), fullerenes
efforts.note: Nobel in Chemistry 1996.

efforts.who: Iijima and Ichihashi; Donald Bethune (IBM), single-wall tubes

sources.title: Iijima 1991, Helical microtubules of graphitic carbon, Nature

3d-printing.summary: Building objects layer by layer from a digital model, first with stereolithography in the 1980s and now in plastic, metal, concrete and cells. It turned prototyping into a desktop task and makes rocket engines and implants that could not be machined.

efforts.who: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute)
efforts.note: Published photopolymer layering but let the patent lapse.
Patent filed 1984, granted 1986.

efforts.who: Carl Deckard and Joe Beaman (UT Austin), selective laser sintering; Scott Crump (Stratasys), fused deposition

efforts.note: Open-source self-copying printers; cheap printers spread after FDM patents expired in 2009.

efforts.who: SpaceX, Relativity, GE Aerospace (LEAP fuel nozzles), Rocket Lab
efforts.note: Printed metal engine parts in flight.

molecular-nanotechnology.summary: Making things with every atom where it is meant to be, as Richard Feynman suggested in 1959 and Eric Drexler argued in 1986. Two routes are live: biology, where designed proteins and DNA frameworks already assemble nanoscale structures, and mechanical positional assembly with microscope tips.
molecular-nanotechnology.criterion: Macroscopic objects (at least a gram) are manufactured to atomic precision, every atom in a specified place, by programmable molecular machinery, at a cost and rate that make the product useful rather than a demonstration.

efforts.who: Richard Feynman, There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom
efforts.note: The founding lecture.

efforts.who: Eric Drexler, Engines of Creation (1986) and Nanosystems (1992)
efforts.note: Disputed by Richard Smalley in 2003 over "fat fingers" and "sticky fingers".

efforts.who: Ben Feringa, Fraser Stoddart, Jean-Pierre Sauvage
efforts.note: Nobel for molecular machines.

efforts.who: David Baker (UW Institute for Protein Design); UK ARIA programmable matter
efforts.note: AI-designed proteins as nanoscale parts.

forecast.note: Read as atomic precision in bulk, not as nanoscale materials, which already exist. On the biological route, designed proteins and DNA origami build precise nanostructures, but nothing joins them into macroscopic objects; UK ARIA started a £50 million programme in 2026 on protein-templated materials. On the mechanical route, tips can do single-site covalent chemistry but no one has built a 3D covalent structure that way, and funding is tiny. A dated snapshot of the Metaculus question on molecular nanotechnology gave roughly 50 percent by 2040, which looks far too fast against the experimental record. I put a gram-scale atomically precise product around 2080, and note this is judgment rather than extrapolation.

sources.title: C&EN: the Drexler and Smalley debate (2003)
Feynman 1959, There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom

routes.name: Biological
routes.note: Build with designed proteins, DNA frameworks and engineered organisms. This is where the money and the results are.

routes.name: Mechanical
routes.note: Drexler's diamond mechanosynthesis, with tips that place atoms covalently, scaled up by machines that build machines.

desalination.summary: Pushing seawater through membranes that pass water but not salt, made practical by Loeb and Sourirajan's membrane around 1960. About 95 million cubic meters a day are now desalinated, supplying most drinking water in Israel and the Gulf.

efforts.note: Asymmetric cellulose acetate membrane; first commercial RO plant at Coalinga, California in 1965.
Thermal desalination, still common where fuel is cheap.

efforts.who: John Cadotte (FilmTec), thin-film composite polyamide membrane
IDE Technologies (Sorek, 2013); ACWA Power; Saudi Water Authority
efforts.note: Seawater RO now takes about 3 kWh per cubic meter.

sources.title: Jones et al. 2019, The state of desalination and brine production, Science of the Total Environment

carbon-capture.summary: Capturing CO2 from gas processing, power plants or factories and burying it deep underground. Norway's Sleipner has stored about a million metric tons a year since 1996, but global capture is only about 50 million metric tons a year, a tiny fraction of emissions.

efforts.note: CO2 injected to push out more oil, not for climate.
Driven by Norway's 1991 carbon tax.
First power plant CCS; below design capture rate.
First cross-border CO2 shipping and storage service.

sources.title: Global CCS Institute, Global Status of CCS 2024

direct-air-capture.summary: Machines that pull CO2 straight out of the air with sorbents or solvents so it can be buried, proposed by Klaus Lackner in 1999. Plants have run since 2017 but capture hundreds to a few thousand tonnes a year, far below their ratings, at several hundred dollars a tonne.
direct-air-capture.criterion: Direct air capture plants worldwide remove and permanently store at least 1 million tonnes of CO2 a year, net of their own emissions and verified by a third party.

efforts.note: Mammoth (designed for 36,000 tonnes a year) captured 105 tonnes in its first ten months with 12 of 72 units installed; all Iceland plants had captured about 2,400 tonnes by May 2025.
Designed for 500,000 tonnes a year in two phases; first-phase commissioning was delayed in mid-2026 with no new date.

effort.note: Stratos alone cost about $1.3 billion. Frontier's buyers (Stripe, Google, Shopify and others) pledged $1 billion in advance purchases from 2022.

forecast.note: Stratos alone would pass the bar if it runs near design, but every plant so far has run far below nameplate, and buyers paid about $340 a tonne on average for durable removal (CDR.fyi). Judgment: about 2033, once Stratos and the US DAC hubs operate for a full year.

sources.title: Gasworld, Climeworks upgrades DAC at Iceland facility after low capture
RBN Energy, Stratos DAC project targets Q2 2026 startup

gigaton-carbon-removal.summary: Removing a billion metric tons or more of CO2 a year with engineered methods such as direct air capture, bioenergy with capture, enhanced weathering and biochar. Climate pathways call for 7 to 9 billion metric tons a year of total removal by 2050; novel methods remove about 1.3 million today.
gigaton-carbon-removal.criterion: Engineered, durable methods (storing carbon for centuries or more) remove at least 1 billion tonnes of CO2 a year, verified.

efforts.who: Frontier advance market commitment (Stripe, Alphabet, Shopify, Meta, McKinsey)

efforts.note: Largest single buyer, tens of millions of tons contracted, mostly BECCS and forestry.

efforts.who: US DAC hubs (DOE); EU Carbon Removal Certification

forecast.note: Durable removal is about 2 million tonnes a year and growing about 40 percent a year (CDR.fyi, 2026); buyers have contracted about 50 million tonnes but only 1.7 million have been delivered. At 40 percent a year, a gigaton takes about 18 years, to the mid-2040s; but removal only sells if policy pays for it, and plants have underperformed (Mammoth). Climate pathways call for several gigatons by 2050. If carbon prices or mandates arrive in the 2030s, the mid-2050s is plausible; otherwise later.

sources.title: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026)
The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 2nd edition (2024)

routes.name: Direct air capture
routes.note: Energy-hungry; pairs with cheap solar, wind and geothermal.

routes.name: Bioenergy with capture
routes.note: Cheapest at scale but limited by land and biomass.

routes.name: Enhanced rock weathering
routes.note: Cheap to spread, hard to measure.

solar-geoengineering.summary: Cooling the planet by reflecting a little sunlight, most plausibly with aerosols sprayed into the stratosphere the way the 1991 Pinatubo eruption cooled Earth by about half a degree. It would be cheap and fast but would not remove CO2, and its governance is unresolved.
solar-geoengineering.criterion: Reflective particles are deliberately put into the stratosphere at scale (on the order of a million tonnes of sulfur dioxide or equivalent a year) for at least a year, with the stated aim of lowering global temperature.

efforts.note: Balloon test cancelled after opposition in Sweden.

efforts.who: UK ARIA Exploring Climate Cooling program
efforts.note: About £57 million for 22 projects, including small outdoor tests that release no particles into the stratosphere.
Raised $60 million in October 2025 ($75 million in all) to develop a reflective particle and delivery system.
Small sulfur balloon releases; Mexico banned such experiments in 2023, and Tennessee (2024) and Florida (2025) passed laws restricting geoengineering.

forecast.note: Technically feasible within about a decade of a decision (Smith and Wagner estimated about $2 billion a year for the first years). The barrier is political: a single country could act, which makes timing depend on climate damage and governance, and opposition grew in 2023 to 2025. Very uncertain.

sources.title: Smith and Wagner 2018, Stratospheric aerosol injection tactics and costs, Environmental Research Letters
MIT Technology Review, How one controversial startup hopes to cool the planet (2025)

nitrogen-fertilizer-scale.summary: The postwar spread of Haber-Bosch ammonia plants, many converted from explosives factories, that took nitrogen fertilizer from about 11 million tons a year in 1961 to over 100 million. Roughly half the world's people are fed by it.

efforts.who: US wartime ammonia plants converted to fertilizer
Yara, CF Industries, Sinopec and Chinese coal-based plants, Nutrien
efforts.note: About 1 to 2 percent of world energy goes into ammonia.

effort.note: Erisman et al. (2008) estimate about 48 percent of humanity depends on synthetic nitrogen. Green ammonia from electrolysis is the main substitute for gas feedstock.

sources.title: Erisman et al. 2008, How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world, Nature Geoscience

center-pivot-irrigation.summary: A long sprinkler arm that rotates around a well, watering a circle of up to a square kilometer, invented by Nebraska farmer Frank Zybach. It turned semi-arid plains into cropland and made the green circles seen from planes.

efforts.note: Patented 1952; Valmont and Lindsay industrialized it.

effort.note: Draws down aquifers such as the Ogallala faster than they recharge.

sources.title: Smithsonian, How center pivot irrigation brought the Dust Bowl back to life

drip-irrigation.summary: Delivering water drop by drop to each plant's roots through plastic tubes and emitters, using far less water than flooding or sprinklers. Simcha Blass and Kibbutz Hatzerim commercialized it as Netafim in 1965.

precision-agriculture.summary: Farming field by field and meter by meter with GPS-steered tractors, yield maps, soil sensors and variable-rate seeding and spraying. It saves seed, fertilizer and fuel and is now standard on large farms.

efforts.note: Yield monitors (1992) and GPS autosteer (late 1990s to 2000s).

efforts.who: Blue River Technology (Deere, See and Spray)
efforts.note: Camera-guided spot spraying of weeds.

sources.title: USDA ERS, Precision agriculture in the digital era (2023)

cultivated-meat.summary: Growing animal muscle and fat cells in bioreactors instead of raising animals. Singapore first approved sales in 2020, the US in 2023, Israel in 2024 and Australia and New Zealand in 2025, but output is tiny, costs are far above conventional meat, and seven US states have banned sales.
cultivated-meat.criterion: Cultivated meat is approved for sale and sold in ordinary retail, rather than in tasting events or single restaurants, in at least three major markets.

efforts.who: Mark Post (Maastricht University), first cultured burger
efforts.note: Cost about $330,000.
The first regulatory approval anywhere, November 2020.

efforts.who: UPSIDE Foods; Mosa Meat; Aleph Farms; Vow; Wildtype; Mission Barns
efforts.note: Five products cleared in the US by 2026; Vow quail approved in Australia and New Zealand in 2025; Florida, Alabama, Indiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska and Texas have banned sales.

forecast.note: Approvals keep coming (Singapore, the US, Israel, Australia and New Zealand, plus UK pet food), but retail distribution does not: products appear in single restaurants and then disappear. Investment fell to $73.9 million in 2025 from nearly $1 billion in 2021, about 140 companies remain, Believer Meats shut down in late 2025, and seven US states ban sales, with Florida's ban upheld on appeal in March 2026. Ordinary retail in three markets looks like the early 2030s; price parity is a separate, much later milestone.

sources.title: GFI: cultivated meat and seafood state of the industry report
FoodNavigator: cultivated meat regulation, where countries stand in 2026
WLRN: appeals court upholds Florida's ban on lab-grown meat (March 2026)
GFI, State of the industry, cultivated meat

research-grant-system.summary: Governments paying universities, through competitive peer-reviewed grants, to do basic research and train scientists, as Vannevar Bush proposed in 1945. The model created the modern research university and was copied worldwide.

efforts.who: Vannevar Bush, Science, the Endless Frontier
efforts.note: Report to President Truman, July 1945, after the wartime OSRD.

efforts.who: NIH extramural grants (1946), Office of Naval Research (1946), National Science Foundation (1950)

efforts.note: Let universities patent federally funded inventions, spurring tech transfer.

efforts.who: Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, UK Research Councils, Japan JSPS, China NSFC (1986), European Research Council (2007)

effort.note: US federal R&D runs about $200 billion a year; world R&D spending passed about $2.5 trillion. Grant writing and administration take a large share of researchers' time; a 2007 US survey put administrative work at about 42 percent.

sources.title: Bush 1945, Science, the Endless Frontier (GPO GovInfo full text)
NSF, National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

darpa.summary: A small agency of temporary program managers with broad freedom to fund risky projects toward specific goals, founded as ARPA in 1958 after Sputnik. It seeded the internet, GPS receivers, stealth and self-driving cars, and has been copied as ARPA-E, ARPA-H and the UK's ARIA.

efforts.who: ARPA-E (2009), IARPA (2006), ARPA-H (2022), UK ARIA (2023), Germany SPRIND (2019)

efforts.note: Time-limited nonprofit teams for tools no lab or startup would build.

sources.title: Azoulay et al. 2019, Funding breakthrough research, the ARPA model

cern.summary: Treaty-based labs where many countries pool money for machines none could build alone, starting with CERN in 1954. The model was reused for ITER, the European Southern Observatory and the ISS.

efforts.note: Tim Berners-Lee invented the web there in 1989.

iso-standards.summary: The International Organization for Standardization, founded in 1947, which sets shared specifications so parts, containers, screws and paperwork work across borders. Its 1968 container standard made global intermodal shipping work.

efforts.note: Electrical, telecom and internet standards bodies.

venture-capital.summary: Funds that buy stakes in young, risky technology companies and expect most to fail and a few to pay for all, begun by Georges Doriot's American Research and Development in 1946. It funded much of semiconductors, computing, biotech and now space and fusion.

efforts.who: Georges Doriot, American Research and Development Corporation
efforts.note: A $70,000 stake in Digital Equipment (1957) became hundreds of millions.

efforts.who: Arthur Rock; Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia (1972)
efforts.note: The 1979 ERISA prudent-man rule let pension funds invest.

efforts.who: Israel Yozma (1993); China state guidance funds

sources.title: Nicholas, VC, An American History (Harvard University Press)

outer-space-treaty.summary: The 1967 UN treaty that declares space free for all to explore, bans claims of national sovereignty and nuclear weapons in orbit, and makes states responsible for their companies' activities. It still frames debates over lunar bases and asteroid mining.

efforts.who: United Nations (US, USSR, UK first signers)

efforts.note: Over 50 signatories by 2025; China and Russia stand apart.

montreal-protocol.summary: The 1987 treaty that phased out ozone-destroying CFCs, ratified by every UN member state. The ozone layer is on track to recover by about 2066, making it the most successful global environmental agreement.

efforts.who: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland (1974); Joe Farman, British Antarctic Survey (1985)
efforts.note: Predicted, then found, the ozone hole.

efforts.who: UNEP and signatories; Kigali Amendment (2016) on HFCs

sources.title: UNEP Ozone Secretariat, The Montreal Protocol
WMO, Ozone layer on track to recover within four decades (2023)

ipcc.summary: A UN body, founded in 1988, in which thousands of volunteer scientists assess published climate research and governments approve the summaries line by line. Its reports set the scientific basis for the Paris Agreement.

efforts.who: World Meteorological Organization and UN Environment Programme
efforts.note: Shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize; Sixth Assessment 2021 to 2023, Seventh cycle under way.

open-source.summary: Licensing software so anyone may use, study, change and share it, organized around Richard Stallman's GNU project (1983) and the term "open source" (1998). Linux and other open projects now run most servers, phones and cloud infrastructure.

efforts.who: Richard Stallman, GNU project and GPL (1989)
Open Source Initiative (Bruce Perens, Eric Raymond)
GitHub (2008); open-weight AI models (Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen)

prediction-markets.summary: Markets where people bet on future events, so prices act as probabilities, plus scored forecasting communities. From the Iowa Electronic Markets in 1988 to Kalshi and Polymarket, they often beat polls and pundits.

efforts.who: University of Iowa, Iowa Electronic Markets
Robin Hanson (idea futures); DARPA Policy Analysis Market (cancelled 2003)
IARPA ACE tournament, Good Judgment Project (Philip Tetlock); Metaculus (2015)

sources.title: Wolfers and Zitzewitz 2004, Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives

inducement-prizes.summary: Paying for results instead of effort: a prize for the first to hit a goal, or a promise to buy a product if someone makes it. The Ansari XPRIZE was won by SpaceShipOne in 2004; a 2009 vaccine commitment and the 2022 Frontier carbon removal fund used the buyer's version.

efforts.who: XPRIZE Foundation (Peter Diamandis), Ansari X Prize
efforts.note: Won by Scaled Composites, funded by Paul Allen.
$1.5 billion; vaccines reached low-income countries years faster.

effort.note: Echoes the 1714 British Longitude Prize.

sources.title: Kremer, Levin and Snyder 2020, Advance Market Commitments, AEA Papers and Proceedings

carbon-pricing.summary: Making emitters pay for CO2, through taxes or capped tradeable permits, so markets find the cheapest cuts. The EU Emissions Trading System began in 2005; about a quarter of world emissions now face some carbon price.

efforts.note: Largest by covered emissions, at low prices.

sources.title: World Bank, State and Trends of Carbon Pricing

mouse-lifespan-drug.summary: Rapamycin fed to genetically mixed mice from 20 months of age (roughly 60 in human terms) extended median and maximum lifespan in both sexes at three independent sites. It was the first drug shown to slow aging in a mammal, and the start of the "geroprotector" idea.

efforts.who: David Harrison, Randy Strong, Richard Miller (NIA Interventions Testing Program)
efforts.where: Jackson Laboratory, UT Health San Antonio, University of Michigan, USA
efforts.note: Lifespan to 90 percent mortality rose 14 percent in females and 9 percent in males.

efforts.who: NIA Interventions Testing Program, later compounds
efforts.note: Acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and canagliflozin also extended lifespan (canagliflozin by 14 percent in males only); fisetin did not.

sources.title: Harrison et al. 2009, full text (PubMed Central)

epigenetic-aging-clocks.summary: Models that estimate biological age from DNA methylation at a few hundred sites. Steve Horvath's 2013 pan-tissue clock was the first to work across tissues; later clocks (GrimAge 2019, DunedinPACE 2022) predict death and disease or the pace of aging, and are now used as exploratory trial endpoints.

efforts.note: Pan-tissue clock from 353 CpG sites; Gregory Hannum and colleagues published a blood clock the same year.

efforts.who: Ake Lu and Steve Horvath (GrimAge); Daniel Belsky and Terrie Moffitt (DunedinPACE)

efforts.note: Its 2024 Nature Medicine paper notes there is still no consensus on how to validate aging biomarkers.

sources.title: Moqri et al., Validation of biomarkers of aging, Nature Medicine (2024)

aging-biomarker-endpoint.summary: The institutional step that makes aging drugs testable in a few years instead of the decades a lifespan trial would take. Without it, every route to rejuvenation has to prove itself one disease at a time.
aging-biomarker-endpoint.criterion: The FDA or EMA accepts a measure of biological aging (a clock, composite or functional index) as a surrogate or primary endpoint that can support approval of a drug whose claim is slowing aging, through biomarker qualification or in an approved drug's label. Use as an exploratory endpoint does not count.

efforts.who: ARPA-H PROSPR program (seven teams including Stanford, UT Health San Antonio, Columbia)
efforts.note: Up to $144 million over five years, awarded February 2026, to find early biomarkers that can serve as surrogates for long-term health outcomes in 1 to 3 year trials.
$101 million prize for restoring muscle, cognitive and immune function by 10 or more years; 20 finalists named in August 2026, results due in 2030.

forecast.note: No aging biomarker has been qualified; only a handful of biomarkers of any kind have ever been fully qualified through FDA's program, and none as surrogate endpoints. PROSPR's cohort and trial data arrive around 2030 to 2031 and XPRIZE results in 2030, so the evidence package could exist by the early 2030s. Biomarker qualification typically takes years more, so I put acceptance around 2036, with a real chance it never comes for clocks and a functional index is accepted instead.

sources.title: Moqri et al., Validation of biomarkers of aging, Nature Medicine (2024)

dog-lifespan-drug.summary: The first drug with a lifespan claim on its label, in any species. Loyal's LOY-002, a daily pill for senior dogs, has passed two of the three major technical sections of FDA review.
dog-lifespan-drug.criterion: A regulator (in practice FDA's Center for Veterinary Medicine) grants conditional or full approval to a drug labeled to extend lifespan or healthy lifespan in dogs.

efforts.note: FDA accepted the effectiveness section (February 2025) and target animal safety section (January 2026); manufacturing is pending. The STAY study enrolled 1,300 dogs at 70 clinics by July 2025.

forecast.note: Loyal says it expects to complete the manufacturing section and apply for conditional approval in 2027. FDA reviews of that section commonly take a year, so 2028 is the likely date.

sources.title: Loyal: LOY-002 target animal safety section accepted (January 2026)
Loyal: LOY-002 target animal safety section accepted (January 2026)

aging-drug-approved.summary: Aging treated as an indication in its own right, the model proposed by the TAME trial of metformin. Several candidate geroprotectors exist (rapamycin, metformin, GLP-1 and SGLT2 drugs); none has been tested this way to completion.
aging-drug-approved.criterion: A major regulator (FDA or EMA) approves a drug for healthy older people on the basis of a randomized trial showing it delays a composite of several age-related diseases (for example cardiovascular disease, cancer, dementia and death), or improves an accepted aging endpoint, rather than treating one disease.

efforts.who: TAME trial (Nir Barzilai, American Federation for Aging Research)
efforts.note: Designed for about 3,000 people aged 65 to 79 over six years with a composite endpoint; still described as awaiting full funding in 2026 and not yet enrolling.
114 people for 48 weeks; missed its primary endpoint (visceral fat), with modest gains in women's lean mass.
In 17,604 adults with obesity, all-cause death fell by about 19 percent (hazard ratio 0.81), a hint of broad protective effects, though not a formally tested result.

efforts.who: VITAL-H (UT Health San Antonio, ARPA-H PROSPR)
efforts.note: A hybrid trial of an SGLT2 inhibitor, rapamycin and semaglutide on healthspan biomarkers.

forecast.note: FDA does not recognize aging as an indication. A TAME-style trial takes about six years after funding, plus a year or two for review, so even a 2027 start gives 2034 at the earliest. A biomarker endpoint (about 2036 in this tree) would let shorter trials support a claim. GLP-1 drugs may get there sideways by accumulating broad outcome labels. I put the first approval whose claim is aging itself around 2040.

sources.title: Moel et al., PEARL rapamycin trial, Aging 17 (2025)
Moel et al., PEARL rapamycin trial, Aging 17 (2025)

senolytics-approved.summary: Drugs that clear senescent cells, which accumulate with age and secrete inflammatory signals. Clearing them extends healthy life in mice, but the first human trials have mostly missed their endpoints.
senolytics-approved.criterion: A drug whose mechanism is selectively killing senescent cells is approved by the FDA or EMA for any indication after meeting its primary endpoint in a randomized trial.

efforts.who: James Kirkland, Sundeep Khosla and colleagues (Mayo Clinic), dasatinib plus quercetin
efforts.note: A 2024 phase 2 bone trial in 60 women missed its primary endpoint; benefit appeared only in those with many senescent cells.
Missed its primary endpoint in diabetic macular edema in 2025; the board approved a plan of dissolution in June 2025.
Early-stage topical and systemic senolytics.
