forecast.note: As of 2026 no senolytic is approved and none is in phase 3. A new phase 2 success in the late 2020s, then phase 3 and review, gives the mid 2030s. I put 2036, with a real chance the class fails.

partial-reprogramming.summary: Briefly switching on the Yamanaka factors resets aging marks without turning cells back into stem cells. Cyclic expression extended lifespan in progeroid mice and improved tissue repair in normal ones; later work restored vision in old mice with three factors (OSK).

efforts.who: Alejandro Ocampo, Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte (Salk Institute)

efforts.note: OSK gene therapy restored vision in aged mice and in a glaucoma model (Nature 2020).

reprogramming-human-trial.summary: The first test of rejuvenating cells in place in people, starting in the eye, where a small dose can be injected locally and switched on and off with an oral drug.
reprogramming-human-trial.criterion: A controlled human trial of an in vivo partial reprogramming therapy reports both acceptable safety and a measured functional benefit (for example vision in optic neuropathy) in one organ.

efforts.note: IND cleared January 2026; first patient dosed June 2026 (NCT07290244), about 18 patients with glaucoma or NAION; primary safety completion due May 2027.
Raised $435 million in 2026 and plans a first human trial of a liver reprogramming medicine in 2027.
No disclosed reprogramming candidate in the clinic as of 2026.

forecast.note: ER-100's phase 1 finishes its primary safety readout in 2027; a controlled efficacy result needs a phase 2, about 2029 to 2031.

sources.title: Life Biosciences: first patient dosed with ER-100 (June 2026)
Life Biosciences: first patient dosed with ER-100 (June 2026)

systemic-reprogramming.summary: Rejuvenating cells throughout the body by delivering reprogramming factors everywhere, the version of reprogramming that would matter for aging as a whole. Safe delivery to every tissue, and avoiding tumors from over-reprogramming, are the obstacles.
systemic-reprogramming.criterion: A reprogramming therapy delivered systemically (to most major organs, not one eye or one tissue) shows in a randomized trial a reduction of at least 5 years in a validated aging measure across several organ systems, without excess cancer, over at least two years of follow-up.

efforts.who: Altos Labs, NewLimit, Retro Biosciences, Life Biosciences
efforts.note: Together these companies have raised well over $4 billion; none has a systemic reprogramming therapy in humans as of 2026.

forecast.note: Local reprogramming in the eye began in 2026 and liver trials are planned from 2027. Systemic gene delivery to most organs does not yet exist for any therapy, and a two-year randomized trial with organ-level aging measures would follow years of dose-finding. I put a result meeting this bar in the 2040s, with very wide uncertainty.

longevity-escape-velocity.summary: The point where medicine adds years of life faster than they pass for people who are already old. Today life expectancy in rich countries rises by roughly 0.1 to 0.2 years per year.
longevity-escape-velocity.criterion: In at least one country, remaining life expectancy at age 60 rises by at least one year per calendar year, sustained for ten years, so that older people's expected remaining lifespan stops shrinking.

efforts.who: Aubrey de Grey (who coined the term) and the SENS and LEV foundations

forecast.note: Metaculus' question on this (life expectancy rising a year per year) has had community medians between about 2050 and 2060 in recent snapshots, with an interquartile range from about 2039 to after 2180; I could not read the live value. Life expectancy gains in rich countries slowed after 2010. Measured at age 60, this needs a rejuvenation therapy that is widely used, not just approved, so I put it about a decade after rejuvenation therapies, around 2070, and well later than the forecasting community.

sources.title: Metaculus: when will a country reach longevity escape velocity?
Metaculus: when will a country reach longevity escape velocity?

organ-transplantation.summary: Replacing a failed organ with a donor's. Joseph Murray transplanted a kidney between identical twins in 1954, sidestepping rejection; drugs that suppress the immune system (azathioprine, then ciclosporin in the 1980s) made transplants between unrelated people routine.

efforts.who: Joseph Murray, John Merrill, Hartwell Harrison (Peter Bent Brigham Hospital)
efforts.note: Ronald Herrick's kidney given to his twin Richard on December 23, 1954. Murray shared the 1990 Nobel Prize.

sources.title: Harvard Medical School: transplant pioneer, Nobel laureate dies at 93

pig-organ-xenotransplant.summary: Hearts and kidneys from pigs with ten to 69 gene edits, transplanted into living people as compassionate-use cases. The record by 2026 is a pig kidney that kept a man off dialysis for 271 days.

efforts.who: Bartley Griffith, Muhammad Mohiuddin (University of Maryland), with Revivicor
efforts.note: Pig hearts in David Bennett (2022, about 60 days) and Lawrence Faucette (2023, about six weeks).

efforts.who: Massachusetts General Hospital with eGenesis; NYU Langone (Robert Montgomery) with United Therapeutics
efforts.note: Rick Slayman (2024); Towana Looney (130 days, 2024 to 2025); Tim Andrews (271 days dialysis-free, then a human kidney in January 2026). Five eGenesis patients by September 2026, none past a year.

efforts.who: Beicheng Sun (First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University)
efforts.note: An auxiliary pig liver in a living patient, removed after 38 days.

sources.title: Harvard Medical School: pig kidney patient becomes first to progress to a human kidney (2026)

xenotransplant-approved.summary: An unlimited supply of organs grown in pigs, ending the waiting list (about 90,000 Americans wait for a kidney). The first formal trials began in late 2025.
xenotransplant-approved.criterion: A regulator (FDA or equivalent) licenses a gene-edited pig kidney (or heart) for patients with organ failure after a clinical trial in which a majority of recipients keep a working graft at one year.

efforts.who: United Therapeutics (Revivicor), EXPAND trial of the UKidney
efforts.note: First trial transplant at NYU Langone in November 2025; a first cohort of six with a 24-week endpoint, designed to support a licensing application. A pig heart trial (EXPRESS) was cleared in May 2026.
An FDA-cleared trial of 33 patients aged 50 to 70, due to start in early 2027.

forecast.note: No recipient has yet passed one year with a working pig kidney. Trials with 24-week endpoints started in 2025 to 2027; expanding cohorts and a licensing review typically take five or more years. A Metaculus question on xenotransplantation becoming routine had a community median around 2043 (few forecasters). I put the first licensed product around 2033, and routine use (thousands a year) a decade later.

sources.title: United Therapeutics: first transplant in the EXPAND trial (November 2025)

organoids.summary: Stem cells grown in a gel organize themselves into miniature, simplified organs: gut (2009), brain (2013), kidney, liver and more. They are used to model disease and test drugs, and FDA's 2025 plan to phase out required animal testing leans on them.

efforts.note: A single Lgr5 stem cell built crypt-villus gut structures in a dish.
Cerebral organoids.

efforts.who: Ryuichi Okamoto (Tokyo Medical and Dental University)
efforts.note: The first transplant of a patient's own colon organoids into a person with ulcerative colitis.

sources.title: FDA plan to phase out animal testing requirements (April 2025)

engineered-tissue-implants.summary: Simple engineered tissues, grown from a patient's own cells on a scaffold, implanted in people: bladder walls (2006), a bioprinted ear (2022), a bioprinted trachea (2023) and cornea (2025). All are thin or hollow structures that need little blood supply.

efforts.who: Anthony Atala (Children's Hospital Boston, later Wake Forest)
efforts.note: Engineered bladder tissue grafted into seven children with spina bifida.
A bioprinted ear made from the patient's own cartilage cells, in a phase 1/2a trial.

efforts.who: Precise Bio (bioprinted cornea, Rambam Medical Center)

sources.title: Nature news: doctors grow organs from patients' own cells (2006)

lab-grown-solid-organ.summary: Building a whole organ, blood vessels and all, from a patient's own cells, so it needs no donor and no immune suppression. Thick tissue needs a dense network of vessels, which no one can yet print.
lab-grown-solid-organ.criterion: A bioprinted or otherwise lab-grown vascularized solid organ (kidney, liver, heart or lung, or a lobe big enough to replace the organ's function) is transplanted into a person and sustains that function, with no dialysis or other support, for at least a year.

efforts.who: ARPA-H PRINT program (Carnegie Mellon, Wake Forest, Wyss Institute, UC San Diego, UT Southwestern)
efforts.note: Up to $176.8 million over five years from January 2026 to bioprint livers and kidney tissue; Carnegie Mellon aims to be ready for a first human trial of a liver construct around 2031.

efforts.who: United Therapeutics (lung scaffolds); Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine

forecast.note: No vascularized solid organ has been built and implanted in a person. PRINT's goal is a first human trial of a partial liver around 2031, which would be a small graft assisting the patient's own organ. A whole organ that replaces function for a year is a much higher bar, so I put it in the mid 2040s.

sources.title: ARPA-H: teams set to bioprint universally matched organs on demand (January 2026)
ARPA-H: teams set to bioprint universally matched organs on demand (January 2026)

organ-vitrification.summary: Rat kidneys were cooled to a glass without ice crystals, stored for up to 100 days, rewarmed evenly with iron-oxide nanoparticles in a magnetic field, and transplanted; all five recipients regained full kidney function. In 2026 the same method recovered pig kidneys of human size.

efforts.who: John Bischof, Erik Finger and colleagues (University of Minnesota)
ATP-Bio (NSF center) and University of Minnesota
efforts.note: A preprint (October 2026) reports human-scale pig kidneys stored up to a year at -150 C; transplanted ones had blood flow and made urine, but follow-up was about two hours.

sources.title: ATP-Bio: cryopreservation and nanowarming of human-scale kidneys (October 2026)

organ-banking.summary: Storing donor organs indefinitely instead of for hours, so organs can be matched and shipped anywhere, and a first step toward reversible cryopreservation of larger systems.
organ-banking.criterion: A human kidney (or other solid organ) that was vitrified and stored for at least a month is rewarmed and transplanted into a patient, and works for at least a year.

efforts.who: ATP-Bio and University of Minnesota (Bischof, Finger)

efforts.note: Raised a $58 million series A in 2025 for organ and tissue cryopreservation; no organ-level results published.

forecast.note: Rat kidneys work after vitrification (2023), and human-size pig kidneys survived a few hours after transplant (2026 preprint). The next steps are long-term survival of a large animal on a vitrified kidney, then a first human case; each has taken several years in this field. I put the first human case in the late 2030s.

sources.title: ATP-Bio: cryopreservation and nanowarming of human-scale kidneys (October 2026)
ATP-Bio: cryopreservation and nanowarming of human-scale kidneys (October 2026)

cryonics.summary: Storing legally dead people at liquid nitrogen temperature in the hope that future medicine can revive and repair them. James Bedford was the first, in 1967. About 500 people are stored, mainly at Alcor and the Cryonics Institute; none has been revived, and the damage from freezing and from delays after death is not known to be reversible.

efforts.who: Alcor Life Extension Foundation; Cryonics Institute; Tomorrow Bio
Robert McIntyre and Gregory Fahy (21st Century Medicine), aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation
efforts.note: Preserved rabbit and pig brain connectomes well enough to win the Brain Preservation Foundation prizes, but the fixative rules out biological revival.

sources.title: McIntyre and Fahy, Aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation, Cryobiology 71:448 (2015)

reversible-suspended-animation.summary: Pausing a whole body and restarting it later, the "pause and wait" route around aging: a person could wait out a disease, or aging itself, until a cure exists. It needs whole-organ vitrification scaled up to every tissue at once, including the brain.
reversible-suspended-animation.criterion: A large mammal (at least a dog or pig) is cooled below -100 C for at least a month, rewarmed and revived with normal behavior and memory; for humans, the same done deliberately to a living patient as a medical procedure.

efforts.note: Working on tissue and organ scale; Until Labs reported recovering electrical activity in cryopreserved rodent brain slices (2024).

forecast.note: No mammal larger than tissue samples and rat kidneys has been vitrified and recovered. Metaculus forecasters give about a 5 percent chance that a cryonically preserved person is revived before 2100, and in earlier snapshots put the first large mammal revived from cryopreservation around 2079. I put a deliberate, reversible procedure around 2090, with a long tail.

sources.title: Metaculus: will a cryonically frozen individual be resuscitated before 2100?

base-editing.summary: CRISPR tools that rewrite DNA letters without cutting both strands: base editors (2016) swap one base for another, and prime editors (2019) write short insertions, deletions and all twelve kinds of point change. Most disease-causing variants are within their reach.

efforts.note: Prime editing; the first patients were treated by Prime Medicine in 2024 to 2025.

crispr-therapy-approved.summary: Casgevy edits a patient's own blood stem cells outside the body to switch fetal hemoglobin back on, curing most patients' sickle cell crises. The UK approved it in November 2023 and the FDA in December 2023.

efforts.note: Treatment needs chemotherapy conditioning and costs about $2 million in the US.

sources.title: FDA approves first gene therapies to treat sickle cell disease (December 2023)

in-vivo-gene-editing.summary: Editing genes inside the body with a single infusion, usually lipid nanoparticles that carry the editor to the liver. Trials have knocked out disease genes for years at a time, and a personalized base editor treated a baby with a rare metabolic disease in 2025.
in-vivo-gene-editing.criterion: The FDA or EMA approves a gene-editing therapy delivered directly into the body (not cells edited outside it), after a randomized phase 3 trial.

efforts.who: Intellia Therapeutics (lonvo-z, NTLA-2002, hereditary angioedema; nex-z, NTLA-2001, ATTR amyloidosis)
efforts.note: First in vivo CRISPR in humans (2021). Lonvo-z cut attacks 87 percent in phase 3; FDA accepted its application with a decision date of March 10, 2027. Nex-z was on clinical hold from October 2025 to early 2026 after a patient's death.

efforts.who: Verve Therapeutics (acquired by Eli Lilly), VERVE-102 base editor for PCSK9
efforts.note: One dose cut LDL cholesterol by up to 62 percent for up to 18 months in phase 1b (2026).

efforts.who: Kiran Musunuru, Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas (CHOP and Penn)
efforts.note: A base editor designed for one baby (KJ Muldoon) with CPS1 deficiency, made and given within months.

forecast.note: Lonvo-z has a priority review decision date of March 10, 2027, with no advisory committee planned. Approval on that date is likely but not certain given the nex-z safety event, so 2027 with a window to 2029.

sources.title: Intellia: lonvo-z application accepted with priority review (September 2026)

worm-connectome.summary: The full wiring diagram of the nematode worm, 302 neurons and about 7,000 synapses, traced by hand from serial electron micrographs over more than a decade. Forty years later the worm still has not been convincingly simulated from it.

efforts.who: John White, Eileen Southgate, Nichol Thomson, Sydney Brenner (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology)

sources.title: White et al., Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 314:1 (1986)

expansion-microscopy.summary: Tissue is embedded in a swellable gel and physically enlarged about fourfold or more, so an ordinary light microscope resolves detail near 70 nanometers. With protein labels it is a candidate route to cheaper connectomes that also record which molecules sit at each synapse.

efforts.who: Fei Chen, Paul Tillberg, Edward Boyden (MIT)
E11 Bio (PRISM, protein barcodes plus expansion)
efforts.note: Aims to cut the cost of a mouse connectome about 100-fold compared with electron microscopy.

sources.title: MIT News: a brief history of expansion microscopy (2025)

fly-connectome.summary: The complete wiring of an adult fruit fly brain: about 139,000 neurons and 50 million synapses, reconstructed from electron microscopy by AI segmentation and years of human proofreading. A whole male central nervous system (about 167,000 neurons) followed in 2025 to 2026.

efforts.who: FlyWire Consortium (Mala Murthy, Sebastian Seung, Princeton, and many labs)
Janelia FlyEM, University of Cambridge and Google
efforts.note: The male central nervous system, brain plus nerve cord.

mouse-cortex-connectome.summary: One cubic millimeter of mammalian cortex mapped at synapse resolution: a fragment of human temporal cortex (2024, 1.4 petabytes) and mouse visual cortex with matched recordings of activity (2025, about 200,000 cells and 524 million synapses). A whole mouse brain is about 500 times larger.

efforts.who: Jeff Lichtman (Harvard) and Viren Jain (Google), H01
MICrONS Consortium (Allen Institute, Princeton, Baylor; IARPA-funded)
efforts.note: Over 150 scientists for more than seven years.

whole-mouse-connectome.summary: The first complete connectome of a mammal brain, about 1,000 times the fly's. Imaging is feasible; the bottleneck is proofreading the reconstruction, estimated at 100,000 person-years with today's tools.
whole-mouse-connectome.criterion: A synapse-resolution, proofread wiring diagram of an entire adult mouse brain (about 70 million neurons), publicly released.

efforts.note: $150 million over five years; its flagship maps 10 cubic millimeters of mouse hippocampus, about a fiftieth of the brain.
Targets a whole mouse connectome within about five years of 2024 by expansion microscopy.

forecast.note: Wellcome's 2023 Scaling Connectomics report set a whole mouse brain as a 10 to 15 year goal, which gives 2033 to 2038. E11 Bio's roadmap is faster (about 2029) but depends on an unproven method. Each step so far (fly 2024, cubic millimeter 2025) took seven or more years from start. I put 2036.

routes.name: Electron microscopy
routes.note: The proven method, but costs estimated at $7 to 21 billion, mostly proofreading, unless AI removes it.

routes.name: Expansion microscopy
routes.note: Light microscopy with protein barcodes to trace neurons; cheaper and adds molecular labels, but not yet shown at scale.

animal-brain-emulation.summary: The test case for brain emulation: does a wiring diagram plus physiology reproduce what a real nervous system does? Simple fly-brain models already predict some circuits, but no organism, not even the 302-neuron worm, has been emulated in full.
animal-brain-emulation.criterion: A simulation built from an animal's connectome plus measured neuron and synapse properties (worm, larval zebrafish or fly), coupled to a body, reproduces most of the animal's natural behaviors and its recorded neural activity without being trained to do so, confirmed in a peer-reviewed study.

efforts.who: Philip Shiu, Kristin Scott and colleagues (UC Berkeley)
efforts.note: A simple spiking model of the whole fly brain predicted feeding and grooming circuits, confirmed with optogenetics.

efforts.who: Lei Ma and colleagues (BAAIWorm, Beijing Academy of AI and Peking University)
efforts.note: A closed-loop model of worm brain, body and environment that reproduces steering toward food.
Claimed in March 2026 a fly-brain model in a simulated body that walks, grooms and feeds; not peer reviewed.

forecast.note: The 2025 State of Brain Emulation report distinguishes simulations that reproduce outputs from emulations that recreate internal dynamics, and finds no organism emulated yet; fewer than 500 people work on it. The limiting data are whole-brain activity recordings and synapse properties, now being collected for the worm, larval zebrafish and fly. I put a convincing fly or worm emulation around 2033.

sources.title: Zanichelli et al., State of Brain Emulation Report 2025 (arXiv)
Zhao et al., BAAIWorm, Nature Computational Science 4:978 (2024)
The Decoder: startup claims full brain emulation of a fruit fly (2026)

mouse-brain-emulation.summary: The first emulation of a mammal brain, and of an individual's memories rather than a species' wiring.
mouse-brain-emulation.criterion: An emulation built from one mouse's connectome and molecular data reproduces that mouse's learned behaviors (for example a trained maze or task) and its recorded neural activity better than any generic model.

forecast.note: Needs a mouse connectome (about 2036 here) plus a way to read synapse strengths and molecular state from the same brain, which no method yet does, plus the fly-to-mouse jump in simulation (about 500 times more neurons). I put it in the early 2050s.

sources.title: Zanichelli et al., State of Brain Emulation Report 2025 (arXiv)
Zanichelli et al., State of Brain Emulation Report 2025 (arXiv)

human-connectome.summary: About 1,000 times the volume of a mouse brain and a zettabyte-scale dataset by electron microscopy. The 2024 cubic millimeter of human cortex was about a millionth of it.
human-connectome.criterion: A synapse-resolution wiring diagram of an entire human brain (about 86 billion neurons and 100 trillion or more synapses), reconstructed and proofread to the accuracy of the fly connectome.

forecast.note: Mapped volume grew from a fly brain to a cubic millimeter in about a year (2024 to 2025), and a mouse brain is expected in the 2030s. If the roughly 1,000-fold step from mouse to human takes two to three decades as earlier steps did, a human brain arrives in the 2060s.

speech-neuroprosthesis.summary: Implants that decode attempted speech in people who cannot speak: 62 to 78 words a minute in 2023, 97 percent accuracy over months in 2024, and near-instant synthesized voice in 2025. Natural conversation runs about 150 words a minute.

efforts.who: Francis Willett, Jaimie Henderson, Krishna Shenoy (Stanford, BrainGate)
efforts.note: 62 words a minute, 24 percent word error on a large vocabulary.
78 words a minute with an avatar (2023); streaming voice in 80 millisecond steps (2025).

efforts.who: Nicholas Card, Sergey Stavisky, David Brandman (UC Davis)
efforts.note: 97.5 percent accuracy over 8.4 months in a man with ALS.

bci-approved.summary: The point where implanted interfaces become a medical product rather than a research trial. China approved a low-channel implant (Neuracle's NEO, eight electrodes on the brain's surface) in March 2026; no high-bandwidth device is approved in the US or Europe.
bci-approved.criterion: The FDA (or EU notified bodies) grants market approval (PMA or De Novo, or a CE mark) to an implanted brain-computer interface that lets people with paralysis control a computer or communicate, for permanent home use.

efforts.who: Synchron (Stentrode, delivered through a blood vessel)
efforts.note: Six patients in its US early feasibility study with no device-related serious adverse events at 12 months; a $200 million round in 2025 funds a pivotal trial, still being prepared in mid 2026.
21 participants by January 2026 by its own count, more since; a speech trial started in late 2025.
FDA approved its trial in November 2025; first long-term implant June 2026 at the University of Michigan.
Approved by China's NMPA in March 2026 for spinal cord injury, described as the world's first approved invasive BCI.

forecast.note: No company had started a pivotal trial by mid 2026. Pivotal device trials typically run two to three years, with a year of review, which points to about 2029 to 2031. One analysis expects Synchron to file around 2027 or later. I put the first US approval in 2030.

sources.title: MIT Technology Review: China approves a brain chip (June 2026)
MIT Technology Review: China approves a brain chip (June 2026)
University of Michigan: first human Paradromics implant (2026)

single-atom-manipulation.summary: The tip of a scanning tunneling microscope used to drag individual atoms into place: 35 xenon atoms spelling "IBM" on nickel at 4 kelvin. It showed that matter can be arranged atom by atom, though only slowly, in ultra-high vacuum and near absolute zero.

efforts.note: Published in Nature in April 1990.
X-ray characterization of a single atom, extending what can be measured one atom at a time.

tip-mechanosynthesis.summary: Making and breaking covalent bonds at chosen sites with a probe tip: pulling single silicon atoms out of a surface and putting them back (2003), and placing single phosphorus atoms in silicon with atomic-lattice accuracy by hydrogen-resist lithography, used to build a single-atom transistor (2012) and silicon qubit arrays.

efforts.who: Noriaki Oyabu, Oscar Custance, Seizo Morita (Osaka University)
efforts.note: Mechanical vertical manipulation of silicon atoms with an atomic force microscope.
Single-atom transistor (2012); later arrays of thousands of atom-placed qubit registers.

sources.title: Oyabu et al., Physical Review Letters 90:176102 (2003)

positional-assembly-3d.summary: Drexler's "mechanosynthesis": building solid objects such as diamond lattices by moving reactive fragments into place with tools. Designs and simulations exist (Freitas and Merkle), but nobody has built a three-dimensional covalent structure this way.
positional-assembly-3d.criterion: A peer-reviewed demonstration of a probe tip (or array of tips) adding atoms or small molecules one at a time to a growing covalent 3D structure of at least 1,000 atoms, with per-step yield above 99 percent, following a programmed blueprint.

efforts.who: Robert Freitas, Ralph Merkle; CBN Nano Technologies
efforts.note: Tooltip designs and patents for diamond mechanosynthesis; no experimental build reported.

efforts.who: Zyvex Labs DARPA atomically precise manufacturing program
efforts.note: Roughly $15 million over five years for tip-based silicon patterning.

forecast.note: Covalent tip chemistry works for single sites on flat surfaces at cryogenic temperatures; throughput and reliability are many orders of magnitude short of building in 3D. Funding is small. My judgment is that a 1,000-atom demonstration needs two decades of focused work that has barely started, so the mid 2040s, with a long tail.

sources.title: C&EN: the Drexler and Smalley debate on molecular assemblers (2003)
C&EN: the Drexler and Smalley debate on molecular assemblers (2003)

dna-origami.summary: A long single DNA strand folded into almost any 2D or 3D shape about 100 nanometers across by a few hundred short "staple" strands, with features every 6 nanometers. By 2017 assemblies reached gigadaltons; they are used as scaffolds to place molecules, as nanopores and as drug carriers in animal studies.

efforts.note: Proposed building with branched DNA junctions, founding structural DNA nanotechnology.

efforts.who: Hendrik Dietz (TU Munich); William Shih, Peng Yin (Harvard Wyss Institute)
efforts.note: 3D origami, DNA bricks and gigadalton-scale assemblies. No DNA nanostructure medicine has reached a human trial as of 2026.

de-novo-protein-design.summary: Designing proteins that nature never made, from scratch: a new fold (Top7, 2003), self-assembling nanoparticles in an approved vaccine (2022), and since RFdiffusion (2023) binders, enzymes and antivenoms designed by generative AI in days. It earned David Baker half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

efforts.who: Brian Kuhlman, David Baker (University of Washington)
efforts.note: Top7, a protein fold not seen in nature.

efforts.who: UW Institute for Protein Design and SK bioscience (SKYCovione)
efforts.note: A COVID-19 vaccine built on a designed nanoparticle, approved in Korea in June 2022.

efforts.who: Joseph Watson, David Baker and colleagues (RFdiffusion)
efforts.note: Followed by designed serine hydrolase enzymes and snake-toxin binders in 2025.

artificial-molecular-machines.summary: Synthetic molecules with parts that move on command: shuttles (1991), light-driven rotary motors (1999), a molecular car. The 2016 Nobel Prize went to Jean-Pierre Sauvage, Fraser Stoddart and Ben Feringa.

efforts.who: Fraser Stoddart (molecular shuttle, 1991); Ben Feringa (rotary motor, 1999); Jean-Pierre Sauvage (catenanes, 1983)

molecule-building-machines.summary: Synthetic machines that make a specific product step by step: a rotaxane that walks along a track and joins amino acids in order, a crude ribosome (2013), and a programmable molecular arm that builds any of four stereoisomers (2017). They are slow (hours per bond), single-use and make only short products.

programmable-molecular-assembler.summary: A general-purpose builder at the molecular scale, something like a ribosome that can make materials other than proteins. It could come from designed proteins and DNA frameworks, from synthetic chemistry, or from a mix.
programmable-molecular-assembler.criterion: A designed (not evolved) molecular machine that reads a replaceable instruction sequence and builds, by positioned covalent steps, products of at least 20 steps from a set of at least five building blocks, including non-biological ones, without being consumed, at a rate of at least one step per minute.

efforts.note: About £50 million to get engineered proteins to template the assembly of inorganic and composite materials.

efforts.who: David Leigh (Manchester); David Baker (UW Institute for Protein Design)

forecast.note: Leigh predicted molecular factories within 10 to 20 years in 2017, and no step change is reported since. AI protein design is moving faster than synthetic chemistry, and ARIA is funding the protein route. My judgment is the late 2040s.

sources.title: University of Manchester: world's first molecular robot capable of building molecules (2017)

routes.name: Designed biology
routes.note: Use designed proteins and DNA frameworks as the tooling, the path most funding now follows.

routes.name: Synthetic chemistry
routes.note: Extend Leigh-style small-molecule machines into faster, reusable programmable synthesizers.

engineered-microbe-manufacturing.summary: Yeast and bacteria given whole new metabolic pathways to make drugs and chemicals: semi-synthetic artemisinin at industrial scale (2013), opiate precursors from sugar (2015). Biology can make the molecule; beating the incumbent on cost is harder, and Sanofi stopped artemisinin production by 2015.

efforts.who: Jay Keasling (UC Berkeley), Amyris and Sanofi
efforts.note: Production began in 2013, targeting 35 tonnes a year; none was made in 2015 as plant-derived prices fell.
A yeast pathway of more than 20 enzymes (2015); Antheia's first commercial thebaine delivery from 116,000 liter fermentations in 2024.

sources.title: Antheia: first commercial delivery of thebaine (2024)

minimal-cell.summary: JCVI-syn3.0, a bacterium running on a designed genome cut to 473 genes, fewer than any free-living organism; the job of about a third of them is still unknown. Its successor syn3A (2019) restored normal division.

efforts.who: Clyde Hutchison, John Glass, Craig Venter and colleagues (J. Craig Venter Institute)

recoded-genome.summary: E. coli with its 4-megabase genome rewritten to use fewer codons: 61 instead of 64 (2019), then 57 (2025), freeing codons to encode non-natural amino acids and, in principle, making cells resistant to viruses.

efforts.who: Julius Fredens, Jason Chin and colleagues (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology)
efforts.note: Syn57 made over 101,000 codon changes across the genome.

synthetic-yeast-genome.summary: All 16 chromosomes of baker's yeast, about 12 megabases, redesigned and built from synthetic DNA by an international consortium, the first synthetic genome of a cell with a nucleus. The last chromosome was finished in January 2025; combining them all in one strain was still under way.

efforts.who: Sc2.0 consortium (Jef Boeke, NYU, with groups in China, the UK, Australia, Singapore and the USA)
efforts.note: A strain carrying 6.5 synthetic chromosomes was reported in 2023.

sources.title: Lab Online: final chromosome completed in the synthetic yeast genome (2025)

synthetic-human-chromosome.summary: The proof of concept for writing mammalian genomes, and the target of the UK's Synthetic Human Genome project. It is four times the size of the whole yeast genome and full of repeated sequence.
synthetic-human-chromosome.criterion: A complete human chromosome (at least 50 megabases, about 2 percent of the genome), written from synthetic DNA, replaces its natural counterpart in a human cell line, which then grows normally.

efforts.who: Synthetic Human Genome Project (SynHG; Jason Chin, Wellcome-funded)
efforts.note: £10 million over five years from June 2025, with a 5 to 10 year horizon for a synthetic chromosome.

forecast.note: SynHG's own horizon is 5 to 10 years from 2025, so 2030 to 2035. Yeast took 2006 to 2025 for 12 megabases, but assembly has sped up since and enzymatic synthesis now delivers 50 kilobase sequence-perfect clones. I put 2034.

sources.title: Wellcome: new project to pioneer human genome synthesis (2025)
Drug Discovery News: Ansa's 50 kb clonal DNA product (2025)
Wellcome: new project to pioneer human genome synthesis (2025)

precision-fermentation.summary: Brewing real milk and egg proteins in microbes rather than taking them from animals. Products are on sale (Perfect Day whey since 2020, Impossible's soy leghemoglobin since 2019), but volumes are small and costs are several times those of the dairy proteins they replace.

efforts.note: FDA GRAS letter in 2018 and color additive approval in 2019, which opened retail sales.
Its existing plant is sold out; a joint-venture plant in Gujarat is due to start in late 2026 and ramp up in 2027.

sources.title: AgFunderNews: Perfect Day's Gujarat facility on track for 2026 (December 2025)
The Spoon: Remilk launches recombinant milk in Israel (2025)

cultivated-meat-parity.summary: The point at which growing meat beats raising animals on cost, which is what would decide whether it ever matters. Cultivated meat is approved in several countries but sells in gram quantities at restaurant prices.
cultivated-meat-parity.criterion: A product that is at least 51 percent cultivated animal cells sells wholesale at or below the price of the conventional meat it replaces (about $6 to $10 per kilogram for ground beef), at a production volume of at least 10,000 tonnes a year.

efforts.who: UPSIDE Foods, GOOD Meat, Mosa Meat, Aleph Farms, Vow, Wildtype, Mission Barns
efforts.note: Investment fell to $73.9 million in 2025 from a peak near $1 billion in 2021, and about 140 companies remain; Believer Meats shut down in December 2025.

forecast.note: David Humbird's 2021 techno-economic analysis puts cell mass at $22 to $51 per kilogram at large scale and argues about $25 is the floor with known bioprocess technology; CE Delft's more optimistic model gives $5.66 per kilogram cost of goods by 2030 for a 10,000 tonne plant. Industry claims of $10 to $15 per kilogram are disputed. With funding down sharply and seven US states banning sales, I put wholesale parity at scale around 2048, and give real weight to it never happening.

sources.title: Humbird, Scale-up economics for cultured meat, Biotechnology and Bioengineering 118:3239 (2021)
GFI: cultivated meat and seafood state of the industry report

gene-edited-crops.summary: Crops with small, targeted DNA edits and no foreign genes, which several countries now regulate like conventional breeding rather than as GMOs: high-oleic soybean (US, 2019), a GABA tomato (Japan, 2021), and crops under England's Precision Breeding regulations (in force November 2025) and the EU's new genomic techniques regulation (adopted June 2026).

efforts.note: England's Precision Breeding Act regulations took effect November 13, 2025; Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 was published June 26, 2026.

sources.title: European Parliament legislative observatory, new genomic techniques (2023/0226(COD))

improved-photosynthesis.summary: Changing how plants handle light and photorespiration to raise yield. Speeding a leaf's recovery from sun protection lifted tobacco biomass about 15 percent (2016) and soybean seed yield by up to 33 percent in field trials (2022). No such crop is grown commercially.

efforts.who: Johannes Kromdijk, Stephen Long and the RIPE project (Illinois, Gates Foundation funded)

efforts.note: Soybean yield up to 33 percent higher across five transformation events, with unchanged protein and oil.

c4-rice.summary: Rewiring rice to use the more efficient photosynthesis of maize and sugarcane, which would raise yield by about half and cut water and nitrogen needs. It means installing both a new leaf anatomy and a new biochemistry, the most ambitious plant engineering project attempted.
c4-rice.criterion: A rice variety running a working C4 photosynthetic cycle yields at least 30 percent more grain per hectare than its parent in multi-season field trials, and is approved for farmers to grow.

efforts.who: C4 Rice Project (IRRI, Oxford, Cambridge; Julian Hibberd, Jane Langdale; Gates Foundation funded)
efforts.note: Five C4 enzymes expressed in rice with labeled carbon showing malate forming (2019), and the bundle sheath made to resemble a C4 plant's; joining anatomy to biochemistry remains undone.

forecast.note: Eighteen years in, the project has the parts but not a working cycle. Project statements have pointed to rice reaching farmers' fields around 2039. Plant breeding and regulatory approval add roughly a decade after a working prototype, so I put approved field use around 2048.

sources.title: Ermakova et al., On the road to C4 rice, Plant Journal (2019)
University of Cambridge, Department of Plant Sciences: Hibberd, Improving crop yield through enhanced photosynthesis (C4 rice)
Ermakova et al., On the road to C4 rice, Plant Journal (2019)

nitrogen-fixing-cereals.summary: Giving grain crops the nitrogen-fixing trick of legumes, which would cut the biggest input cost in farming and a large share of farming's emissions. Microbial products deliver perhaps a fifth of a maize crop's nitrogen today.
nitrogen-fixing-cereals.criterion: A commercial cereal variety (maize, wheat or rice) that, through its own genes or an engineered symbiosis, supplies at least half its nitrogen from the air, cutting applied fertilizer by 50 percent or more at equal yield in multi-season field trials.

efforts.note: More than 15 million cumulative acres; university studies find up to 35 to 40 pounds of nitrogen per acre, about a fifth of a maize crop's need.

efforts.who: Alan Bennett, Allen Van Deynze (UC Davis), Sierra Mixe maize
efforts.note: A landrace maize whose aerial-root mucilage hosts nitrogen-fixing bacteria supplying 29 to 82 percent of its nitrogen.

efforts.who: Guntur Subbarao and colleagues (JIRCAS and CIMMYT), nitrification-inhibiting wheat
efforts.note: A wild-grass chromosome segment roughly doubled root nitrification inhibition, raising yield and cutting nitrous oxide.
Gene-edited rice exuding more apigenin, which recruits nitrogen-fixing biofilms.

forecast.note: Microbial products are commercial but cover only about a fifth of a crop's nitrogen, and the trend in their performance is slow. Putting nitrogenase, which is poisoned by oxygen, into plant organelles has been attempted for over a decade without a working cereal. Half of a crop's nitrogen from the air, at field scale, looks like the 2040s.

sources.title: Van Deynze et al., PLOS Biology 16:e2006352 (2018)
Pivot Bio: peer-reviewed study of its nitrogen-fixing microbes (2025)
Van Deynze et al., PLOS Biology 16:e2006352 (2018)

routes.name: Engineered microbes
routes.note: Give soil bacteria that already live on roots a working nitrogenase, the approach now sold commercially.

routes.name: Engineered plants
routes.note: Change the plant itself, by recruiting nitrogen-fixing bacteria with root exudates, copying the Sierra Mixe maize mucilage trait, or putting nitrogenase into plant organelles.

trapped-ion-qubits.summary: Qubits stored in single charged atoms held by electric fields and controlled with lasers or microwaves. They have the best gate fidelities of any platform but run slowly, and scaling means shuttling ions between zones on a chip.

efforts.note: Proposed a quantum computer built from cold trapped ions.

efforts.who: Christopher Monroe, David Wineland and colleagues (NIST)
efforts.note: First two-qubit quantum logic gate, on a single beryllium ion.

efforts.who: Quantinuum; IonQ (with Oxford Ionics); AQT; Oxford Ionics

sources.title: Monroe et al. 1995, Demonstration of a Fundamental Quantum Logic Gate, Physical Review Letters

superconducting-qubits.summary: Qubits made from tiny superconducting circuits with Josephson junctions, cooled near absolute zero and made with chip fabrication methods. They are fast and the most developed platform (Google, IBM, USTC), but need wiring and refrigeration for every qubit.

efforts.who: Yasunobu Nakamura, Yuri Pashkin and Jaw-Shen Tsai (NEC)
efforts.note: Coherent control of a single-Cooper-pair box, the first superconducting qubit.

efforts.who: Google Quantum AI; IBM; USTC (Zuchongzhi); Rigetti; AWS

sources.title: Nakamura, Pashkin and Tsai 1999, Coherent control of macroscopic quantum states in a single-Cooper-pair box, Nature

photonic-qubits.summary: Computing with single photons in optical circuits. Photons barely interact, so gates are probabilistic and built from measurement, but chips can be made in ordinary silicon photonics foundries and work at room temperature apart from the detectors.

efforts.who: Emanuel Knill, Raymond Laflamme and Gerard Milburn
efforts.note: Showed that linear optics plus photon detection is enough for efficient quantum computing.

efforts.who: Jeremy O'Brien and colleagues (University of Queensland)
efforts.note: First all-optical controlled-NOT gate.

efforts.who: Pan Jianwei and Lu Chaoyang (USTC), Jiuzhang
efforts.note: Quantum advantage on Gaussian boson sampling with 76 detected photons.

sources.title: Knill, Laflamme and Milburn 2001, A scheme for efficient quantum computation with linear optics, Nature
O'Brien et al. 2003, Demonstration of an all-optical quantum controlled-NOT gate, Nature
Zhong et al. 2020, Quantum computational advantage using photons, Science

neutral-atom-arrays.summary: Uncharged atoms held in grids of laser tweezers and entangled by exciting them to large Rydberg states. Atoms can be moved mid-computation, which suits error-correcting codes, and arrays grew from dozens to thousands of atoms in under a decade.

efforts.who: Thad Walker and Mark Saffman (Wisconsin); Antoine Browaeys (Institut d'Optique)
efforts.note: First neutral-atom controlled-NOT gate using Rydberg blockade (Wisconsin, 2010).

efforts.who: Browaeys group; Mikhail Lukin and Markus Greiner (Harvard)
efforts.note: Defect-free arrays assembled atom by atom with movable tweezers.

sources.title: Isenhower et al. 2010, Demonstration of a Neutral Atom Controlled-NOT Quantum Gate, Physical Review Letters
Barredo et al. 2016, An atom-by-atom assembler of defect-free arbitrary two-dimensional atomic arrays, Science

logical-qubit-processors.summary: Running algorithms on dozens of error-corrected logical qubits at once rather than on bare physical qubits. The codes were small and the circuits short, but it showed the machinery of fault tolerance working together.

efforts.who: Dolev Bluvstein, Mikhail Lukin and colleagues (Harvard, MIT, QuEra)
efforts.note: Up to 48 logical qubits on 280 atoms, with entangling gates between them.
November 2025: 98 barium-ion qubits with 99.92 percent two-qubit fidelity, encoding a claimed 48 error-corrected logical qubits (a 2:1 ratio some observers question).
A 3,000-atom array run continuously for over two hours, and a fault-tolerant architecture with dozens of logical qubits below threshold (Nature, 2025).

sources.title: Quantum Computing Report, Quantinuum launches Helios (2025)
Chiu et al. 2025, Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system (arXiv)
Bluvstein et al. 2023, Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays, Nature

optimized-stellarator.summary: A twisted magnetic bottle whose coils are shaped by computer optimization so the plasma stays confined without a large current flowing through it, which avoids the sudden disruptions of tokamaks. Wendelstein 7-X showed in 2021 that the optimization works.

efforts.note: Invented the stellarator; early ones lost heat too fast and were eclipsed by the tokamak.

efforts.who: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Wendelstein 7-X
efforts.note: First plasma 2015; reduced neoclassical heat loss confirmed in Nature (2021); record long-pulse triple product sustained for 43 seconds in May 2025.

efforts.who: Proxima Fusion; Type One Energy; Thea Energy
efforts.note: Startups designing stellarator power plants with high-temperature superconducting magnets.

sources.title: Beidler et al. 2021, Demonstration of reduced neoclassical energy transport in Wendelstein 7-X, Nature
EUROfusion, Wendelstein 7-X sets world record for long plasma triple product (2025)

hts-fusion-magnets.summary: Large magnets wound from high-temperature superconducting tape that reach about 20 tesla. Fusion power density rises with the fourth power of field strength, so these allow tokamaks and stellarators tens of times smaller than ITER for the same performance.

efforts.who: Commonwealth Fusion Systems and MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center
efforts.note: A 20 tesla large-bore magnet test on September 5, 2021, the design used in SPARC.
Energy Singularity's HH70, the first all-HTS tokamak, made its first plasma in 2024.

sources.title: MIT News, MIT-designed project achieves major advance toward fusion energy (2021)

magneto-inertial-fusion.summary: A middle path between magnetic and laser fusion: a magnetized plasma is squeezed in a fast pulse by a collapsing liner, colliding plasmas or magnetic fields. It needs neither steady confinement nor huge lasers, and it is the route of several of the best-funded startups.

efforts.who: Sandia National Laboratories, MagLIF on the Z machine
efforts.note: Magnetized liner inertial fusion produced thermonuclear neutrons at fusion-relevant temperatures.

Aims to recover electricity directly from the expanding plasma. Its Polaris machine reached 150 million degrees and in January 2026 became the first private device to run deuterium-tritium fusion; it has not yet claimed electricity.
LM26 made first plasma in March 2025; laid off about a quarter of staff in May 2025, then listed on Nasdaq in July 2026 and reported 1.1 keV electron temperature in October 2026.
FuZE-3 reached about 1.6 gigapascals of plasma pressure (November 2025).

sources.title: Helion, Helion achieves new fusion energy milestones
General Fusion, 1 keV electron temperature milestone (2026)
Gomez et al. 2014, Experimental Demonstration of Fusion-Relevant Conditions in Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion, Physical Review Letters

hydride-superconductors.summary: Hydrogen-rich compounds squeezed in diamond anvils to over a million atmospheres superconduct at up to about 250 K, close to room temperature, as theory predicted. They prove high critical temperatures are possible but are useless at ordinary pressure.

efforts.who: Mikhail Eremets and colleagues (Max Planck Institute for Chemistry, Mainz)
efforts.note: Sulfur hydride superconducting at 203 K at about 150 gigapascals.

efforts.who: Eremets group; Russell Hemley group (George Washington University)
efforts.note: Lanthanum hydride at about 250 K and 170 gigapascals.

sources.title: Drozdov et al. 2015, Conventional superconductivity at 203 kelvin at high pressures in the sulfur hydride system, Nature
Drozdov et al. 2019, Superconductivity at 250 K in lanthanum hydride under high pressures, Nature

mars-oxygen-moxie.summary: A toaster-sized unit on the Perseverance rover that split Martian carbon dioxide into oxygen, the first use of another planet's resources to make something useful. A return trip would need about a thousand times its output, mostly as oxidizer for rocket fuel.

efforts.who: MIT Haystack Observatory and NASA JPL (Michael Hecht, principal investigator)
efforts.note: 16 runs from April 2021 to August 2023 made 122 grams of oxygen at up to 12 grams an hour, 98 percent pure.

sources.title: NASA, NASA's oxygen-generating experiment MOXIE completes Mars mission (2023)
Hoffman et al. 2022, Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment (MOXIE), Science Advances

ai-discovered-results.summary: Language models paired with automatic checkers that search for new programs and constructions, finding results that beat the best known human ones on open problems. The answers are narrow but new, and each can be verified by a machine.

efforts.who: Google DeepMind, FunSearch (Bernardino Romera-Paredes, Pushmeet Kohli and colleagues)
efforts.note: Found larger cap sets than any known, the first discovery on an open math problem by an LLM-based search (Nature, December 2023).

May 2025: multiplied 4x4 complex matrices with 48 multiplications, beating Strassen's 1969 method; improved the best known answer on about 20 percent of 50-plus open problems; a scheduling heuristic recovers 0.7 percent of Google's compute.

sources.title: Romera-Paredes et al. 2023, Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models, Nature
Google DeepMind, AlphaEvolve, a Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms (2025)

starship-orbital-refueling.summary: Pumping cryogenic propellant from one spacecraft to another in orbit, so a ship can leave Earth orbit with full tanks. Both US lunar landers and SpaceX's Mars plans depend on it, and it has not yet been done at scale with cryogenic fuel.
starship-orbital-refueling.criterion: One spacecraft transfers cryogenic propellant (liquid oxygen and methane or hydrogen) to another in orbit at the scale of tens of tonnes or more, as NASA's lunar lander contracts require before an uncrewed landing.

efforts.who: SpaceX (Starship Human Landing System for NASA)
efforts.note: Moved propellant between tanks inside one ship on its third flight (March 2024); a tanker-to-depot demonstration was scheduled for early 2027 as of NASA's October 2026 update. A lunar landing needs an estimated 4 to 14 tanker flights.

efforts.who: Blue Origin (Blue Moon Mark 2 with a refueling transporter)
efforts.note: The smaller Mark 1 cargo lander had not flown by October 2026, with launch no earlier than early 2027.
Routine transfer of storable (not cryogenic) propellant to space stations since 1978.

forecast.note: SpaceX's first orbital Starship flight came only in September 2026, and the ship-to-ship test has already slipped from 2025 to 2027. Boil-off, docking of two very large ships and fast tanker turnaround all have to work. I expect the first transfer demonstration in 2027 to 2028 and treat 2028 as the date it is done at the scale a landing needs.

propellant-depot.summary: Tanks parked in orbit that collect propellant from many launches and store it for weeks to months, the space equivalent of a fuel station. They turn launch cost, not rocket size, into the limit on how far missions can go.
propellant-depot.criterion: A depot holds at least 100 tonnes of cryogenic propellant in orbit for a month or more with low boil-off, and then refuels a vehicle that departs for the Moon or beyond.

efforts.who: SpaceX (depot ship filled by tanker Starships)
efforts.note: Part of the lunar lander plan; the first fill-up flights were scheduled for 2027.
Proposed depots around the Centaur upper stage in the 2000s and 2010s; never flown.

forecast.note: A depot needs a working transfer first, then storage for weeks, which no one has shown for cryogenic propellant. SpaceX's lunar lander plan uses exactly this (a depot ship filled by several tankers), and the first crewed US landing (Artemis IV, targeted 2028) depends on it. If transfers work in 2027 to 2028, a depot follows within a year or so. Judgment: 2029, with slips likely.

commercial-lunar-landers.summary: Private companies landing robotic craft on the Moon under fixed-price NASA delivery contracts. The first landed tipped on its side in 2024; Firefly's Blue Ghost made the first fully successful one in 2025.

efforts.note: First private soft landing, February 22, 2024, near Malapert A; broke a leg and tipped over. IM-2 (March 2025) also tipped over, so its PRIME-1 ice drill never ran.
Landed upright in Mare Crisium on March 2, 2025 and operated for two weeks.
Both landers crashed (April 2023 and June 2025).

lunar-water-mining.summary: Extracting water ice from permanently shadowed craters near the lunar poles for drinking, oxygen and rocket fuel. It is the main reason both the US and China aim for the south pole, but no one has yet drilled into lunar ice.
lunar-water-mining.criterion: Equipment on the Moon extracts at least one tonne of water (or the oxygen from it) from lunar soil or ice within a year, for use there.

efforts.who: NASA (PRIME-1 drill on IM-2; VIPER rover)
efforts.note: PRIME-1's drill was extended but never operated after the lander tipped over in March 2025.
Planned to test in-situ resource use in 2028 as a step toward the International Lunar Research Station.
Aims to mine helium-3 rather than water; claims over $500 million in purchase orders.

forecast.note: The ice has been mapped from orbit, but its form and concentration on the ground are unknown, and the only drill sent so far never ran. Tonne scale needs a powered, long-lived plant near a crater, which in turn needs a lunar base program (the US targets 2029 to 2036, China's ILRS construction runs 2026 to 2035). Judgment: late 2030s.

lunar-base.summary: A base near the lunar south pole where crews live in rotation, like Antarctic stations, supplied from Earth at first and later partly from local ice. NASA paused its lunar-orbit Gateway in 2026 to focus on a surface base; China plans one with partner countries.
lunar-base.criterion: People live on the Moon continuously for at least a year, with crews rotating and no gap of more than a few weeks.

efforts.note: In March 2026 NASA paused the Gateway station "as designed" and refocused on a surface base built from 2029 to 2036, with about one landing a year from Artemis V (late 2028).

efforts.who: China and partners, International Lunar Research Station
efforts.note: Construction phase 2026 to 2035, missions ILRS-1 to 5 in 2031 to 2035, use from 2036.
In February 2026 Musk said Mars missions would wait five to seven years while SpaceX focuses on a lunar base.

forecast.note: Agency schedules put early base elements in the early 2030s, but continuous occupancy needs reliable landings every few months, surface power through the two-week lunar night and habitats that do not yet exist. Antarctica took about 45 years from the first expeditions to year-round stations (1911 to 1956). Judgment: around 2040.

closed-loop-life-support.summary: Habitats that recycle nearly all their air and water and grow much of their own food, so crews far from Earth are not tied to supply ships. The ISS recycles 98 percent of its water but no oxygen-food loop has run for years with people.
closed-loop-life-support.criterion: A crew of at least four lives for a year in a sealed habitat (on Earth, in orbit or on another world) with at least 98 percent of water and oxygen recycled and at least half of food grown inside, with no resupply of those.

efforts.note: Total water recovery reached 98 percent with the brine processor (June 2023); oxygen is made by electrolysis of resupplied water.
Eight people sealed in for two years (1991 to 1993); oxygen fell so low that air had to be pumped in.
Rotating crews of four lived in a ground facility for 370 days (2017 to 2018) with oxygen and water fully recycled and much of the food grown inside.

forecast.note: Ground tests have come close for a year, but not in space or under partial gravity, and no space agency has funded a flight-scale bioregenerative system. A Mars settlement or a permanent lunar base would force the issue. Judgment: mid-2040s for a flight-proven system.

sources.title: NASA, NASA achieves water recovery milestone on International Space Station (2023)
NASA, NASA achieves water recovery milestone on International Space Station (2023)

mars-propellant-production.summary: Making methane and oxygen on Mars from atmospheric carbon dioxide and buried ice, so ships can fly home without hauling return fuel from Earth. MOXIE made 122 grams of oxygen; a return Starship needs hundreds of tonnes of propellant.
mars-propellant-production.criterion: A plant on Mars produces at least 10 tonnes of rocket propellant (oxidizer and fuel) and loads it into a vehicle.

efforts.note: Its Mars architecture assumes Sabatier-process methane plants powered by large solar arrays; Mars missions were pushed back by five to seven years in February 2026.

efforts.who: NASA (MOXIE follow-ons in the Moon to Mars architecture)

forecast.note: The step from 12 grams an hour to tonnes needs uncrewed cargo landings with power plants, ice mining and automation, all before crews arrive, since SpaceX's plan relies on it for the trip home. Mars launch windows come every 26 months. Judgment: about 2040, on uncrewed precursor flights.

nuclear-space-propulsion.summary: Rockets heated by a fission reactor (nuclear thermal), or electric thrusters powered by one (nuclear electric), which could halve Mars trip times compared with chemical rockets. NERVA engines ran on the ground in the 1960s; none has flown.
nuclear-space-propulsion.criterion: A spacecraft in space is propelled by a fission reactor, either by heating propellant directly or by powering electric thrusters.

efforts.who: NASA and the Atomic Energy Commission, Rover and NERVA
efforts.note: Ground tests from 1959 to 1969 reached about 850 seconds of specific impulse, twice chemical engines; cancelled January 1973.
A nuclear thermal flight demonstration cancelled in 2025; DARPA cited falling launch costs.
Announced March 2026, a nuclear electric pathfinder reusing the Gateway power module, proposed for launch in December 2028 with two Mars flybys.

forecast.note: Nuclear propulsion has lost funding every time chemical alternatives looked good enough, most recently in 2025. SR-1 Freedom's 2028 date is a proposal; new nuclear flight hardware usually slips several years. Judgment: early 2030s.

artemis-accords.summary: Bilateral agreements, led by the US, on how countries behave on the Moon and beyond, including that extracting space resources is allowed without claiming territory. They build on a 2015 US law letting citizens own resources they mine in space.

efforts.who: US Congress, Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act
efforts.note: Signed November 25, 2015; lets US citizens own space resources they obtain, without claiming sovereignty.

efforts.who: NASA and the US State Department with seven founding partners
efforts.note: Signed October 13, 2020 by eight nations; 77 signatories by October 2026. China and Russia have not signed.

sources.title: Wikipedia, U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act

electric-regional-aircraft.summary: Fixed-wing airliners with 9 to 30 seats flying short routes on battery power, or batteries plus a small fuel reserve. Batteries hold about 50 times less energy per kilogram than jet fuel, so range, not motors, is the limit.
electric-regional-aircraft.criterion: A battery-electric or battery-hybrid airliner with at least 19 seats holds a type certificate and flies scheduled paying passengers.

efforts.note: First flight September 2022; on indefinite pause since 2025.
Its X1 demonstrator first flew on August 12, 2026; aims for type certification of the 30-seat hybrid by the end of the 2020s.
Conventional-takeoff electric aircraft in FAA certification; went public in November 2025.

forecast.note: New airliner certifications usually slip by years, Heart's ES-30 has moved from all-electric to hybrid, and Eviation paused. Batteries near 400 Wh/kg would help. Judgment: first 19-plus seat service in the early to mid 2030s.

superhuman-coder.summary: AI that does all the coding work of a frontier AI lab better and much faster than its best engineers, so that human researchers only choose what to build. It is the first step in most forecasts of AI speeding up its own development.
superhuman-coder.criterion: The AI 2027 "superhuman coder" bar: a frontier AI company could run the system on 5 percent of its compute as about 30 times as many agents as it has human researchers, each doing the company's coding tasks about 30 times faster than its best human engineer, at equal or better quality. A lab saying it has stopped hiring software engineers for research because AI does that work would be strong evidence.

efforts.who: Anthropic (Claude Code, Claude Opus and Mythos models)
efforts.note: Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026) was the first model METR measured above an 8-hour, 50 percent time horizon; an early Mythos Preview reached about 17 hours (April 2026).
METR found GPT-5.6 Sol (June 2026) cheated on tasks more often than any public model it had tested and judged it would not enable fully automated AI research.

efforts.who: Google DeepMind; xAI; DeepSeek; Cursor; Cognition

forecast.note: METR's 50 percent time horizon on software tasks crossed 1 hour in February 2025 and 8 hours in February 2026 (Claude Opus 4.6, about 12 hours, 95 percent interval 5 to 61 hours), doubling about every 4.3 months since 2023. The 80 percent horizon is four to six times shorter (about 3 hours for the best model), and METR says its tasks cannot measure beyond about 16 hours, so the trend is now hard to check. Carried forward, a 50 percent horizon of a work-month arrives around 2027 to 2029. The AI 2027 scenario put the superhuman coder in early 2027; in August 2026 its authors' medians for the similar "automated coder" were November 2027 (Kokotajlo) and January 2030 (Lifland), and the AI Futures model's December 2025 median was late 2031, and its August 2026 default run reaches it around October 2027. I put it at 2028, allowing for the reliability gap between finishing half of long tasks and doing a lab's work.

sources.title: METR, benchmark results (time horizons by model)
AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 timelines update (August 2026)
AI Futures Project, AI Futures Model December 2025 update
AI 2027, takeoff forecast (definitions of superhuman coder and researcher)

ai-autonomous-science.summary: AI agents that form hypotheses, run experiments through automated labs or simulations, and reach discoveries in physics, chemistry or biology on their own. By 2026 AI had proved significant math results, but its lab discoveries still relied on humans to run the experiments.
ai-autonomous-science.criterion: An AI system, with humans only supplying resources and checking the work, makes a discovery in a natural science that is published in a leading journal with the AI as the main contributor, and that experts rank among the important results of its field that year.

efforts.note: A multi-agent system proposed ripasudil as a treatment for dry macular degeneration (May 2025), with humans running the lab work; published in Nature in May 2026.
Proposed drug-repurposing candidates for leukemia and independently arrived at an unpublished, already validated mechanism of gene transfer in bacteria (February 2025).
A fully AI-written paper passed peer review at an ICLR 2025 workshop and was withdrawn as planned.
Runs of about 12 hours were judged equal to months of human research; about 79 percent of report statements were accurate.

forecast.note: Math, where answers can be checked by machine, fell first: in May 2026 an unreleased OpenAI model disproved Erdős's 1946 unit distance conjecture, a result Tim Gowers said he would have recommended for the Annals of Mathematics. Natural science also needs physical experiments, which are slower and need lab automation. If automated coders arrive near 2029, AI-led discovery in simulation-heavy fields should follow within a year or two. Judgment: around 2030.

sources.title: Quanta Magazine, Why the legendary Erdős problems are falling to AI (August 2026)
FutureHouse, Robin, end-to-end scientific discovery with a multi-agent system
Google Research, Accelerating scientific breakthroughs with an AI co-scientist (2025)
Sakana AI, The AI Scientist generates its first peer-reviewed scientific publication (2025)
Kosmos, an AI scientist for autonomous discovery (arXiv 2025)

continual-learning-ai.summary: AI that keeps learning from its own experience after it is deployed, building up skill and context the way a new employee does, rather than staying frozen between training runs. Many researchers see this, or learned world models, as the missing piece that scaling alone may not supply.
continual-learning-ai.criterion: A deployed AI system improves at a new job from its own experience and feedback over days to weeks, about as fast and as lastingly as a capable human hire, without its developer running a new training run, across white-collar work in general.

efforts.note: Memory and long context let 2026 agents carry notes between sessions, but their weights stay fixed between releases.

efforts.who: Yann LeCun, AMI Labs (Advanced Machine Intelligence)
efforts.note: Founded December 2025 after LeCun left Meta, to build world models that learn how the physical world works; raised $1.03 billion in March 2026.

forecast.note: Dwarkesh Patel argued in June 2025 that the lack of continual learning is the main reason models do not yet replace human workers, and gave 2032 as his 50 percent date for AI that learns on the job as easily as a human. Lab research on test-time training and memory is active but no lab has shipped it. Judgment: early 2030s, with wide uncertainty.

sources.title: Dwarkesh Patel, Why I don't think AGI is right around the corner (June 2025)
Dwarkesh Patel, Why I don't think AGI is right around the corner (June 2025)

general-purpose-robots.summary: Humanoids and mobile robot arms run by foundation models that can be put to many jobs, in factories, warehouses and homes, instead of one programmed task. Thousands were built by 2026, mostly for pilots and research.
general-purpose-robots.criterion: At least 100,000 general-purpose robots (humanoids or mobile manipulators driven by learned models, not fixed single-task arms) are doing paid work worldwide, or a home robot that does chores such as laundry and dishes in unfamiliar homes sells tens of thousands of units.

efforts.note: Shipped over 5,500 humanoids in 2025, mostly for research, education and display; filed for a Shanghai listing in March 2026.
Over 350 Figure 03 robots delivered by April 2026, building about one an hour, and about 740 operating by the end of June 2026.
Fremont production lines were being installed in 2026; no output reported.
Home humanoid offered for preorder in October 2025 at $20,000 or $499 a month.

efforts.who: Physical Intelligence; Google DeepMind (Gemini Robotics); Nvidia (GR00T)
efforts.note: Robot foundation models; Physical Intelligence released pi0.7 in April 2026 and an API in October 2026.

forecast.note: From a few thousand working units in 2026, reaching 100,000 needs about five doublings; at a doubling a year (fast for hardware) that is about 2031. Reliability in unstructured places, cost (a car-like price per robot) and safety around people are the main hurdles. Judgment: early 2030s for the work count, later for homes.

robotaxis-at-scale.summary: Driverless taxi fleets large enough to be an ordinary way to get around in many cities. Waymo reached about 500,000 paid rides a week in 2026, Tesla removed safety monitors in several Texas and Florida cities, and Baidu, Pony.ai and WeRide run driverless fleets in China and the Gulf.
robotaxis-at-scale.criterion: Robotaxis with no safety driver or monitor on board give at least one million paid rides a week in one country, spread over at least ten metropolitan areas.

efforts.note: About 500,000 paid rides a week and 3,871 vehicles in June 2026; full service in Phoenix, the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Austin, Atlanta, Miami, Nashville, Dallas, Houston, and from October 2026 San Antonio, San Diego and Tampa.
Camera-only; no safety monitor in Austin from January 2026, then Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa; about 420 vehicles in Texas.
Driverless commercial service in Beijing, Wuhan, Shenzhen, Guangzhou and other Chinese cities, and in Abu Dhabi and Dubai.
Purpose-built vehicles; paid rides in Las Vegas from August 2026.

forecast.note: Waymo reached about 500,000 paid rides a week by mid-2026 and opened eight new metros in 2026 alone; one more doubling, likely within about a year at that pace, would pass a million a week in the US alone, so 2027 is likely. China may get there first if Apollo Go's growth continues, but its ride counts were not published for 2026.

personal-self-driving-cars.summary: Cars that people own and that drive themselves anywhere in a large region with no one watching the road, so the owner can sleep or work. In 2026 consumer systems, including Tesla's Full Self-Driving, still required a supervising driver.
personal-self-driving-cars.criterion: At least 100,000 privately owned cars are legally allowed to drive themselves door to door, including on highways and city streets across at least a whole metropolitan area, with no human required to watch the road (SAE level 4 in private ownership).

efforts.note: Still sold as "Supervised" for consumers in 2026, while unsupervised in Tesla's own robotaxi fleets in some cities.

efforts.who: Waymo and car makers (lidar, radar and detailed maps)
efforts.note: The sensor-heavy approach that works in robotaxis is costlier per car, which is why it has stayed in fleets.

forecast.note: Robotaxis work in mapped, geofenced cities with remote support; personal cars must handle any road and weather, and makers would carry the liability. Expect the first unsupervised personal-car offers late in the 2020s and 100,000 such cars in the early to mid 2030s. Judgment.

ai-safety-institutes.summary: Government bodies that test the most capable AI models before and after release, and the first laws aimed at general-purpose models, notably the EU AI Act. They give states a way to see dangerous capabilities coming, though their powers are mostly voluntary.

efforts.who: UK AI Safety Institute (AI Security Institute from February 2025)
efforts.note: Founded November 2023 around the Bletchley Park summit.

efforts.who: US AI Safety Institute (Center for AI Standards and Innovation from June 2025)

efforts.note: In force August 1, 2024; obligations for general-purpose AI models from August 2, 2025.

topological-qubits.summary: Qubits that store information in exotic states (Majorana zero modes) spread across a superconducting nanowire, so local noise cannot easily disturb them. If they work they would need far less error correction; whether anyone has made one is disputed.
topological-qubits.criterion: A qubit whose protection comes from topological states, confirmed by independent groups (for example through braiding or parity measurements), with error rates below those of the best conventional qubits.

efforts.note: Announced Majorana 1 with eight "topological qubits" in February 2025, but the accompanying Nature paper said its measurements did not by themselves show the states were topological. Microsoft is in the final stage of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative.

forecast.note: Two decades of Majorana claims have not yet produced an agreed working qubit. Microsoft says it can reach useful scale quickly once one works; DARPA's program will judge by 2033. Low confidence; it may be overtaken by other platforms before it matures.

sources.title: Microsoft Quantum team 2025, Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs-Al hybrid devices, Nature
Microsoft, Majorana 1 chip carves new path for quantum computing (2025)

useful-quantum-advantage.summary: A quantum computer doing a calculation someone actually needs, in physics, chemistry or materials, better than any classical computer can. Earlier "supremacy" tasks were contrived; in 2025 and 2026 Google and IBM claimed the first verifiable or useful advantages, and classical researchers are testing each claim.
useful-quantum-advantage.criterion: A quantum computer solves a problem of scientific or commercial value (not a benchmark designed for quantum hardware) faster, more cheaply or more accurately than the best known classical method, and the claim survives at least a year of attempts to match it classically.

efforts.who: Google Quantum AI (Quantum Echoes on Willow)
efforts.note: Claimed the first verifiable quantum advantage in October 2025, measuring an out-of-time-order correlator about 13,000 times faster than supercomputers (Nature).

efforts.who: IBM with the University of Chicago, Qedma and Algorithmiq
efforts.note: Published three advantage claims in July 2026 on its Quantum Advantage Tracker. Within two weeks a classical team reproduced the University of Chicago result in 37 minutes on GPUs; the other two had not been matched.

forecast.note: IBM predicted the first advantages would be found by the end of 2026 and set up a public tracker for claims and rebuttals. Classical simulation has overturned most earlier claims within months, so I expect a claim to survive a year of scrutiny around 2027, with the first commercially valuable one (chemistry or materials) later.

sources.title: IBM Quantum blog, The dawn of quantum advantage (2025)
Manabe, Gu and Pan 2026, classical reproduction of the IBM and UChicago result (arXiv)
Google Quantum AI 2025, Observation of constructive interference at the edge of quantum ergodicity, Nature
Google, Our quantum hardware demonstrates verifiable quantum advantage (2025)
IBM and University of Chicago demonstrate quantum advantage (July 2026)

backside-power-delivery.summary: Moving a chip's power wiring underneath the transistors, so the wires on top carry only signals. It frees space and cuts power losses, and is the biggest change in chip wiring in decades.

efforts.note: Intel says it reached high-volume manufacturing on 18A by the end of 2025 in Arizona and Oregon, claiming up to 18 percent more performance or 38 percent less power than Intel 3.
Nanosheet transistors with a backside power rail, scheduled for the second half of 2026.

cfet-transistors.summary: Stacking the n-type and p-type transistor of each logic pair on top of each other instead of side by side, roughly halving the area of a logic cell. It is the planned successor to gate-all-around nanosheets once sideways shrinking runs out.
cfet-transistors.criterion: Chips built with stacked complementary FETs are in high-volume manufacturing for commercial products.

efforts.note: Showed CFET test devices at IEDM in December 2023 (Intel an inverter at 60 nm pitch, TSMC at 48 nm).
Its scaling roadmap puts CFET after forksheet transistors.

forecast.note: Engineers quoted in 2023 expected production 7 to 10 years out, about 2030 to 2033. New transistor architectures have usually arrived later than first expected (gate-all-around came in 2022 to 2025), so I put it in the mid-2030s.

sources.title: IEEE Spectrum, Intel, Samsung and TSMC demo stacked CFET transistors (2023)
imec, Smaller, better, faster, imec presents chip scaling roadmap (2023)
IEEE Spectrum, Intel, Samsung and TSMC demo stacked CFET transistors (2023)

magnetic-fusion-gain.summary: A magnetically confined plasma that makes more fusion power than the heating power put into it (Q above 1), which laser fusion passed in 2022. JET reached Q of 0.67 in 1997; compact high-field tokamaks under construction aim to pass 1 around 2027.
magnetic-fusion-gain.criterion: A magnetic confinement device (tokamak, stellarator or other) produces more fusion power than the external heating power absorbed by the plasma (Q above 1), with deuterium-tritium fuel.

efforts.note: Q of 0.67 with 16 MW of fusion power in 1997; a record 69 MJ in October 2023 before closing.
First of 18 magnets installed January 2026 and about 80 percent complete by July 2026; first plasma and Q above 1 targeted for 2027, design Q about 11.
Compact superconducting tokamak due for completion in 2027, aiming at Q of about 5.
Deuterium-tritium operation now planned for 2039, aiming at Q of 10.

forecast.note: SPARC and BEST both target 2027. New fusion machines take a year or more from first plasma to full field and tritium operation, and SPARC has already slipped from 2025. Judgment: first Q above 1 in 2028.

sources.title: Nuclear News Network, CFS SPARC tracker
Nuclear News Network, China BEST tracker
Creely et al. 2020, Overview of the SPARC tokamak, Journal of Plasma Physics
TechCrunch, Commonwealth Fusion Systems installs reactor magnet (January 2026)

fusion-drivers.summary: Lasers or pulsed-power machines efficient enough, and fast enough to fire many times a second, to turn laser-style fusion into a power plant. NIF's flashlamp lasers fire a few times a day and waste most of the power they draw.
fusion-drivers.criterion: A driver delivers fusion-class energy (megajoule scale) to targets at least once a second for hours, with wall-plug efficiency of about 10 percent or better.

efforts.who: DOE inertial fusion energy hubs (LLNL-led STARFIRE, with Focused Energy and Xcimer)
efforts.note: $42 million for three research hubs announced December 2023.
Krypton fluoride laser; its Phoenix prototype started operating in June 2026, with a larger Anvil system planned for 2028 and a plant in the mid-2030s.

efforts.who: Focused Energy (with RWE at Biblis); Marvel Fusion
efforts.note: Focused Energy raised a $240 million Series A in May 2026 and plans a plant in the mid-2030s.
Uses pulsed power instead of lasers; raised over $900 million and broke ground in New Mexico in August 2026, aiming at net facility gain by 2030.

forecast.note: Company plans converge on demonstration drivers around 2028 to 2030 and plants in the mid-2030s. Each needs a new laser or pulser architecture plus cheap mass-produced targets. Judgment: 2035.

sources.title: POWER, Xcimer starts operations of prototype for laser fusion architecture (2026)
New Mexico governor, Pacific Fusion campus announcement (2025)
US DOE, $42 million for inertial fusion energy hubs (2023)

tritium-breeding-blanket.summary: Lithium-bearing walls around a fusion plasma that capture its neutrons and turn the lithium into tritium. The world has only a few tens of kilograms of tritium, so deuterium-tritium plants must make their own fuel; no large breeding system has yet been tried.
tritium-breeding-blanket.criterion: A blanket in a fusion neutron environment breeds more tritium than the plant burns (tritium breeding ratio above 1), measured over a full operating campaign, and the tritium is extracted for reuse.
