efforts.who: ITER test blanket modules (EU, Japan, China, Korea)
efforts.note: Four mock-up blanket designs to be tested in two ports during deuterium-tritium operation.
About £220 million (2023 to 2030) for a breeding test facility using a 14 MeV neutron source in the old JET power building; Commonwealth Fusion Systems joined in July 2026.

forecast.note: Breeding can only be shown at full scale in a deuterium-tritium plant or a strong neutron source; ITER's tests start in 2039 and the first pilot plants (ARC, STEP) aim for the 2030s. Judgment: about 2040.

fusion-net-electricity.summary: A fusion machine that sends out more electricity than the whole facility draws, if only for a test run. Scientific gain counts only the heating energy reaching the fuel; here the lasers, magnets, pumps and conversion losses all count against it.
fusion-net-electricity.criterion: A fusion device produces more electrical energy than the entire facility consumes over the same period (engineering gain above 1), measured and published, even for a single run of seconds to minutes.

efforts.note: Promised Microsoft at least 50 MW from its Orion plant by 2028 under a 2023 agreement; it had earlier expected Polaris to make electricity in 2024, which it did not.
A 400 MW plant near Richmond, Virginia, planned for the early 2030s; Google has agreed to buy half its output and Eni over $1 billion of power.
Aims at facility gain by 2030, a step short of net electricity.

forecast.note: Private fusion has raised about $14 billion (FIA, July 2026) and most firms say the early 2030s; Helion says 2028. Those dates have slipped before, and engineering gain needs a Q well above 5 to 10 for magnetic routes or much higher target gains for inertial ones. Judgment: the first net-electric run around 2034, by whichever route gets there.

routes.note: Commonwealth Fusion Systems (SPARC then ARC), China (BEST then CFEDR), Tokamak Energy, UKAEA STEP.

routes.note: Proxima Fusion (Alpha, early 2030s), Type One Energy (Infinity Two at TVA), Thea Energy.

routes.note: Helion (direct electricity recovery, Orion plant for Microsoft), General Fusion, Zap Energy.

smr-series-production.summary: The point of small modular reactors: building the same design over and over so costs fall, the way they did for ships and aircraft. First units are expensive; Ontario's first four BWRX-300s are budgeted at C$20.9 billion.
smr-series-production.criterion: At least ten reactors of one small modular design (under 300 MWe each) are in commercial operation, and the later units were each built in under four years at a lower cost per kilowatt than the first.

efforts.who: Ontario Power Generation and GE Vernova Hitachi (BWRX-300, Darlington)
efforts.note: Four units for C$20.9 billion, the first C$7.7 billion; basemat set May 2026, first grid power targeted for the end of 2030.
Plan for up to 6 GW announced September 2025; no power purchase agreement signed by August 2026.

efforts.who: Kairos Power with Google; X-energy with Dow; TerraPower Natrium
efforts.note: Google agreed to buy up to 500 MW from Kairos (2024); TerraPower started building its 345 MWe Natrium plant in Wyoming in April 2026.

forecast.note: Western first units reach the grid around 2030, and a design needs several more units before it shows a learning curve; Darlington's four are the nearest fleet. China's Linglong One could be copied faster. Judgment: about 2040 for ten units of one design.

sources.title: World Nuclear News, What is the budget for Canada's first SMR project?

round-the-clock-solar.summary: Solar panels plus batteries sized to supply a constant load day and night nearly all year, which turns cheap daytime solar into firm power. In sunny places this cost about $104 per MWh in 2024, falling about a fifth a year.
round-the-clock-solar.criterion: Unsubsidized solar plus batteries can deliver a constant load for at least 97 percent of hours of the year in a sunny region for under $60 per MWh, below the cost of new coal or nuclear power.

efforts.note: Found that 6 GW of solar and 17 GWh of batteries in Las Vegas could have met a constant 1 GW for 97 percent of hours at $104 per MWh with 2024 prices, down from $132 a year earlier; new coal was about $118 and new nuclear about $182.
Module prices about $0.11 per watt in October 2026; stationary battery packs averaged $70 per kWh in 2025.

forecast.note: The cost fell 22 percent in a year as battery prices fell 45 percent for stationary packs (BNEF 2025); modules, at about 11 cents a watt, fall more slowly now. A continued 10 to 15 percent a year would reach $60 by about 2028 to 2030. Land, grid connection and financing costs fall less, so judgment: 2030.

BloombergNEF, Lithium-ion battery pack prices fall to $108 per kilowatt-hour (2025)
Ember, Solar electricity every hour of every day is here (2025)

compressed-air-storage.summary: Storing energy by pumping air into salt caverns or mines and releasing it through turbines, now with the heat of compression kept and reused. China's plants of 300 to 600 MW and 1.5 to 2.4 GWh, with about 70 percent round-trip efficiency, made it a grid-scale rival to batteries.

efforts.note: 300 MW and 1,500 MWh, about 70 percent efficient, fully grid-connected in January 2025.
600 MW and 2.4 GWh in two units, fully operating by March 2026.

sources.title: ESS News, World's largest compressed air storage facility in full operation (2025)
ESS News, World's largest compressed air storage station fully operational (2026)
Hydrostor, Willow Rock Energy Storage Center

closed-loop-geothermal.summary: Circulating fluid through sealed, radiator-like loops of deep horizontal wells, so heat is taken from rock without fracturing it or needing natural hot water. It avoids induced earthquakes but extracts heat more slowly.
closed-loop-geothermal.criterion: A closed-loop geothermal plant delivers at least 5 MW of electricity to a grid for a year.

efforts.note: Designed for about 8.2 MW of electricity and 64 MW of heat; drilling and technical updates through May 2026.

forecast.note: Geretsried's first loop delivered power to the grid in December 2025, in partial operation, and the second loop began construction in March 2026. Each loop is about a quarter of the plant's 8.2 MW, so 5 MW needs about three loops running, and the criterion then needs a year of output. Judgment: about 2029.

superhot-rock-geothermal.summary: Drilling to rock above about 374 °C, where water becomes supercritical and carries several times more energy per well. It would make geothermal cheap almost anywhere, but needs drills and well materials that survive those temperatures, possibly by vaporizing rock with millimeter waves.
superhot-rock-geothermal.criterion: A plant produces electricity commercially from wells in rock above 374 °C (supercritical water conditions).

efforts.note: Project Obsidian in central Oregon (announced April 2026) plans 50 MW, then 250 MW, then over 1 GW; a confirmation well toward 15,000 feet and 700 °F was under way in October 2026.

forecast.note: Millimeter-wave drilling has not yet been proven at depth, and well casings and pumps must last at supercritical conditions. Judgment: mid-2030s for a first commercial plant.

sources.title: Quaise Energy, Confirming the resource at Project Obsidian (2026)

geothermal-at-scale.summary: Engineered geothermal plants, no longer limited to volcanic hot springs, adding firm, carbon-free power by the gigawatt. Fervo's Utah plant began commercial operation in October 2026 with about 900 MW contracted.
geothermal-at-scale.criterion: At least 1 GW of new-type geothermal capacity (enhanced, closed-loop or superhot) is operating in one country.

efforts.note: First 33 MW block in commercial operation October 1, 2026; about 100 MW by January 2027 and a 400 MW next phase targeted for 2028; about 900 MW contracted, including 396 MW for Google.

forecast.note: Fervo alone plans about 500 MW by 2028. Reaching a gigawatt needs a second large site or another developer, and drilling costs must keep falling. Judgment: 2031.

sources.title: ThinkGeoEnergy, Fervo reports first power at Cape Station (2026)
ThinkGeoEnergy, Fervo reports first power at Cape Station (2026)

routes.note: Fervo, Utah FORGE, Sage Geosystems.

routes.note: Eavor.

beccs.summary: Burning or fermenting plants for energy and burying the CO2, so carbon the plants pulled from the air stays underground. It can run at large scale with today's equipment, but competes for land and biomass.
beccs.criterion: A BECCS plant removes and permanently stores at least 500,000 tonnes of biogenic CO2 a year, verified by a third party.

efforts.who: Stockholm Exergi (Värtaverket combined heat and power plant)
efforts.note: Under construction (foundation finished September 2026), planned to remove 7.83 million tonnes over its first ten years, with €180 million from the EU Innovation Fund and over SEK 20 billion of Swedish support.

efforts.who: Microsoft and other carbon removal buyers
efforts.note: BECCS makes up most of the tonnes contracted in large removal deals.

forecast.note: Stockholm Exergi's plant is the first large one with financing in place; at about 800,000 tonnes a year it would meet the bar once running, expected near the end of the decade. Judgment: 2029.

enhanced-weathering.summary: Spreading crushed basalt or similar rock on farmland so that rain turns CO2 into dissolved bicarbonate, speeding a reaction that controls the climate over geological time. It is cheap to spread but hard to measure.
enhanced-weathering.criterion: Enhanced weathering projects deliver at least one million tonnes a year of third-party verified CO2 removal.

efforts.note: 5,160 registry-certified tonnes issued by December 2025, then the largest such issuance.
Has spread about 358,000 tonnes of rock, which it expects to remove about 79,000 tonnes of CO2 over time.

forecast.note: Verified tonnes are in the thousands a year, and measurement methods are still being settled. Durable removal overall is growing about 40 percent a year (CDR.fyi, 2026); at faster rates typical of a young market, a million verified tonnes a year comes around the early 2030s. Judgment.

rebco-coated-conductor.summary: Thin films of rare-earth barium copper oxide grown on metal ribbon, the form of high-temperature superconductor that carries very high currents in strong magnetic fields. Fusion demand turned it from a specialty product into one made by the thousand kilometers.

efforts.who: SuperOx; Faraday Factory Japan; Fujikura; Shanghai Superconductor; SuperPower
efforts.note: SuperOx made over 300 km of 4 mm tape in nine months, mostly for Commonwealth Fusion Systems, which it called the largest order the industry had seen. SPARC needs about 10,000 km.

sources.title: Molodyk et al. 2021, Development and large volume production of extremely high current density YBa2Cu3O7 superconducting wires for fusion, Scientific Reports
MIT News, Tests show high-temperature superconducting magnets are ready for fusion (2024)

cheap-superconducting-tape.summary: High-temperature superconducting tape cheap enough per unit of current carried to be used widely, in grid cables, wind generators, motors and MRI machines as well as fusion magnets. Makers aim at tens of dollars per kiloampere-meter.
cheap-superconducting-tape.criterion: REBCO tape sells in volume for under $20 per kiloampere-meter of current capacity (at the operating conditions of a fusion or motor magnet, about 20 K).

efforts.who: SuperOx; Faraday Factory Japan; Shanghai Superconductor; Fujikura
efforts.note: Scaling production lines for fusion customers; SuperOx's stated goal is "tens of dollars per kiloampere-meter".

forecast.note: Public prices are scarce. Fusion orders of thousands of kilometers are what drives the scale-up, so the date tracks fusion financing. Judgment with low confidence: early 2030s.

genome-100-dollars.summary: A 30x human genome for under $100 all in, the price at which sequencing everyone at birth becomes routine. Vendors already claim reagent costs near or below $100 (Ultima's Solaris, 2025, about $80); NHGRI's fuller production cost, which counts labor, instruments and overhead, was $525 when it last reported, in 2022.

sources.title: Ultima upgrades sequencer to enable $80 genome (GenomeWeb, 2025)

solar-module-1-dollar-watt.summary: Solar panels for under a dollar per watt of capacity (in 2025 dollars), long held up as the point where solar could compete with grid power without subsidy. Chinese wafer and module factories scaling up after 2008 pushed prices through it.

solar-module-20-cents-watt.summary: Solar modules for under 20 cents a watt, after a glut of Chinese production capacity cut prices by almost two thirds from 2022 to 2024.

solar-module-10-cents-watt.summary: Solar modules for under 10 cents a watt on the European benchmark that the series follows.

solar-1-terawatt.summary: One terawatt of solar capacity installed worldwide, up from about 1.2 gigawatts in 2000. It took three more years to pass 2 TW.

solar-power-5-cents-kwh.summary: New utility-scale solar farms, averaged worldwide, producing electricity for under 5 cents a kilowatt-hour over their life (2025 dollars). It was 41 cents in 2010.

wind-power-5-cents-kwh.summary: New onshore wind farms, averaged worldwide, producing electricity for under 5 cents a kilowatt-hour over their life (2025 dollars), helped by taller towers and longer blades that raised output per turbine.

battery-pack-100-dollars-kwh.summary: The average lithium-ion pack, across cars, buses, two-wheelers and grid storage, for under $100 a kilowatt-hour, the price long cited for electric cars to match combustion cars on sticker price. Segments are already there: in 2025 stationary storage packs averaged $70 and all packs sold in China $84, while the global average was $108.

sources.title: BloombergNEF, Lithium-ion battery pack prices fall to $108 per kilowatt-hour (December 2025)

battery-pack-50-dollars-kwh.summary: The average lithium-ion pack for under $50 a kilowatt-hour, cheap enough for batteries to shift solar power into the night almost everywhere.

ai-training-1e25-flop.summary: A model trained with ten trillion trillion operations. The EU's AI Act (2024) presumes any general-purpose model trained with more than this poses systemic risk. GPT-4 (2023) used about 2e25.

sources.title: EU AI Act, Article 51 (classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk)

ai-training-1e26-flop.summary: A model trained with 10^26 operations, the reporting threshold in the US executive order on AI of October 2023. Grok 3 and GPT-4.5 (2025) are estimated to have passed it.

ai-training-1e27-flop.summary: A model trained with 10^27 operations, about 50 times GPT-4.

forecast.note: The 2010-2026 trend crosses 1e27 in late 2025, but frontier compute has grown more slowly since GPT-4 (about 3 times a year rather than 4 to 5). The largest estimate in Epoch's data, GPT-6 Astra (September 2026), is 9.4e26 with an interval of about 5e26 to 2e27, so the threshold may already have been passed; at 3 times a year the next frontier models clear it in 2027.

sources.title: Epoch AI, Notable AI Models dataset

ai-gpt4-level-1-dollar.summary: A model as good as the original GPT-4 on MMLU for under a dollar per million tokens (about 750,000 words). Gemini 2.0 Flash (February 2025) did it for $0.175, half a percent of GPT-4's launch price two years earlier.

ai-horizon-1-hour.summary: A frontier AI agent succeeding half the time at software tasks that take a skilled person an hour, on METR's benchmark. Claude 3.7 Sonnet was the first measured there, in February 2025.

ai-horizon-1-workday.summary: A frontier AI agent succeeding half the time at software tasks that take a skilled person a full working day (8 hours), on METR's benchmark. Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026) was measured at about 12 hours, though with a confidence interval from about 5 to 60 hours.

ai-horizon-1-week.summary: A frontier AI agent succeeding half the time at software tasks that take a skilled person a 40-hour working week. Measuring this needs longer tasks than METR's current suite, which it calls unreliable above 16 hours.

ai-horizon-1-month.summary: A frontier AI agent succeeding half the time at software projects that take a skilled person a month (167 working hours), the scale of a typical feature or a small research project.

ai-horizon-1-year.summary: A frontier AI agent succeeding half the time at projects that take a skilled person a working year (2,000 hours).

launch-1000-dollars-kg.summary: A rocket on sale that puts payload in low Earth orbit for under $1,000 a kilogram (2021 dollars), a third below Falcon Heavy's list price.

forecast.note: The record line in the CSIS data halves only every 22 years because it stalled from 1967 to 2010, so its trend (about 2032) says little. Falcon Heavy (2018) sits at $1,500 and SpaceX's internal cost with booster reuse is likely already lower, but no listed price is. The step below $1,000 most likely comes with Starship: it first reached orbit and deployed Starlink satellites on its 14th flight on 28 September 2026, but no customer price has been published. I put the likely date at 2029 for the first published price under $1,000, allowing for a few years of flights before outside payloads.

sources.title: CSIS, Space launch to low Earth orbit: how much does it cost?

launch-100-dollars-kg.summary: Launch to low Earth orbit for under $100 a kilogram, cheap enough for space-based solar power, large orbital stations and mass cargo to the Moon and Mars to start to make economic sense.

forecast.note: The CSIS record line's 22-year halving would put this near 2105, but that line is from expendable rockets. A fully reusable Starship refuelled and reflown many times is the only design aimed at this price; it reached orbit for the first time in September 2026 and its upper stage has not yet been recovered and reflown. I assume a tenfold fall takes about a decade after the first sub-$1,000 price once both stages are reused routinely, which gives about 2040, with a long tail if full reuse proves hard.

dna-synthesis-1-cent-base.summary: Synthetic genes at a list price of 1 cent per base pair, so a typical 1,500-base gene costs $15 and a whole bacterial genome tens of thousands of dollars.

forecast.note: The fitted trend (halving about every 2.6 years) would say this already happened, but it rests on Carlson's 2016 and 2017 values of 2 to 3 cents, which no list price matches: Twist sells gene fragments from 7 cents a base in 2026 and GenScript cloned genes from 15 cents, so list prices have been nearly flat for a decade. Array-made oligos already cost far under a cent a base, and enzymatic synthesis companies aim to turn that into genes; I assume list prices resume falling at their pre-2014 rate (about halving every 3 years) once those reach market, which gives about 2034.

sources.title: Rob Carlson, DNA cost and productivity data (2022)

fusion-triple-product-ignition.summary: A magnetically confined plasma with a triple product (density times temperature times confinement time) of about 3e21 keV·s/m³, enough for deuterium-tritium fusion to heat itself without outside power. The best so far, TFTR in 1995, reached about a quarter of that. Laser fusion at NIF reached ignition by its own measure in 2021 and 2022.

forecast.note: The record rose almost a million-fold from 1957 to 1995 and then stalled, as no later machine has surpassed TFTR, so the trend (which would put ignition around 2000) is no guide. The next two machines are designed to pass it: SPARC (Commonwealth Fusion Systems, projected 6.2e21 at full performance), which aims for net energy (Q above 1) in 2027, and ITER (projected 7.4e21), whose 2024 schedule puts deuterium-tritium operation in 2039. Reaching full performance usually takes a new machine several years, so I put SPARC at likely 2032, with ITER as the backstop.

sources.title: Wurzel and Hsu, Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain (2025)

quantum-gate-three-nines.summary: An entangling gate between two qubits that fails less than once in a thousand tries, reached with trapped ions at Oxford and NIST in 2016.

quantum-gate-four-nines.summary: A two-qubit gate that fails less than once in ten thousand tries, claimed by IonQ in October 2025 with electronically controlled trapped ions (a preprint, measured by a newer benchmarking method).

hdd-1-dollar-gb.summary: Hard disk storage for under a dollar a gigabyte (2020 dollars), about 100 million times cheaper than IBM's first disk drive in 1956.

life-expectancy-80.summary: A country (of at least a million people) whose newborns could expect to live 80 years on average at that year's death rates. Japan was first.

life-expectancy-85.summary: A country or territory of at least a million people with a life expectancy at birth of 85 years for both sexes together. Hong Kong was first.

life-expectancy-90.summary: A country of at least a million people with a life expectancy at birth of 90 years for both sexes. The record line has risen about a quarter of a year each year since 1840; whether it can keep doing so without slowing aging itself is the central question of longevity research.

cereal-yield-4-tonnes.summary: The world's farms averaging 4 tonnes of grain per hectare, three times the 1961 average.

cereal-yield-5-tonnes.summary: The world's farms averaging 5 tonnes of grain per hectare.

forecast.note: Cereal yields have grown in a straight line rather than exponentially: about 0.045 tonnes a hectare a year from 1961 to 2024, but only about 0.03 a year from 2014 to 2024 (3.89 to 4.21). Carried forward from 4.21 in 2024, those rates give 5 tonnes between about 2042 and 2050, later than the exponential trend's date; I put the likely date at 2045.

sources.title: Our World in Data, Cereal yield (FAO)

cart-wagon.summary: Wheeled vehicles pulled by oxen, appearing across Europe and the Near East within a few centuries of the wheel. Wooden wagonways for mine carts were the direct ancestors of the railway.

efforts.note: The Bronocice pot (Poland, about 3500 BC) shows a four-wheeled wagon.

chariot.summary: A light two-wheeled war vehicle with spoked wheels, pulled by horses. It spread from the steppe across Eurasia within a few centuries.

gears.summary: Toothed wheels that transmit and convert rotation. They made the watermill, windmill, clockwork and calculating machines possible.

efforts.who: Greek engineers (Ctesibius, Archimedes, Philo of Byzantium)

firearms.summary: Metal tubes that use gunpowder to fire a projectile. Boring cannon barrels accurately led to the precision cylinder boring that made Watt's steam engine work, and armory practice led to interchangeable parts.

efforts.note: The Heilongjiang hand cannon is dated to about 1288; the Xanadu gun to 1298.

pendulum-clock.summary: Christiaan Huygens's clock, regulated by a pendulum, cut clock errors from about fifteen minutes a day to about fifteen seconds. It remained the most accurate timekeeper until the 1930s.

efforts.who: Christiaan Huygens, with clockmaker Salomon Coster

bicycle.summary: John Kemp Starley's Rover: two equal wheels, chain drive to the rear, and soon pneumatic tires. Bicycle makers developed the ball bearings, steel tubing and mass production the car industry inherited, and the Wright brothers were bicycle makers.

modern-synthesis.summary: The reconciliation of Darwinian selection with Mendelian genetics through population genetics, by Fisher, Haldane, Wright, Dobzhansky and others. It is the statistical basis of quantitative genetics, breeding and genome-wide association.

efforts.who: Ronald Fisher, J. B. S. Haldane, Sewall Wright
Theodosius Dobzhansky, Ernst Mayr, Julian Huxley
efforts.note: Huxley's 1942 book gave the synthesis its name.

x-ray-crystallography.summary: Working out where the atoms in a crystal are from how it diffracts X-rays. It revealed the structures of salt, DNA, proteins and most of the drugs in use.

efforts.who: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg

dna-synthesis.summary: Making DNA of a chosen sequence from chemical building blocks. Khorana's group built the first synthetic gene in 1970; Beaucage and Caruthers's phosphoramidite chemistry (1981) made it automatic, and it still supplies the primers for PCR and the parts for synthetic genomes.

television.summary: Pictures sent by radio and drawn on a cathode-ray tube. Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first all-electronic image in 1927; by the 1960s most homes in rich countries had a set.

efforts.note: Mechanical television, with a spinning disc; it lost to electronic systems.

life-expectancy-world-75.summary: The average newborn on Earth expected to live 75 years at that year's death rates, up from 32 in 1900 and 73 in 2023. Most of the remaining gain is in Africa and South Asia, from fewer child, infectious and heart disease deaths.

forecast.note: The straight line since 1970 (about 3.1 years a decade) would cross 75 around 2027, but gains have been slowing as countries converge. The UN's median crosses 75 around 2034, with a 95 percent interval from about 2029 to 2047. IHME's reference forecast (73.6 in 2022 to 78.2 in 2050) crosses around 2031 to 2033 if its gains are steady. I use the UN's dates.

sources.title: UN World Population Prospects 2024, probabilistic projections of life expectancy at birth

life-expectancy-world-80.summary: The world as a whole living as long as Japan did around 1996. Reaching it means poorer countries closing most of the gap with the leaders, and the leaders' old-age death rates continuing to fall.

forecast.note: The UN's median reaches 80 around 2080, its 95 percent interval from about 2062 to after 2100; IHME's upper bound for 2050 is 80.3. The straight-line trend (about 2043) overstates it. In the tree's model, rejuvenation therapies arriving in 2062 and spreading as HIV therapy did bring it to 2071 (2060 if they arrive in 2045). I put it a little before the UN, around 2078.

sources.title: UN World Population Prospects 2024, probabilistic projections of life expectancy at birth

life-expectancy-65-25.summary: A country where 65-year-olds can expect to live to 90 on average, at that year's death rates. The record was 23.2 years (Hong Kong) in 2023, up from 15.7 in 1970, mostly from fewer deaths from heart disease and stroke.

forecast.note: The line since 1970 (1.5 years a decade) crosses 25 around 2035, but since 2000 the pace has been about 1.2 a decade, which gives 2040, and the UN's medium path for Hong Kong reaches 25 in 2041. The tree's geroprotector and senolytic drugs (about 2036 to 2040 here) could bring it a few years earlier if they work.

sources.title: UN World Population Prospects 2024, demographic indicators, medium variant

life-expectancy-65-30.summary: A country where 65-year-olds can expect to reach 95 on average. This is where gains depend most on slowing aging itself rather than curing particular diseases.

forecast.note: Without new aging biology the UN's medium path for Hong Kong reaches 30 only around 2096, and the line since 1970 around 2070. In the tree's model, a 10-year rejuvenation arriving in 2062 (node aging-reversal) adds about 7.5 years at 65 as it spreads and brings it to about 2070, or 2055 with arrival in 2045. I put it around 2080, between the two, since the therapy's date is so uncertain.

sources.title: UN World Population Prospects 2024, demographic indicators, medium variant

life-expectancy-100.summary: A country of at least a million people where the average newborn could expect to reach 100 at that year's death rates, 14.5 years above the 2023 record. Olshansky and colleagues call this radical life extension and argue it is implausible this century unless aging itself is slowed.

forecast.note: The sources disagree by decades. Metaculus forecasters put the median at 2062 (interquartile range 2045 to after 2075). Oeppen and Vaupel's record line, a quarter year per year, gives 2081. The UN's median for the leading country never reaches 100 this century; the top of its 95 percent band does around 2084. The tree's model, with rejuvenation therapies in 2062, gives about 2085, since a single 10-year reset adds only about 7 years at birth. I put it around 2090.

sources.title: Metaculus: when will any country have a life expectancy at birth of at least 100 years?
Olshansky et al., Implausibility of radical life extension in humans in the twenty-first century, Nature Aging 4:1635 (2024)
Oeppen and Vaupel, Broken limits to life expectancy, Science 296:1029 (2002)

lifespan-123.summary: Breaking Jeanne Calment's record of 122 years and 164 days, set in 1997 and unbroken for almost 30 years. Counted when a validated supercentenarian reaches 123, which on this chart shows when they die.

forecast.note: The oldest living person in October 2026, Ethel Caterham, is 117.2, so 2032 is about the earliest possible date. Medford and Vaupel (2019) put the chance that Calment's record survives to 2050 at about one in five; Metaculus forecasters expect the record on 1 January 2050 to be about 126 (interquartile range about 123 to 130); Pearce and Raftery (2021) put the chance of someone dying at 124 or older by 2100 at 99.9 percent. Dong et al. (2016) argued for a limit near 115, which makes the record an outlier unlikely to be repeated. I put the likely date around 2043.

sources.title: Medford and Vaupel, Human lifespan records are not remarkable but their durations are, PLOS ONE 14:e0212345 (2019)
Metaculus: longest verified human lifespan on record on January 1, 2050

lifespan-125.summary: A validated human lifespan of 125 years, the age Dong, Milholland and Vijg (2016) put as the practical upper limit, with a chance in any year of under 1 in 10,000.

forecast.note: Pearce and Raftery's Bayesian forecast puts the chance of someone dying at 126 or older between 2020 and 2100 at 89 percent and at 124 or older at 99.9 percent, so 125 is likely this century, mostly late, once the large post-war birth cohorts reach 110 (from about 2056). Metaculus forecasters are more optimistic, with a median record of about 126 by 2050. A rejuvenation therapy (about 2062 here) given to people over 100 would make it sooner. I put it around 2070.

sources.title: Pearce and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasting of maximum human lifespan by 2100, Demographic Research 44:1271 (2021)
Dong, Milholland and Vijg, Evidence for a limit to human lifespan, Nature 538:257 (2016)

swe-bench-verified-50.summary: An AI agent resolving half of SWE-bench Verified, 500 real bug reports and feature requests from open-source Python projects, graded by the projects' own tests. OpenHands, an agent built on Claude 3.5 Sonnet, reached 53 percent in October 2024. In practice: AI could take a well-described ticket in an unfamiliar codebase and often close it unaided.

swe-bench-verified-95.summary: AI resolving 95 percent of SWE-bench Verified, about all that is left once flawed and ambiguous tasks are allowed for. Anthropic reported 95.5 for Claude Mythos 5 (June 2026) and Vals.ai measured 97.0 for Claude Opus 5 independently. In practice: routine, well-specified fixes in real codebases became something AI does reliably, and the benchmark stopped separating models, so labs moved to harder ones such as SWE-bench Pro.

osworld-human-level.summary: An AI agent completing as many of OSWorld's 369 tasks on a real desktop (spreadsheets, documents, browsers, file management) as the people tested, 72.36 percent. A best-of-10 agent system passed it in December 2025 and single models in 2026. In practice: AI can operate ordinary software through the screen, mouse and keyboard, so it is not limited to tools with an API.

frontiermath-50.summary: AI solving half of FrontierMath's tiers 1 to 3, unpublished problems from advanced undergraduate to early research level. GPT-5 did it in August 2025 on Epoch AI's revised version 2 (on the original version, GPT-5.4 Pro reached 50 in March 2026). In practice: AI became useful for the routine but hard calculations and arguments inside research mathematics.

frontiermath-tier4-50.summary: AI solving half of FrontierMath tier 4, research-level problems written by mathematicians. GPT-5.4 Pro reached 58.5 percent in March 2026 on Epoch AI's revised version 2 (on the original version the best was 47.9 in May 2026, against an AI Digest survey median of 62 for the end of 2026). In practice: AI could solve many problems that would be a project for a professional mathematician.

frontiermath-tier4-solved.summary: AI solving essentially all of FrontierMath's research tier: GPT-6 Astra scored 97.6 percent in September 2026 and GPT-6.1 Sol all 41 problems. Epoch AI had written in 2025 that the benchmark "could be solved as early as 2027". In practice: on hard math problems with checkable answers, AI matches strong research mathematicians; the open question moved to proving new theorems and choosing what to prove.

hle-50.summary: AI answering half of Humanity's Last Exam, 2,500 expert-written questions at the edge of knowledge in dozens of fields, without tools, as run independently by Scale AI. GPT-6 Astra scored 54.8 percent in September 2026 (Anthropic reported 56.8 for Claude Mythos Preview in April). In practice: AI answers many questions only a specialist in that narrow area could.

hle-80.summary: AI answering 80 percent of Humanity's Last Exam without tools, about as high as the benchmark can go given its answer-key errors. In practice: on closed questions an AI would match the specialist in almost any field, the "last exam" of its name.

forecast.note: Scale AI's no-tools runs rose about 25 points a year from 2024 to 2026, which would reach 80 in late 2027, but gains slow near the top and FutureHouse estimated that 29 percent of the chemistry and biology answers conflict with the literature, so the last points may be unreachable. Polymarket gives 6 percent to 80 or more in 2026; Manifold's thin market on the first year above 80 (any published score, tools allowed) gives 36 percent to 2026 and 43 percent to 2027. Labs' own scores with tools were already 68 to 70 in late 2026. Judgment: 2028 for an independent no-tools run, earlier if lab reports count.

sources.title: Polymarket, Highest score on Humanity's Last Exam in 2026?
Manifold, When will Humanity's Last Exam be saturated? (>80%)
FutureHouse, About 30% of Humanity's Last Exam chemistry and biology answers are likely wrong (July 2025)

remote-labor-index-50.summary: AI completing half of the Remote Labor Index, 240 real projects that freelancers were paid to do (design, software, architecture, data analysis; a median of 11.5 hours and $200 each), at a quality a client would accept. The best was 21 percent in September 2026. In practice: for a typical remote freelance job, handing it to an AI would usually work, the clearest sign on any benchmark of AI replacing paid work rather than helping with it.

ai-lab-revenue-100b.summary: OpenAI and Anthropic together selling AI at a rate of $100 billion a year, passed by the third quarter of 2026 (OpenAI $50 billion in September, Anthropic $65 billion in July). Forecasters in the AI Digest survey had put the end of 2026 at $100 billion including xAI. In practice: AI became a large industry in its own right, able to pay for the next rounds of data centers from sales rather than only from investors.

ai-lab-revenue-1t.summary: The two leading AI labs selling AI at a rate of a trillion dollars a year, ten times their 2026 level. In practice it would mean AI doing a large share of paid work, since revenue on this scale would most likely come from replacing labor rather than selling software seats. Epoch AI's 3-times-a-year trend reaches it in late 2028; the Forecasting Research Institute's superforecasters expected $770 billion only by 2040.

sources.title: Forecasting Research Institute, LEAP wave 11 report
Epoch AI, What will AI look like in 2030? (September 2025)

ai-training-1e28-flop.summary: A model trained with ten times GPT-6 Astra's estimated compute and about 500 times GPT-4's. In practice it needs a gigawatt-scale data center campus; Epoch AI put the power limit for 2030 at 1e28 to 3e29 FLOP.

ai-training-1e29-flop.summary: A model trained with 100 times GPT-6 Astra's estimated compute, the scale Epoch AI expected by 2030 (it judged about 2e29 feasible). In practice it needs gigawatts of power and clusters costing over $100 billion, so it tests whether money and electricity, not ideas, set the pace of AI.

sources.title: Epoch AI, Can AI scaling continue through 2030? (August 2024)

electrolysis.summary: Splitting compounds with electric current, first done to water weeks after Volta announced his pile. Humphry Davy used it to isolate sodium and potassium in 1807, and Faraday worked out its laws in 1833.

efforts.note: Isolated potassium and sodium.

chromatography.summary: Separating a mixture by how fast its parts move through a medium. Mikhail Tsvet separated plant pigments this way in 1903; Martin and Synge's partition chromatography (1941) made it a general laboratory tool.

efforts.note: Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1952.

particle-accelerator.summary: Accelerators that keep particles in step as they gain energy, then rings that collide two beams head on. They made the particle discoveries behind the Standard Model possible.

efforts.note: Phase stability, the principle behind the synchrotron.
The first hadron collider.
